title: Known issues and caveats
summary: Known issues include dead placeholder links, AJAX‑populated values, spelling inconsistencies, duplicate entries, and data‑coverage caveats in the Vahan portal.
body:
These are quirks captured on **6 August 2026**. They help you avoid misreading the portal — and they're the things most likely to change, so treat this page as living.

## Dead / placeholder links
- Footer **TERMS OF USE**, **SITEMAP** and **FAQS** all point to `#` — no destination.
- Header parents **Reports, Public Dashboard, Public Report, Login** are `#` toggles; only their child items lead anywhere.

## Values that need JavaScript (can't be read from static HTML)
- **RTO, Maker,** and **part of Class** populate by AJAX after a selection — their full option lists load only in a browser.
- **Y-Axis / X-Axis** options are AJAX-populated. The lists in [section 3]([[03-Report-Filters|03-report-filters]].md) come from third-party scrapers and a methodology note, **not** the live rendered dropdown — treat as **medium confidence** and confirm in a browser.
- The live "All Vahan4 Running States (n/36)" numerator could not be verified.

## Spelling & formatting inconsistencies
- **"Snorked Ladders"** (Class) is almost certainly a typo for "Snorkel Ladders".
- **EV Type** renders with punctuation on the report page (`ELECTRIC(BOV)`) but without it on the dashboard (`ELECTRIC BOV`).
- **Emission** entries mix capitalisation styles (`BHARAT STAGE VI` vs `Bharat Trem Stage III`).
- **"Andaman & Nicobar Island"** is singular on the portal.
- **Maker** names are known to carry spelling inconsistencies in the underlying data.

## Duplicate / overlapping values
- **EV Type** duplicates four values that also appear in **Fuel**.
- **Category Group** overlaps conceptually with **Sub-Category** (both split goods/passenger/weight).
- **"Excavator (Commercial)"** and **"Excavator (NT)"** cover the same machine under different use types.

## Values with unclear meaning
- **"Snorked Ladders"** — not clearly defined on the site; best read as a misspelling of a snorkel/aerial fire ladder.
- The precise distinction between **Vehicle Class**, **Category Group** and **Sub-Category** isn't defined on the page; the meanings in this guide are inferred from the Motor Vehicles Act category scheme.

## Data-coverage caveats
- The portal covers only RTOs running on **Vahan 4.0 and Sarathi 4.0**, with data from **1970**.
- **Telangana** historically sat outside the VAHAN database and began integrating only in **2025**; its series may be missing or partial.
- All-India totals may **not exactly match** the sum of individual state figures, owing to refresh timing and archival reclassification.
- Report generation is **CAPTCHA-gated and session-bound**; long idle sessions may time out.
- Figures are **registrations, not sales** — see the [glossary]([[04-Glossary|04-glossary]].md#key-terms).

## Confidence summary
Everything captured as a value in sections 2–3 was read from the served HTML on the review date and is **high confidence**, except the AJAX-populated lists flagged above. Meanings in the [glossary]([[04-Glossary|04-glossary]].md) are sourced from the portal and from MoRTH / NIC / Motor Vehicles Act material; where no official source defines a term, the guide says so rather than guessing.

---

## Help keep this current
Option lists change whenever MoRTH updates the portal — a new fuel, a new emission norm, a new state joining Vahan 4. If you notice a change:
1. Note the **exact wording** as it appears on the portal and the **date** you saw it.
2. Open an issue or a pull request with the filter name and the old → new value.
3. For AJAX-only values (RTO, Maker, Y/X-Axis), please mention that you confirmed it **live in a browser**.

title: Research methods for product managers
summary: Research methods for product managers covers primary vs secondary research, sequencing, bias, question design, and frameworks for PMs.
body:
# Research Methods for Product Managers

## Core purpose
Research exists to kill assumptions before spending engineering time. Every method is a tool to discover you were wrong.

## Seven research types a PM performs
| Type | Question it answers | Typical output |
|------|--------------------|----------------|
| User research | What are the user's needs, pain points and behaviours? | Personas, pain-point list, journey map |
| Market research | Is this market viable? What are the trends and size? | TAM/SAM/SOM, trend brief, opportunity sizing |
| Competitor research | What are competitors shipping, at what price, with what features? | Feature matrix, pricing comparison, gap analysis |
| Customer research | Who are the segments and personas, what do they expect? | Segmentation, persona set, expectation map |
| Technical research | Can we actually build this with what exists today? | Feasibility note, tech constraint list |
| Product‑market fit research | Is this product a genuine fit for the target market? | PMF survey scores, retention curves |
| Financial viability research | Will this make money for us? | Unit economics, pricing model, business case |

Technical research stops you writing PRDs for impossible tech. Financial viability stops you shipping a feature that bankrupts the company.

## Primary vs secondary research
- **Primary**: data you generate first‑hand (interviews, surveys, usability tests, your own analytics, A/B tests on your product).  
- **Secondary**: data that already exists (market reports, competitor analysis, app‑store reviews, academic papers, internal data, government data).  

Same method can be either: your own A/B results are primary; reading a competitor’s published A/B is secondary.

## Sequencing rule: secondary first
1. Look at your own data (analytics, reviews, support tickets).  
2. Form a testable hypothesis from that data.  
3. Use the data to decide which cohort to talk to.  
4. Then run primary research to confirm or kill the hypothesis.  

Example: Myntra data showed women in Tier 1 cities browse 6‑7 PM but rarely buy. Asking that cohort “what would make you buy instantly?” would be wrong; the conversion‑focused cohort is the opposite group.

## Know your output before you ask
Microsoft’s Excel PM team gets 30 minutes with the top 20 power users twice a year and may ask only two questions. If you do not know what decision the answer will inform, you waste the scarce access.  
Principle: decide the decision first, then craft questions that will inform it without revealing your goal to the participant.

## Bias is the enemy
During a Swiggy diabetes exercise a participant suggested diabetics already know what to order; that was labeled 100 % bias. A relative with diabetes orders pizza weekly, proving the opposite assumption is also bias. Bias feels like common sense; the only defence is data plus real‑user talk, which is why secondary research comes first.

## Needs versus behaviour
- **Need**: what the user says they want.  
- **Behaviour**: what the user actually does (logged actions).  

When they diverge, trust the behaviour. PhonePe UPI Lite example: friends asked to raise the no‑PIN limit from ₹2 000 to ₹5 000, but analytics showed they never used UPI Lite. The stated need was useless because the behaviour was zero.

## Question wording decides the answer
A single word changes the framing:  
- “exploring a life with them” → Shaadi.com (matrimony)  
- “exploring something fun with them” → Tinder/Bumble (casual)  

Leading, intrusive, or solution‑asking questions produce useless data. In the Swiggy diabetes survey exercise, almost every question failed on at least one of six checks (see below).

## Six‑check survey question test
Run every survey question through these filters; rewrite if any fail.

| Check | Fails if… |
|-------|-----------|
| 1 | Asks for a solution (“which feature would you want”) |
| 2 | Is leading (pre‑loads an opinion) |
| 3 | Is intrusive (asks sensitive data without trust) |
| 4 | You already have the answer in your own analytics |
| 5 | Labels the respondent (names condition, income, identity) |
| 6 | Cannot invalidate your hypothesis (no possible answer would make you abandon the idea) |

**Good example** (Swiggy diabetes):  
“When you ordered food last time on Swiggy, what was your biggest concern?”  
Options: no concerns; health impact; body‑sugar impact; delivery/packaging/food quality; other reason not listed.  
It mentions no feature, no label, anchors to a real event, includes an escape hatch, and can kill the hypothesis if most pick “no concerns”.

## Interview techniques
- Start with “Tell me about…” not “Do you…”.  
- Keep silence; users reveal more when you pause.  
- Probe “why?” three times.  
- Record and transcribe with consent.  
- Group insights into jobs‑to‑be‑done, frustrations, motivations.  

**Bad questions** to avoid:  
- “Which feature do you like the most?”  
- “Which feature do you hate the most?”  
- “If you were a PM, what feature would you build?”  
- “How good is my product?”  

These validate your own thesis; if the user could do your job, why pay you a PM salary?

**Substitution test** (powerful opening):  
“What happens if you wake up tomorrow and you cannot find [my product] on any of your devices?”  
Responses reveal criticality, switching cost, and emotional load without naming those concepts.

## Frameworks & models

### Classification grid (qual/quant vs primary/secondary)

| Method | Qual/Quant | Primary/Secondary |
|--------|------------|-------------------|
| Survey | Quant (counts, ratings) | Primary |
| Interviews | Both (text + any scales) | Primary |
| A/B test | Quant | Primary if your own data; secondary if competitor’s published result |
| FGD | Both | Primary |
| Usability study | Mostly qual (observation, text) | Primary |
| Data analytics | Quant | Primary (your own product) |
| Customer feedback | Both (stars quant, free text qual) | Primary |
| Ethnographic study | Qual | Primary |

Use this grid to name a method and instantly state the evidence type and whether you must generate the data.

### 1:1 interview flow (≈40 min)
1. Warm‑up (5 min): rapport, lower defences.  
2. Context (10 min): background, situation.  
3. Core (20 min): pain points, workflows, decisions.  
4. Wrap‑up (5 min): feedback, follow‑up permission.  

Tips: ask “Tell me about…”, keep silence, probe why three times, record with consent, theme insights.

### Survey flow
1. Define the decision the survey will inform.  
2. Target the right audience (segment first).  
3. Keep it short (7–10 questions max).  
4. Mix Likert, multiple choice, open‑ended.  
5. Pilot with five people, watch confusion.  

Pitfalls: leading questions, too long, sampling only active users.  
Best practice: neutral language (“How satisfied are you?”), 5‑ or 7‑point scale, incentivise, close the loop.

### A/B testing steps
1. Define single metric (conversion, click‑through, retention, etc.).  
2. Build variant A (control) and B (change).  
3. Split large, random, comparable users (e.g., 25 k vs 25 k).  
4. Run defined period; do not peek early.  
5. Flip groups (show A to former B, B to former A).  
6. Compare across both runs; if winner holds, it is real.  
7. Make winner default.  

Political value: A/B results are your Brahmastra — evidence that ends stakeholder debates.

### Data analytics (always first step)
Look at: acquisition sources, funnel drop‑offs, action points, session counts/frequency/recency, clickstream, heatmaps.  
External sources that count: Play Store/App Store reviews, Twitter threads, Amazon reviews.  
Example: Ola/Uber‑style ride data shows cancellations spike at a time/zone → you know which drivers/riders to interview and what to ask.

### Customer feedback
Structured post‑transaction signals: ratings (quant) and free text (qual).  
Swiggy/Zomato ask delivery experience, agent behaviour, food quality, store preference, etc.  
Zomato’s karma score built from feedback patterns to detect fraudulent refund claims — feedback becomes a revenue‑protecting mechanism.

### Which method for which question (decision table)

| Your question | Method | Qual/Quant | Why | Concrete example |
|---------------|--------|------------|-----|------------------|
| Which steps in our onboarding confuse users most? | Usability interview | Qual | Direct observation finds nuanced pain points | 8 users think aloud through onboarding |
| Did our release move engagement? | Data analytics | Quant | Large‑scale behavioural data quantifies change | Compare churn pre/post feature |
| Which of 10 features matter most to a broad base? | Survey | Quant | Statistically meaningful input from many users | Ranking survey to 500 customers |
| How do segments feel about new pricing? | FGD | Qual | Captures live debate and reasoning | 3 virtual groups of 6‑8 on pricing tiers |
| Why do users do this strange thing our data shows? | 1:1 interview | Qual | Conversation surfaces motivation | “Walk me through the last time you did X” |
| What really happens in the user’s environment? | Ethnographic study | Qual | Behaviour is situational, cannot be recalled in a chair | Sitting in a clinic; flying in aircraft; two weeks on support calls |
| Which of these two designs converts better? | A/B test | Quant | Isolates one variable at scale with control | Red vs blue CTA on 25 k each, then flipped |
| Can users complete the core task at all? | Usability study | Both | Task completion rates + observed confusion | 5‑8 users, 4 tasks, measured and observed |
| Is this problem even worth solving? | Survey with invalidating option | Quant | One well‑posed question can kill hypothesis cheaply | “When you last ordered, what was your biggest concern? — I had no concerns” |
| What is the market and who else is in it? | Secondary research | Both | Data already exists; generating yourself is waste | Industry reports, competitor teardowns, app‑store reviews |

### Commitment test
Check whether enthusiasm for an unbuilt product is real.  
1. Build hypothesis from data, not enthusiasm.  
2. Create a prototype (pen‑and‑paper, Figma, AI‑generated).  
3. Give it to the user who claims to love the idea.  
4. Ask them to commit something real (time, attention, deposit, pilot slot).  
5. Observe if enthusiasm drops.  
If they make excuses, that is your retention forecast; they will not adopt the product later.

## Common mistakes to avoid
1. Asking users to design the product.  
2. Writing leading questions without noticing (use the Amitabh Bachchan test).  
3. Skipping secondary research because primary feels more exciting.  
4. Trusting what a friendly user tells you; cross‑check stated needs against usage data.  
5. Confusing adoption with retention (novelty spikes fade).  
6. Running a focus group without managing the room (dominant voices skew results).  
7. Using FGDs for sensitive topics (health, money, embarrassment).  
8. Asking for sensitive data you have not earned trust for.  
9. Writing surveys longer than 7–10 questions (completion rate drops).  
10. Sampling only happy, active users (excludes churned users you need to hear from).  
11. Stopping an A/B test when it shows the result you wanted; run full duration then flip cohorts.  
12. Confusing “can’t do it” with “doesn’t want it” (Copilot story: feature worked but users couldn’t find it).  
13. Treating a question as neutral because it feels neutral to you; read it aloud as the respondent.  
14. Doing research that cannot change your mind (rubber stamp).  

## Interview & portfolio angle
**In a PM interview**  
- Name the decision first: “I’d want to know whether this problem is worth solving, so I’d start with…”.  
- Sequence secondary before primary: “First I’d look at our analytics and support tickets, then design interviews around the gap.”  
- State how you’d know you were wrong: “If fewer than 30 % pick the sugar‑related option, I’d conclude the hypothesis is dead.”  

**Portfolio artefacts**  
1. Filled classification grid with a sentence per method on when you’d use it.  
2. Survey design with annotations: take the Swiggy diabetes brief, write five questions, note which of the six checks each passes and why.  
3. One‑page research plan for a real product: business question, secondary findings, hypothesis, cohort, two primary methods with justification, and the result that would kill the idea.  

Posting these on LinkedIn tags the school and builds a visible track record.

## Glossary (selected)
- **A/B testing** – Showing two variants to comparable groups and measuring which performs better on one defined metric.  
- **Attitudes (user)** – Perceptions and opinions about a product or brand.  
- **Behaviour (user)** – What a user actually does inside a product; the truth when it contradicts what they say.  
- **Cohort** – Defined group sharing a characteristic or behaviour, used as unit of comparison.  
- **Cohort flip** – Swapping which group sees which variant partway through an A/B test to confirm the variant caused the result.  
- **Escape‑hatch option** – Survey answer such as “my reason is not listed here” that reveals when your option set was wrong.  
- **FGD (Focus Group Discussion)** – Moderated discussion with 5‑8 users exploring shared perceptions; not for sensitive topics.  
- **Hypothesis** – Single testable belief about user behaviour, stated so a specific result would prove it false.  
- **Invalidation** – Designing research so some possible outcome would kill your idea; research without it is a rubber stamp.  
- **Leading question** – Question that pre‑loads an opinion, making agreement the easy path.  
- **Likert scale** – Rating scale, usually 1‑5 or 1‑7, capturing degree of agreement or satisfaction.  
- **Mom Test** – People who like you will lie to protect feelings; ask questions that make lying impossible.  
- **Needs (user)** – Problems users say they are trying to solve.  
- **Primary research** – Data you generate yourself, first‑hand, that nobody else has.  
- **Qualitative research** – Text‑ and observation‑based with small samples answering why and how.  
- **Quantitative research** – Number‑based with large samples answering how many and how much.  
- **Sampling** – Choosing who is included; poor sampling (e.g., only active users) invalidates work.  
- **Secondary research** – Data that already exists and you read to extract information; always the first step.  
- **Substitution test** – Interview question “what happens if this product disappears tomorrow?” to reveal criticality and switching cost.  
- **Task completion rate** – Percentage of usability study participants who finish a defined task.  
- **Technical research** – Whether the thing you want to build can be built with existing technology.  
- **Time on task** – How long a usability participant takes to complete a defined task.  
- **UAT (User Acceptance Testing)** – Small group runs real end‑to‑end flow before GA to confirm build is acceptable.  
- **Usability study** – Watching real users attempt defined tasks with a product or prototype to find where they struggle; typically 5‑8 participants.  
- **User research** – Systematic study of target users and their requirements to add realistic context and insight to the design process.

title: Personas empathy maps and user journeys
summary: Personas empathy maps and user journeys teach how to synthesize user research into actionable insights for product decisions.
body:
# Session 05 — Personas, Empathy Maps & User Journeys

I learned that user empathy in product management is not about being nice; it is about discovering what users will pay for. If I cannot connect empathy to revenue, retention or cost, I am doing support work, not product work.

## Empathy redefined  
I must be able to answer three questions for any user problem:  
1. Should my product or feature solve this?  
2. Why will the user pay if I solve it?  
3. If I solve it, will my product be the best choice, or will alternatives remain?  

If I only say I understand users and want to solve their problems, I belong in a support role.

## Latent needs  
A latent need is a hidden or unknown need that users feel but cannot articulate. They describe small improvements to what they already use.  
*Example:* Users asked for more iPod storage; Apple built a cloud music library.  
*Example:* Users asked for more accurate ChatGPT responses; the product built agentic workflows that do the work instead of describing it.  
To uncover latent needs I take every stated need and generalise it into one or two capabilities that cover all of them.

## Needs vs wants  
- **Need**: output the user can name (e.g., “give me order tracking”).  
- **Want**: outcome the user cannot name (e.g., “100% predictability and control over my order”).  
Users know needs; I must discover wants. If I build only what users say they need, I miss the real value.

## Reading user feedback – three rules  
1. **One solution only?** If a stated problem has only one possible solution, it is a feature in disguise, not a pain point.  
2. **Many asks in one sentence?** If the user bundles several requests, it is a confused response; I can drop it.  
3. **Whose problem is it?** If the issue belongs to Finance, Strategy, Growth, Marketing or Operations, I route it; I do not build it as a product PM.

## Bucketing (affinity clustering)  
After collecting raw statements I:  
1. **Collect** every verbatim need.  
2. **Cluster** into 4–6 themed buckets.  
3. **Generalise** each bucket into one insight sentence.  
4. **Converge** all buckets into one or two lines that express the want (the outcome).  
5. **Quantify** frequency and impact on core metrics.  
6. **Prioritise** with Impact × Effort or Frequency × Severity.  
The deliverable is a Pain Map showing high‑impact issues on top of the unmet needs they signal.  
*Example:* 22 Blinkit/Zepto needs collapsed to the want “100% predictability and control over my order.”

## Knowing a problem is worth solving  
I look for four signals, three of them measurable:  
1. **Withdrawal test** – if users panic when the product disappears, it is worth building.  
2. **Organic adoption** – new users come without heavy marketing.  
3. **Repeat transactions** – high repeat usage, not just sign‑ups.  
4. **Price resilience** – users stay after a price increase.

## Outcomes – one outcome only  
Multiple outcomes mean leadership never clarified why they hired me. I ask for the single outcome I am meant to move at 3, 6 and 12 months.  
Outcome = want. The persona narrows the outcome; the outcome narrows the roadmap.

## Persona  
A persona is a **generalised representation** of my ideal user, not a fictional character and not a 1:1 copy of a real person. It has four blocks:  
- **Demographics** – age, gender, earnings, city, digital literacy, occupation.  
- **Psychographics** – pains, gains, motivations, values, fears.  
- **Tech proficiency** – devices, OS, app habits, social media usage, internet constraints, accessibility needs.  
- **Product‑specific** – touchpoints, usage, most‑used features, struggles, alternatives, purchase drivers, satisfaction, switching barriers, the success metric they care about.  

I need at most three personas (primary, secondary, tertiary).  
*Example (Excel):* Primary persona Priya (Bangalore data analyst) wants to find trends quickly, automate tasks, present findings clearly. Secondary persona David (Houston small‑business owner) wants simple expense tracking and readable reports. The tension between them shows why both are needed.

## User journey  
A journey map shows the same user across time, stage by stage, with emotions, pain points and opportunities logged at each stage. Persona is the static photo; journey is the moving film.  
Stages can be Awareness → Consideration → Onboarding → Retention → Loyalty (or Awareness → Adoption → Engagement → Revenue → Referral).  
For each stage I record:  
- **Actions** – what the user does.  
- **Touchpoints** – where they meet the product.  
- **Experience** – feeling + a short quote.  
- **Pain points** – specific friction + a short quote.  
- **Opportunities** – “How might we …” ideas.  
I attach a metric to each stage so the map is measurable.

*Example (Netflix):*  
- Awareness: sees ads, hears from friends – curious, mild FOMO.  
- Adoption: starts free trial, watches first series – excited, low‑risk.  
- Engagement: watches new releases, follows recommendations – hooked, entertained.  
- Revenue: renews out of habit, values no ads – comfortable, habitual.  
- Referral: shares a coupon, starts Teleparty – connected, sociable.  

*Example (Zepto):*  
- Awareness: sees Instagram ads, asks friends – curious, hopeful.  
- Consideration: compares Blinkit, checks delivery time – interested, comparing.  
- Onboarding: installs app, places first order – excited, confident.  
- Retention: reorders essentials, browses deals – convenient, routine.  
- Loyalty: refers friends, buys weekly groceries – proud, connected.  

From the journey I derive prioritised recommendations, each tied to a metric and effort estimate.

## Jobs to be Done (from deck)  
Users hire a product to get a job done. The job statement format: “When I [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome].”  
Job types: functional, emotional, social, financial.  
*Example (milkshake):*  
- Functional: keep me engaged on my commute as a single‑item breakfast.  
- Emotional: make me feel full with enough quantity.  
- Social: be seen drinking from a reputed outlet in acceptable packaging.  
- Financial: be affordable for an average American.  

Every job is tied to a business consequence (e.g., drives engagement, strengthens retention).

## Needs vs pain points (from deck)  
- **Need**: stable desire pulling a user toward a goal (e.g., “I want to connect with people I care about”).  
- **Pain point**: specific, situational frustration blocking that need (e.g., “It takes too long to upload stories”).  
Needs define what to build; pain points define what to fix. I should not just treat the pain – I must uncover the underlying need it signals.

## Voice of the User  
VoU is the discipline of systematically recording user pains, gains and unmet needs so the team agrees on real truths.  
It captures:  
- **User pains** – barriers, frustrations, negative emotions.  
- **User gains** – positive outcomes and delights.  
- **Unmet needs** – indirect desires, often phrased as “I wish it could…”.  
Sources: surveys, interviews, app‑store reviews, social comments, support tickets, analytics anomalies.

## Frameworks (condensed but complete)

### 1. The Three Empathy Questions  
Apply to any user problem before it enters the backlog.  
Steps:  
1. Is this something my product or feature should solve for?  
2. Why will my user pay if I solve this problem?  
3. If I solved it, would my product be the best choice, or would the user still have alternatives?  
*Mini‑example:* “Users want to see product reviews on Blinkit.”  
1. Yes – trust at the shelf is ours.  
2. They currently won’t buy expensive items here; reviews enable a higher‑value basket (payment is basket size).  
3. Only if reviews are quick‑commerce specific (freshness, packaging, real condition); generic star ratings would push users to check Amazon anyway.

### 2. The Pain Point Sentence  
Template:  
> I, as a user, want to **[goal]**, but on **[product]** I am not able to do this because **[specific blocker]**, hence I am not able to achieve **[consequence in my life]**.  
After writing it I test:  
- Can I think of at least three different solutions? If no → feature in disguise.  
- Is it one clear struggle, or five? If five → confused response.  
- Is it a product problem, or Finance/Growth/Marketing/Operations? If not product → route it.  
*Worked example:*  
Bad: “I want to add items after placing my order.” (one solution)  
Good: “I, as a user, want to order my full weekly grocery list in one go, but on Blinkit I am not able to because I remember missed items only after checkout, hence I end up paying delivery fees twice or dropping the items entirely.” (multiple solutions: order‑edit window, “frequently forgotten” nudge, free merge of a second order within 10 min, persistent list).

### 3. Needs → Buckets → Wants → Outcome  
Steps (as in Bucketing above).  
*Worked mini‑example:* Blinkit’s 22 stated needs → five buckets (ETA & tracking, scheduling, charges, product attributes, reviews & returns) → each generalised → converged to the want “100% predictability and control over my order.”

### 4. The Persona (filled‑in example)  
When to use: at the start of any new product, feature or team; when onboarding; before prototype testing.  
Steps:  
1. Gather qualitative (interviews, support tickets) and quantitative (analytics) data.  
2. Cluster users by behaviour, not just demographics.  
3. Decide if one persona suffices; otherwise add secondary (and tertiary only if genuinely needed).  
4. Fill the four blocks.  
5. Add one verbatim quote that captures the worldview.  
6. Add the success metric the persona personally cares about.  
7. Revisit quarterly against fresh data.  

*Primary persona (Excel):* Priya, 25‑30 y, Bangalore, Senior Data Analyst, ₹80k‑1.2L/mo, lives with flatmates, high digital literacy. Pains: large slow datasets, formula errors, presenting to non‑technical people. Gains: finding trends quickly, automating work with macros, impressing stakeholders with dashboards. Motivations: career advancement via data‑driven insights. Values: accuracy, efficiency, innovative analysis. Fears: analysis mistake affecting business strategy. Devices/OS: Windows laptop with secondary monitor, Windows 11. App habits: fluent across MS Office, explores new data tools. Social media: high on LinkedIn. Internet: high‑speed fibre. Alternatives: Python, Tableau, SQL (used alongside Excel). Usage frequency: daily; primary tool. Purchase drivers: corporate standard, powerful functions, industry norm. Satisfaction: high, though some features feel complex. Switching barriers: dependence on built macros/templates, industry norms. Success metric she cares about: accuracy and speed of delivering insights to stakeholders. What she wants: find key trends quickly, automate repetitive tasks, present findings clearly.  

*Secondary persona (Excel):* David, 45‑55 y, Houston, owner of independent hardware store, $60‑80k/yr, married with children, moderate digital literacy. Pains: remembering complex formulas, losing track of files, hard to understand simple charts. Gains: knowing best‑selling products, expense tracking without an accountant, simple monthly sales summaries. Motivations/Values/Fears: saving money on software, keeping business afloat, simplicity/cost‑effectiveness, losing financial data or tax errors. Tech: Windows 10 desktop + smartphone, email, basic accounting/spreadsheet apps, low social media, basic broadband. Alternatives: QuickBooks; pen and paper. Switching barriers: comfort with current system, data already in Excel format. Success metric: correctness of basic financial numbers. What he wants: keep track of expenses, know product popularity, reports he can actually read.

*Instagram Creator Persona (from deck):* Claire, 26, lifestyle creator, urban city (Mumbai/LA). Tech: iPhone, editing apps, analytics tools; active on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts; daily use of Reels, Stories, Insights. Psychographics: seeks creativity, validation and growth; enjoys self‑expression; values social recognition. Pain points: algorithm unpredictability, follower drop, time spent editing. Goals: grow audience, earn through brand collaborations, engage community. Quote: “I want to create content that resonates, grow my community authentically, and turn my passion into a sustainable career.” This persona shaped Creator Mode and the Professional Dashboard.

### 5. The Empathy Map (filled‑in)  
Use straight after an interview while the transcript is fresh.  
Steps:  
1. Pick one user and one situation (e.g., “Rahul ordering weekly groceries on a Sunday evening”).  
2. **Says** – verbatim quotes only.  
3. **Does** – observed behaviour only (no inference).  
4. **Thinks** and **Feels** – inference, marked as inference.  
5. Extract **Pains** and **Gains** at the bottom.  
6. Cross‑check: any pain must trace back to a quote or observed behaviour.  

*Filled‑in example (quick‑commerce grocery user):*  
- **Says**: “I can't compare the same product across brands and pack sizes side by side.” • “I can't tell if the fruit is fresh until it arrives.” • “Half my regular list is out of stock.” • “I don't know what the final bill will be until checkout.”  
- **Thinks** (inferred): Am I overpaying for this pack size? • If the tomatoes are bad again I'm going back to the local shop. • Why do I have to check two apps for one grocery list? • There's a charge in here I didn't expect.  
- **Does** (observed): Opens two apps and switches back and forth to compare prices. • Adds unwanted items to cross the free‑delivery threshold. • Places a second order 10 min later for forgotten items. • Photographs bad produce for the returns flow.  
- **Feels** (inferred): Suspicious at the price breakdown. • Anxious between checkout and doorbell. • Irritated when a staple is out of stock. • Relieved when the order arrives complete and fresh.  
- **Pains**: Cannot verify quality before paying. • Cannot predict the final bill. • Cannot complete one full list in one app. • Cannot fix an order after placing it.  
- **Gains**: Ten‑minute delivery when it works. • No trip to the market. • Repeat‑order convenience for staples.  
- **Generalised want**: “Give me complete confidence in what I will receive, when, and at what price.”

### 6. The User Journey Map (filled‑in)  
Use when I need to locate a problem in time, before prioritising work, or when a metric like retention drops.  
Steps (from deck):  
1. For each stage write what the user is **doing** and **feeling**.  
2. Identify **pain points** – what frustrates them or stops progression.  
3. Brainstorm **opportunities** – how each pain could be solved.  
4. Attach a **metric** to each stage so the map is measurable.  

*Stage reference table:*  
- **Awareness** – channels, message recall, targeting → CTR, reach → optimise ad creative, SEO, social presence.  
- **Consideration** – website/app exploration → time on page, bounce rate → improve landing pages and CTAs.  
- **Onboarding** – signup, setup completion → activation rate → simplify flows, guided tutorials.  
- **Retention** – frequency and recency → DAU/MAU, churn → add habit loops, push notifications.  
- **Loyalty** – advocacy and referrals → NPS, referral rate → reward programmes, communities.  

*Full worked journey (Netflix):*  

| Row \ Stage | Awareness | Adoption | Engagement | Revenue | Referral |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Actions** | Sees ads; hears about a show from friends; scrolls past clips on social media | Starts free trial; watches first series (Money Heist); buys trial pack, then subscription | Watches new releases; follows recommendations; explores international content; watches series forwarded by friends | Renews month after month; upgrades plan; watches weekly drops | Shares recommendations; starts a Teleparty; passes on coupons; shares a plan |
| **Thoughts** | “Everyone's talking about this show.” “Is this worth ₹500 a month?” | “Let me just try it free first.” “One episode won't hurt.” | “There's always something new.” “It knows what I like.” | “I'd notice if this were gone.” “No ads is worth it.” | “You have to watch this.” “We can watch it together.” |
| **Feelings** | Curious, mildly left out (FOMO) | Excited, low‑risk | Hooked, entertained, relaxed | Comfortable, habitual, unbothered | Connected, sociable |
| **Pain points** | Doesn't know what's actually on it; ad noise from many streamers | Payment friction; not sure trial is genuinely free; unclear what to watch first | Recommendation fatigue; content leaves platform; endless scroll before picking | Price rises; overlapping subscriptions; “am I using this enough?” | Password‑sharing restrictions; no easy shared‑watch on mobile; nothing in it for the referrer |
| **Opportunities** | I lead with the one show a person will actually care about, not the catalogue | I provide a zero‑friction trial with a curated first‑watch, matched to the acquisition trigger | I reduce time‑to‑play; warn before favourites expire; strengthen the “because you watched” logic | I make weekly value visible (“you watched 14 hours this month”); tiered pricing tied to real usage | I build the co‑watch feature properly; reward the referrer, not only the referred |

*Second worked journey (Zepto – generated with AI prompt):*  

| Row \ Stage | Awareness | Consideration | Onboarding | Retention | Loyalty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Customer actions** | Sees Instagram ads; asks friends | Compares Blinkit; checks delivery time | Installs app; places first order | Reorders essentials; browses daily deals | Refers friends; buys weekly groceries |
| **Touchpoints** | Instagram Reels; WhatsApp shares | App Store; Google Search | Mobile app; UPI checkout | Push notifications; home feed | Referral page; loyalty rewards |
| **Experience** | Curious, hopeful — “Fast enough?” | Interested, comparing — “Worth switching?” | Excited, confident — “Easy checkout” | Convenient, routine — “Forgot groceries” | Proud, connected — “Love recommending” |
| **Pain points** | Trust concerns, brand confusion — “Too expensive” | Price comparison, offer overload — “Better elsewhere” | Coupon issues, signup friction — “Code failed” | Notification fatigue, forgets the app — “Too many alerts” | Weak rewards, referral friction — “Nothing special” |
| **Opportunities (HMW)** | How might we build trust quickly? | How might we simplify comparisons? | How might we shorten first checkout? | How might we trigger habitual reorders? | How might we reward loyal customers? |

*Top‑4 recommendations (tied to goal and metric):*  
1. Smart replenishment reminders – fix forgotten reorders @ Retention → Repeat orders per user per month (Effort: M)  
2. Personalised loyalty rewards – fix weak incentives @ Loyalty → 30‑day retention (M)  
3. AI‑powered offer personalisation – fix irrelevant promotions @ Retention → Repeat purchase rate (L)  
4. One‑tap recurring baskets – fix reorder effort @ Retention → Weekly active purchasers (M)  

*Journey snapshot (≤12 words):* Problem → hard to get daily essentials quickly. First convenience → 10‑minute delivery saves time. Trusted habit → Zepto becomes my go‑to weekly habit.

### 7. Generalising pain points into a Pain Map  
Five‑step method: Collect → Cluster → Generalise → Quantify → Prioritise.  
Deliverable: Pain Map showing high‑impact issues on top of the unmet needs they signal.  
*Worked example (Instagram):* Pains – “Algorithm is unpredictable, my reach drops suddenly.” “Too many ads in feed.” “Hard to manage multiple accounts.” → clustered into Control, Clarity, Simplicity → generalised insight: “Users want more transparency and control over visibility.” → shipped features: Account Status (clarifies algorithm impact), Professional Dashboard (analytics transparency), simplified multi‑account switching → improved creator trust and fewer complaints about algorithm opacity.

### 8. Jobs to be Done applied (worked mini‑example – Instagram)  

| Job type | User's job statement | Instagram's solution | Business value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Functional | “I want to share photos and videos quickly with friends.” | Easy post creation and sharing tools | Drives daily engagement |
| Emotional | “I want to feel inspired and appreciated for my creativity.” | Likes, comments, algorithmic reach | Strengthens creator retention |
| Social | “I want to be part of trends and look relevant.” | Reels, trending audio, hashtags | Boosts viral growth and content supply |
| Emotional | “I don't want to feel left out when others share moments.” | Story rings, peer notifications | Increases habitual check‑ins |

Every job is tied to a business consequence, embodying the rule that empathy without business value is not product work.

### 9. The two AI prompts  

**Prompt A – Visual Persona Designer**  
```
You are a visual persona designer. Ask me only these two questions in one line,
then proceed without further questions:
  1. What is the product (name + 1-line what it does)?
  2. Do you want one persona or two (primary + secondary)?

After my reply, generate an image (1920x1080 PNG) with a clean poster layout:
title "CASE STUDY — USER PERSONA", subtle paper texture background, two rounded
persona cards (left = Primary, right = Secondary; if I choose "one", center a
single large card). Include a small product logo placeholder top-right. Use
modern typography, clear section headers, bullet points, and high contrast. Add
friendly, diverse face placeholders (no real people). Keep language respectful
and stereotype-free.

For each persona card, fill these sections with crisp, specific bullets tailored
to the product's market (invent realistic details when missing):
  - Name + short 1-line life with the product (“A day in one sentence”).
  - Demographics: Age range, Location, Occupation, Income band, Household if
    relevant, Digital literacy.
  - Psychographic: Pains (top 3), Gains (top 3), Motivations, Values, Fears.
  - Tech Proficiency: Devices, OS, App habits, Social media usage, Internet
    constraints, Accessibility needs if any.
  - Product-Specific: Current alternatives, Usage scenarios & frequency,
    Purchase drivers, Satisfaction level, Switching barriers, Success metric
    they care about.
  - What they want: 3-5 crisp outcome-oriented statements.

Visual formatting rules:
  - Use the section labels exactly: Demographics, Psychographic, Tech
    Proficiency, Product-Specific, What they want.
  - Keep each bullet <= 12 words; 4-6 bullets per section.
  - Highlight Pains and Gains with small icons or bold labels.
  - If two personas, make the Secondary clearly distinct.

Output:
  - Primary deliverable: a single 1920x1080 PNG containing the persona card(s).
  - Also include a compact, copyable JSON block mirroring all fields.

Do not ask more questions. If any info is unknown, infer plausibly and state
assumptions in the JSON under "assumptions". Avoid stereotypes; use generic
faces, not identifiable people.

Begin now by asking only: "Product (name + 1-liner)? One persona or two?"
```

**Prompt B – Senior Journey-Mapping Assistant**  
```
You are a senior journey-mapping assistant.
First, ask ONLY these in ONE line, then wait:
  1) Product (name + 1-line)
  2) Goal (engagement/adoption/revenue/retention/other)
  3) Core problem
  4) Region/persona (market, segment, traits)

After I answer, produce:
=== OUTPUT (<=280 words, Markdown only) ===
Keep every cell crisp. Max 2 bullets per cell, each <= 7 words. Prefer real
customer words: include one short quote in Experience and Pain Points cells per
stage (e.g. "Too many steps", "Feels risky", "Can't find X").

## Customer Journey Map
Stages: Awareness | Consideration | Onboarding | Retention | Loyalty
Rows:
  - Customer actions   — concrete verbs
  - Touchpoints        — exact channels/surfaces
  - Experience         — 1 feeling + 1 quote
  - Pain points        — specific friction + 1 quote
  - Opportunities (HMW)— 1 "How might we ..." idea

## Top 4 Recommendations (1-liners, prioritized)
Tie each to my goal and a single metric.
Format: 1) [Action] to fix <pain @ stage> => Metric (Effort: S/M/L)

## Journey Snapshot (<=12 words)
Outcome from problem -> first value -> habit.

=== RULES ===
- Be region/persona-specific (local channels, norms, language).
- No fluff, no extra sections, no explanations.
- Prefer strong verbs, concrete nouns, plain English.

title: Vahan Data API plan part 1
summary: Vahan Data API plan outlines government and private approaches to sell aggregated vehicle registration data.
body:
> **Scope:** An end-to-end plan (requirements → design → build → deploy) plus a full financial plan for an **aggregate** Vahan vehicle-registration **Data API**, from two angles: **(A) the Government operating it** (MoRTH/NIC, aiming for self-sufficiency) and **(B) a private company** building a product on top.
> ⚠️ **Read this first.** All forward-looking figures are **illustrative estimates on stated assumptions**, not official budgets, forecasts, or a MoRTH/NIC plan. The only hard facts are cited (e.g. the 2019 policy's ₹111.4 cr / 142 buyers).

## Executive Summary

The Vahan Data API presents a timely opportunity to revolutionize access to vehicle registration data in India. Currently, numerous industries — including vehicle financiers, manufacturers, dealers, insurers, researchers, and data aggregators — rely on fragmented and often unreliable data sources for critical business decisions. 

This situation stems from the retirement of the existing dashboard and the lack of an official, structured interface for accessing aggregate vehicle registration information.  Currently, demand is met through fragile web scraping practices and third-party resellers, leading to inconsistencies, security risks, and ethical concerns.

The Vahan Data API addresses these challenges by providing a secure, standardized, and transparent platform for accessing de-identified, aggregate vehicle data. This initiative can be pursued through two distinct but complementary lenses: 

1. **Government-operated API:**  A self-sufficient public service directly managed by the government, ensuring data sovereignty and control over its usage.
2. **Private product built on top of the API:** A commercial offering leveraging the government's open data infrastructure to provide tailored solutions and value-added services to specific industry segments.

Designed in strict compliance with the DPDP Act 2023, the Vahan Data API prioritizes user privacy by providing only aggregated, anonymized data, eliminating any risk of personal information exposure. This robust framework ensures responsible data governance and fosters trust among users.

The overarching goal is to establish a sustainable and self-financing public data service that empowers businesses, fuels innovation, and contributes to India's digital economy. Detailed financial projections outlining the potential revenue streams and cost structure are presented in the subsequent sections. 




---

## Customer base

The addressable market for a Vahan Aggregate Data API spans financial services, automotive commerce, insurance, logistics, and research. Because the underlying regulatory environment strictly limits access to personal identifiable information (PII) under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023, the product design focuses entirely on non-personal, aggregated, time-series, and spatial-registration datasets (e.g., fuel-type distribution by RTO, EV penetration velocity, brand market share by district, and vintage decay curves).

The following segment-by-segment breakdown details the counts, specific data needs, and estimated willingness to pay (WTP) for each group:

### 1. NBFCs & Vehicle Financiers
*   **Segment Count:** ~300 active serious vehicle financiers (out of ~9,000 registered NBFCs; vehicle finance constitutes ~50% of NBFC retail credit).
*   **Data Needed:** RTO-level default and saturation rates, asset concentration by fuel type/maker, vintage curves of commercial vs. passenger vehicles, and geographical default-risk mapping.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹3 Lakh to ₹12 Lakh / year (Enterprise subscription).

### 2. Commercial Banks (Auto & Retail Lending)
*   **Segment Count:** ~50 major scheduled commercial banks active in retail auto and CV lending.
*   **Data Needed:** District-level EV adoption rates, macro-registration trends for target commercial vehicle segments, and competitive market share shifts across national footprints to calibrate lending targets.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹5 Lakh to ₹20 Lakh / year (Enterprise multi-seat license).

### 3. General Insurance Companies
*   **Segment Count:** ~30 active general/motor insurers (out of 34 total).
*   **Data Needed:** State/RTO-level insurable population breakdowns by vehicle class, age, fuel type, and accident-prone zone cross-referencing to optimize geographic underwriting and pricing risk models.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹5 Lakh to ₹15 Lakh / year (Data feed integration).

### 4. Auto OEMs & Tier-1 Suppliers
*   **Segment Count:** ~100 active entities (Passenger vehicles, 2W, 3W, CV manufacturers, and major Tier-1 component makers).
*   **Data Needed:** Real-time segment market share tracking by district/RTO, competitive dispatch-to-registration velocity, fuel-type shifts (ICE to EV/CNG), and capacity utilization planning.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹10 Lakh to ₹30 Lakh / year (Advanced analytics dashboard + API access).

### 5. Auto Dealership Networks & Associations
*   **Segment Count:** ~15,000 dealerships / ~30,000 outlets represented via bodies like FADA (~50 major dealer groups buy bulk analysis; local dealers consume through downstream platforms).
*   **Data Needed:** Localized micro-market demand for specific models, competitor discounting impact visible via registration surges, and used-vs-new ratio analytics.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹50,000 to ₹2 Lakh / year (Aggregated dealer-portal access).

### 6. Used-Car & Marketplace Platforms
*   **Segment Count:** ~20 to 50 platforms (e.g., Cars24, Spinny, OLX Auto, CarTrade).
*   **Data Needed:** Historical valuation benchmarking based on regional registration volumes, age-distribution of scrap/deregistered vehicles, and liquidity indices of specific models by geography.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹3 Lakh to ₹10 Lakh / year.

### 7. Fintechs & Data Aggregators
*   **Segment Count:** ~50 to 100 players (e.g., Surepass, Signzy, EKO, Karza, credit bureaus).
*   **Data Needed:** Raw aggregated streams to embed inside risk-scoring models, macro-economic dashboards, and alternative credit assessment engines for logistics and transport operators.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** Usage-based pricing scaling from ₹2 Lakh to ₹15 Lakh / year.

### 8. Market Researchers, Consultancies & Think Tanks
*   **Segment Count:** ~100+ institutions (e.g., CRISIL, ICRA, EY, McKinsey, TERI, CSE).
*   **Data Needed:** Historical data (dating back to 1970 where available), multi-variable cuts (State x Fuel x Maker x Year), and electric vehicle transition velocity indicators.
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹1 Lakh to ₹5 Lakh / year (Ad-hoc export licenses or research tier).

### 9. Fleet Operators, Logistics & Supply Chain
*   **Segment Count:** ~50+ large institutional fleet owners and logistics networks.
*   **Data Needed:** Commercial vehicle saturation indices, toll-to-registration correlation data, and infrastructure density indicators (e.g., EV charging station viability mapping based on local EV registrations).
*   **Willingness to Pay (WTP):** ₹1 Lakh to ₹4 Lakh / year.

---

### Total Addressable Customer (TAC) Table

| Segment | Estimated Count | Target Addressable Count | Average WTP (INR / Year) | Potential Annual Market Size (Illustrative) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **NBFCs & Financiers** | ~9,000 (Reg.) | 300 | ₹6,00,000 | ₹18.00 Cr |
| **Commercial Banks** | ~100 | 50 | ₹12,00,000 | ₹6.00 Cr |
| **General Insurers** | ~34 | 30 | ₹10,00,000 | ₹3.00 Cr |
| **Auto OEMs & Tier-1** | ~100 | 80 | ₹20 lakh | ₹16.00 Cr |
| **Dealer Groups (FADA/Large)**| ~15,000 dealerships | 200 (Enterprise groups) | ₹1,50,000 | ₹3.00 Cr |
| **Used-Car Marketplaces** | ~50 | 35 | ₹5,00,000 | ₹1.75 Cr |
| **Fintechs & Aggregators** | ~100 | 70 | ₹7,50,000 | ₹5.25 Cr |
| **Research / Consultancies** | ~200+ | 100 | ₹2,50,000 | ₹2.50 Cr |
| **Fleet & Logistics** | ~100+ | 50 | ₹2,00,000 | ₹1.00 Cr |
| **Total** | **~24,584** | **915** | — | **₹56.50 Cr / year** |

*(Note: Figures are illustrative estimates based on current enterprise SaaS benchmarks in the Indian financial-data sector).*

### Key assumptions in this section:
1. Enterprise willingness to pay is tied to regulatory risk avoidance and compliance with the DPDP Act 2023, driving demand away from raw PII lookups toward compliant, aggregate macro data.
2. The addressable market filters out micro-entities (small unorganized dealers, individual transport operators) who rely on free public portals rather than paid enterprise APIs.
3. Market sizing assumes 1,000+ RTOs and 36 states/UTs are fully harmonized under the aggregate data release architecture.

---

## Demand & request-volume estimation

To design an API infrastructure capable of handling systemic load without degradation, request volumes are projected bottom-up across distinct customer tiers. Unlike real-time per-vehicle RC verification (which handles transactional lookups like EKO's ~₹3.00/verification), aggregate analytics APIs are driven by automated batch pulls, dashboard refreshes, and scheduled reporting pipelines.

### Segment-by-Segment Request Volume Model (Illustrative Estimates)

| Segment | Active Accounts | Avg. Requests / Day / Account | Peak Multiplier | Annual Request Volume (Illustrative) | Primary Interaction Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **NBFCs & Financiers** | 300 | 500 | 3x | 54,750,000 | Scheduled ETL / Portfolio Risk Dashboards |
| **Commercial Banks** | 50 | 1,000 | 2.5x | 18,250,000 | Macro-economic Credit Modeling |
| **General Insurers** | 30 | 800 | 2x | 8,760,000 | Underwriting Risk Mapping |
| **Auto OEMs & Tier-1** | 80 | 2,500 | 4x | 73,000,000 | Market Share & Competitor Tracking |
| **Dealer Groups** | 200 | 100 | 2x | 7,300,000 | Localized Demand Queries |
| **Used-Car Marketplaces** | 35 | 1,500 | 3x | 19,162,500 | Valuation & Liquidity Indexing |
| **Fintechs & Aggregators** | 70 | 5,000 | 5x | 127,750,000 | White-label Risk Engine Feeds |
| **Research / Consultancies**| 100 | 200 | 1.5x | 7,300,000 | Periodic Report Generation |
| **Fleet & Logistics** | 50 | 150 | 2x | 2,737,500 | EV Transition Planning |
| **Total Aggregate Demand** | **915** | — | — | **319,010,000 (~319M requests/yr)** | — |

### Core Assumptions & Calculations:
*   **Base Pool Growth:** The system processes approximately **~319 million API queries annually** across all paid commercial tiers.
*   **System Load Profile:** Unlike transactional payment gateways, aggregate query loads are front-loaded during business hours (09:00 to 18:00 IST) and peak sharply on the 1st and last business days of every month when enterprise dashboards execute automated reconciliation scripts.
*   **Data Freshness Constraints:** New registrations (~26 million per year) are ingested continuously from 1,000+ RTOs, translating to an average ingestion velocity of ~71,000 records/day. API caching layers must refresh nightly to serve consistent aggregate views.

---

## API product & packaging

The Vahan Aggregate Data API product is structured to balance open-access transparency mandates (for citizens, media, and academia) with high-value enterprise data monetization. Personal data (owner names, precise addresses, hypothecation specifics linked to individuals) is strictly redacted to maintain alignment with the DPDP Act 2023.

### Endpoint & Product Architecture
1.  `/v1/aggregate/national` — Macro totals (Total active fleet, YoY growth, EV penetration).
2.  `/v1/aggregate/state/{state_code}` — State-level filtering (Fuel mix, vehicle class distribution).
3.  `/v1/aggregate/rto/{rto_code}` — Micro-market RTO intelligence (District saturation, monthly registration velocity).
4.  `/v1/aggregate/timeseries` — Historical trends dating back to available archives (1970+ baseline aggregations).

---

### Packaging Tiers & Rate Limits

| Tier Name | Target Audience | Pricing (Illustrative) | Rate Limits | Data Granularity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 0: Public / Open** | Citizens, Media, Academia, Students | **Free** | 100 requests / day (Token-authenticated) | National & State-level summaries only (Monthly aggregated CSV/JSON). |
| **Tier 1: Standard Developer** | Startups, Small Fleet Operators, App Developers | **₹25,000 / year** or ₹2,500 / month | 1,000 requests / hour | State & District-level filters; basic fuel/class splits. |
| **Tier 2: Business Pro** | Used-car platforms, Mid-tier NBFCs, Regional Dealers | **₹3,00,000 / year** | 10,000 requests / hour | Full RTO-level granularity, maker/model aggregate breakdowns, monthly history. |
| **Tier 3: Enterprise Scale** | Tier-1 OEMs, Major Banks, National Insurers, Fintechs | **₹12 lakh to ₹25 lakh / year** | Custom / Unlimited (Burst up to 50,000 req/hr) | Real-time batch feeds, multi-year historical archives (from 1970), custom webhook alerts, dedicated account support. |

---

title: Access control and segregation of duties
summary: Access control and segregation of duties outlines current flaws, a six‑role model, permission matrix, enforcement steps, conflicting duties, and review processes.
body:
# Access control and segregation of duties

Status: draft for review
Created: 16 Sep 2026
Related: [[00-Policy-Framework-Overview]] · [[01-Role-Policy-Manager]] · [[07-Policy-Gap-Register]]

---

## Current state

Three findings from reading the code, not from theory.

**Permissions are advisory.** `ROLE_PERMISSIONS` and `hasPermission()` in `src/lib/auth.ts` are client-side objects. Nothing on the server consults them. Any caller holding the anon key and a session can reach any PostgREST endpoint the RLS policies allow, regardless of what role the UI thinks they have. The UI hides buttons; it does not withhold capability.

**RLS is written but not applied.** `sql/009_rls_policies.sql` exists and is thorough. It has never been run. Until it is, row-level security is off across every table.

**Roles are coarse.** Four roles — `admin`, `credit_officer`, `reviewer`, `viewer` — and `admin` carries everything including `manage_users` and, implicitly, policy write. There is no role that can author policy without also being able to decision cases, and no role that can approve a policy change as a distinct act.

## Target role model

Six roles. The two new ones are `policy_manager` and `credit_head`.

| Role | Real-world designation | Core purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `credit_officer` | Underwriter | Decision cases within a sanction limit |
| `credit_manager` | Manager | Decision above officer limit; case-level override and deviation |
| `credit_head` | Credit Head | Approve policy changes, rate grid, model promotion; high-value sanction |
| `policy_manager` | Policy Manager | Author policy, rules, pricing parameters. No case decisions |
| `compliance` | Compliance / Audit | Read everything including PII and audit; change nothing |
| `admin` | System Admin | Users, roles, configuration. No policy write, no case decisions |

Splitting `admin` matters. A single super-role that can both create users and change credit rules can grant itself whatever it needs and erase the distinction the rest of this document depends on.

## Permission matrix

| Permission | officer | manager | head | policy_mgr | compliance | admin |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| `view_assigned` | own | team | all | aggregate | all | none |
| `create` (application) | yes | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| `evaluate` (run assessment) | yes | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| `approve` / `decline` | ≤ limit | ≤ limit | yes | **no** | no | no |
| `override` (case deviation) | no | yes | yes | **no** | no | no |
| `policy_author` | no | no | yes | **yes** | no | no |
| `policy_approve` | no | no | **yes** | **no** | no | no |
| `policy_simulate` | no | no | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `rate_grid_author` | no | no | yes | yes | no | no |
| `model_propose` | no | no | yes | yes | no | no |
| `model_approve` | no | no | yes (+CRO) | no | no | no |
| `reveal_pii` | own cases | team | all | **no** | all | **no** |
| `view_reports` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `audit` (read trail) | no | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `manage_users` | no | no | no | no | no | yes |
| `export` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |

Two cells deserve comment. `admin` has no `reveal_pii` — a system administrator has no business reason to see a borrower's PAN, and denying it removes a standing risk. And `policy_manager` has no `reveal_pii` for the reason in [[01-Role-Policy-Manager]]: the role works on parameters, never on named borrowers.

## Enforcement, in order of dependence

Client-side checks stay — they make the UI coherent — but they stop being the control.

1. **Apply RLS.** Run `009_rls_policies.sql`. Nothing below matters until this is done, because without it every table is open to the anon key.
2. **Put role checks inside SECURITY DEFINER functions.** `fn_officer_decision`, `fn_customer_pii`, and any future `fn_policy_*` should read the caller's role from `users` via `auth.uid()` and raise on mismatch. `fn_customer_pii` already does this — it is the pattern to copy.
3. **Enforce sanction limits server-side.** `users.max_sanction_amount` exists in the schema. Nothing checks it. An officer decisioning a case above their limit should be rejected by the database, not by a disabled button.
4. **Make policy writes go through an RPC.** Revoke direct UPDATE on `policy_rules` and `rate_grid` from `authenticated`. All changes route through the workflow in [[03-Policy-Change-Management]].
5. **Log every privileged act.** Decisions, overrides, PII reveals, policy changes, role changes. `audit_events` already exists and takes `actor_id` and `actor_type`.

## Conflicting duty pairs

Combinations that must never sit with one person. Worth checking as a query against `users` periodically, not just asserting here.

| Pair | Why |
|---|---|
| Author policy + approve policy | Removes the second pair of eyes entirely |
| Author policy + decision cases | Lets a rule be shaped around a specific borrower |
| Decision a case + approve the same case's override | Self-approval of one's own deviation |
| Manage users + any policy or decision right | Can self-grant the rights needed to do either |
| Operate the system + audit it | Cannot review one's own trail |

## Access review

- Quarterly: every active user's role, against their actual job. Recertified by the role owner, not by the user.
- On exit or transfer: revoke same day. A transferred employee accumulating a second role is the most common way these matrices quietly break.
- Semi-annual: a report of anyone holding a conflicting pair above. Should return zero rows.
- Annual: review of `max_sanction_amount` and `daily_case_limit` per officer.
- Every privileged account gets MFA. This includes `policy_manager` and `credit_head`.

## Known gaps to close

These are tracked with owners in [[07-Policy-Gap-Register]].

- RLS not applied
- No server-side role enforcement
- Sanction limits unenforced
- `[email removed]` bypasses authentication even when Supabase is configured
- No `policy_manager` or `credit_head` role exists yet
- No periodic access review process
- No MFA on any account

title: Technical changes moving from Vahan4Dashboard to Vahan Public Report
summary: The move from Vahan4Dashboard to the new Vahan Public Report/Dashboard introduces CAPTCHA‑gated AJAX filters, richer granular options, and a one‑year‑per‑query limit, making some analyses easier and automation harder.
body:
The move from the old **Vahan4Dashboard** to the new **Vahan Public Report / Dashboard** is not just a new address — the way you interact with the data changed. This page summarises the technical shape of the new portal (documented from the live site on 6 Aug 2026) and reasons through what that makes easier and harder.

> **Note on confidence:** the *new* portal's behaviour below is observed and documented. Some *old*-portal comparisons are general recollection and are marked *(inferred)* — verify against the old page while it is still up (before 15 Aug 2026) if the distinction matters to you.

## The new portal's technical shape (observed)

- **Two separate public pages** inside one `analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics` app:
  - a **visual Dashboard** — headline cards (Total Registration / Revenue / Permit), chart panels, view toggles (**Registration / Revenue / Comparison**), and a value-scale toggle (**Actual / Crore / Lakh / Thousand**);
  - a **Report builder** — the filter-driven cross-tab documented in this guide.
- **CAPTCHA-gated and session-bound** report generation — you solve an image CAPTCHA, and long idle sessions can time out.
- **Cascading AJAX dropdowns** — **State drives RTO**; Maker and the Y/X-Axis lists load only *after* the page/selection, via JavaScript.
- **Cross-tab control** — you choose the **Y-Axis (rows)** and **X-Axis (columns)** to shape the output table.
- **Expanded, granular filter set** — Archived Flag, EV Type, Fitness-valid toggle, Delhi-NCR toggle, detailed Fuel blends (E20, hybrids, dual-fuel), full Emission-norm ladder (incl. tractor/CEV), and a long Owner-Type list. See [Report filters]([[03-Report-Filters|03-report-filters]].md).
- **Scope** — registration data from **1970**, covering RTOs on Vahan 4.0 / Sarathi 4.0; **one-year span per query**.

## ✅ What becomes easier

- **Quick visual reads without building a query** — the public Dashboard gives charts and headline totals with a couple of toggles; no login needed.
- **Finer slicing** — the richer filter set lets you isolate, say, *E20 petrol two-wheelers*, *pure-EV three-wheelers*, or *BS VI heavy goods vehicles* directly, rather than post-processing a coarse export.
- **EV and emissions analysis** — dedicated EV Type plus the detailed fuel/emission lists make clean-mobility cuts much more direct.
- **Clear table shaping** — explicit Y-/X-axis choice makes the output cross-tab predictable.
- **One long history in one place** — data back to 1970 under a single portal.

## ⚠️ What becomes harder

- **Automation / bulk extraction** — CAPTCHA + session binding, and dropdowns that only populate via JavaScript, make programmatic or scripted access harder than the old page *(inferred: the old Vahan4Dashboard was widely scraped)*. Prefer the on-screen UI; if you need bulk data, check with NIC for an official data route rather than working around the CAPTCHA.
- **Multi-year time series** — the **one-year-per-query** limit means you run one query per year and stitch the results yourself.
- **Findability** — several footer links (**Terms of Use, Sitemap, FAQs**) are dead `#` [[Placeholders|placeholders]], there's no on-page search/sort, and **RTO / Maker** lists appear only after you make a selection.
- **Consistency across pages** — the same value can be spelled differently on the Dashboard vs the Report page (e.g. `ELECTRIC(BOV)` vs `ELECTRIC BOV`), and a few labels are inconsistent or typo'd (e.g. `Snorked Ladders`). See [Known issues]([[05-Known-Issues|05-known-issues]].md).
- **Breakage of old setups** — any bookmarks, saved queries, or scripts pointing at `vahan4dashboard` stop working after **15 August 2026**.

## Impact on scraping and enterprise use

The old Vahan4Dashboard was widely scraped — many open-source scrapers and paid "registration intelligence" services were built on it. The new portal changes that:

- **Casual scraping gets materially harder.** CAPTCHA-gating, session binding, and dropdowns that only populate via JavaScript mean a simple HTTP scraper no longer works — you'd need a full headless browser plus CAPTCHA handling. This appears deliberate.
- **Existing enterprise pipelines break.** Auto OEMs tracking competitor registrations, NBFCs and insurers scoring markets, and used-car platforms sizing supply — anyone who automated the old page has to re-engineer after 15 Aug 2026, at higher cost and fragility (any label or layout change breaks a scraper).
- **But only aggregates are exposed.** The public portal serves **anonymised, aggregate** statistics — no owner personal data. Scraping it yields market/registration aggregates, not the personal RC/DL details the old *bulk-data* policy once sold (and that privacy law now restricts).
- **The sustainable enterprise path is official access, not scraping** — especially under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023. That points toward a paid/official data service; see the illustrative **[Paid API scenario]([[07-Paid-API-Scenario|07-paid-api-scenario]].md)**.

## Migration tips

1. **Swap the URLs** — replace old `vahan4dashboard` links with the new [Public Report](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/vahanpublicreport?lang=en) and [Public Dashboard](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/publicdashboard/vahan?lang=en). See [What's changing]([[01-Whats-Changing|01-whats-changing]].md).
2. **Re-plan any automation** — expect to redo old scripts against the new AJAX/CAPTCHA flow, or seek an official bulk-data option from NIC (`parivahan[dot]analytics[at]nic[dot]in`).
3. **For trends over years**, budget one query per year (the 1-year limit) and combine the outputs.
4. **Re-verify your filters** — the option lists are richer and some names differ; confirm the exact values you rely on against [Report filters]([[03-Report-Filters|03-report-filters]].md).

title: Vahan4Dashboard discontinuation and new public dashboard
summary: Vahan4Dashboard will be discontinued on 15 August 2026 and replaced by the new Public Dashboard on analytics.parivahan.gov.in.
body:
## The official notice

MoRTH has posted this on the old Vahan4Dashboard:

> 📢 **IMPORTANT NOTICE:** The new Public Dashboard is now available. **Vahan4Dashboard will be discontinued after 15 August 2026.** Please use the new dashboard for the latest data and features. For any issues, please contact: **[email removed]**

## Old → New

| Thing | Old location (retiring) | New location |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive report builder | `vahan.parivahan.gov.in/vahan4dashboard/vahan/view/reportview.xhtml` | [`analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/vahanpublicreport`](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/vahanpublicreport?lang=en) |
| Visual charts dashboard | (old app) | [`analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/publicdashboard/vahan`](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/publicdashboard/vahan?lang=en) |

Both new pages live inside the same **`analytics.parivahan.gov.in`** application. The **Public Report** is the report *builder* (pick filters → get a data table); the **Public Dashboard** is the *visual* view (headline cards and charts).

## Timeline

- **Now:** both old and new work.
- **After 15 August 2026:** the old Vahan4Dashboard is discontinued. Move any bookmarks, saved queries, or scraping scripts to the new portal before then.

## What stays the same

- The underlying data is still **VAHAN / Vahan 4.0** — MoRTH's national vehicle-registration database, built by NIC. State Registers feed a National Register.
- Coverage is still RTOs running on **Vahan 4.0 and Sarathi 4.0**, with data from **1970**.
- It still counts **registrations**, not sales.

title: Six sigma core concepts
summary: Six sigma core concepts cover quality, Y = f(x), process stability, cause validation, wastes, and RTY.
body:
## Quality The ISO 9000 definition I work from: **quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of an object fulfils requirements.** ### Stated and unstated needs | Type | Rough share | What it means | |------|-------------|---------------| | Stated | 20% | What the customer explicitly asks for | | Unstated / implied | 80% | What the customer expects but never says | Stated needs are about a fifth of what a customer wants. Unstated does not mean unknown. It means implied: things the customer assumes will happen and only mentions when they don't. The company that wins is the one that delivers the unstated needs at the most economical and sustainable cost, and works them out before the customer complains. ### Quality management cycle ```mermaid graph LR A[Measure
Data] --> B[Monitor] B --> C[Review] C --> D[Improve /
Action] D --> E[Control] E --> A ``` Data that passes through several hands without changing the customer's outcome is non-value-added work. Collecting and processing data nobody acts on is waste too. ## Process and system - **Process:** a sequence of activities that converts input into something the customer wants. - **System:** a chain of inter-related processes that starts with the customer and ends with the customer. The test for value added is simple: would the customer pay for this step? | | What it is | What I do with it | |---|---|---| | **Input** | The X's: causes, controllable factors | Control | | **Output** | The Y: result, response | Measure | ## Measuring performance - **Efficiency** = Output / Input × 100. How much I got out of what I put in. - **Effectiveness** = **DIRFT**, Do It Right First Time. No rework, no second attempt. ### TGR and TGW | | Stands for | Direction | |---|---|---| | **TGR** | Things Gone Right | Increase these | | **TGW** | Things Gone Wrong | Decrease these | TGW shows me what to fix. TGR shows me what is working and worth copying into the next product or process. Tracking both turns experience into something the next team can use. The principle underneath all of it: **output is measured, input is controlled.** I can't change the output directly. I change the inputs and the output follows. ## Y = f(x) > **Y = f(x)**: the output (Y) is a function of the inputs (X's). In Six Sigma I control only the X's, never the Y directly. - X = the controllable causes, where I can act - Y = the result I measure - The problem sits in the X's ### 7M + 1E input categories | # | Factor | Lending example | Controllable? | |---|--------|-----------------|---------------| | 1 | Men | Field and credit officer skill, officer capacity | Yes | | 2 | Material | Documents, KYC papers, application forms | Yes | | 3 | Money | Sanction limits, funds available for disbursement | Yes | | 4 | Management | Approval authority, delegation matrix | Yes | | 5 | Machine | Loan origination system, CRM, portals | Yes | | 6 | Method | SOP for credit appraisal or collections | Yes | | 7 | Measurement | TAT tracking, MIS, defect counts | Yes | | +1 | Environment | Regulation, market conditions, competition | No, uncontrollable (UC) | ### Ishikawa (fishbone, cause and effect) diagram ```mermaid graph LR Men --> Y["Effect (Y)"] Material --> Y Money --> Y Management --> Y Machine --> Y Method --> Y Measurement --> Y Environment["Environment
(UC)"] -.-> Y ``` - Group every cause under one of the 7M + 1E branches - All branches point at the effect (Y) - The point of the diagram is to separate controllable causes from uncontrollable ones ## Process stability ### Two types of cause | Cause type | Also called | Controllable? | What to do | |------------|-------------|---------------|------------| | **Special cause** | Assignable cause | Yes | Find it and fix it | | **Common cause** | Chance cause | No, tied to the environment | Expensive and very hard to fix | I list every X and mark it **C** (controllable, special) or **UC** (uncontrollable, common). **A process is stable when only common (chance) causes are acting on it, with no special causes present.** ### Automation rule - Don't automate for the sake of automating - **Automate only stable processes.** Then the gain shows up as a better TAT - **Never automate an unstable process.** Automation hides the real problems and makes them run faster ### Process control ```mermaid graph LR A[Controllable X's] --> B[Identify
Critical X's] B --> C[Control] C --> D[Monitor] D --> E[Review /
Improve] E --> F[Sustain] F --> D ``` Process control plus a protected stable process gives an efficient process. Once a process is stable: monitor it, track TGR, identify the critical X's and sustain them. ## Problem-solving method | Step | Tool | Output | |------|------|--------| | 1 | Brainstorming | A long cause list, often around 100 | | 2 | Ishikawa diagram | Causes organised by 7M + 1E | | 3 | Cause validation | Data-backed check that finds the critical X's | | 4 | Identify critical X's | The red ones from the funnel | | 5 | Analytical tools | Use data to confirm and solve | ### Cause validation table For each cause, compare actual data against the specification (the SOP) and colour-code it. | S.No | Category | Cause | Specification (SOP) | Actual | Remark | Colour | |------|----------|-------|---------------------|--------|--------|--------| | 1 | Man | Turnaround time | 20 days | 25 days | Not good | Red | | 2 | Man | Turnaround time | 20 days | 20 days | Borderline | Yellow | | 3 | Man | Turnaround time | 20 days | 10 days | Good | Green | | 4–9 | Machine, Money, Management, Method, Measurement, Material | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | | 10 | Environment | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | The colour decides the order of action. ### The cause funnel ```mermaid graph TD A["100 causes
(brainstorming)"] --> B["70 green
within spec"] A --> C["20 yellow
borderline"] A --> D["10 red
critical X's"] D --> E["Fix these first"] ``` Most brainstormed causes turn out to be within spec. A few are borderline. The handful that fail are the critical X's, and those get fixed first. ## Why-why analysis: three rules 1. **Specific problems only.** Why-why doesn't work on a generic problem. Narrow the scope to one specific failure first. 2. **Occurrences and deductions.** Use it for things that happened ("why did this fail?") and for things that should have happened ("why wasn't this done earlier, why was no action taken?"). 3. **It must end at a manual issue or a system issue.** Manual means human error, a skill gap or a compliance gap. System splits into system design, process design or product design. If my chain ends anywhere else, I haven't gone deep enough. ## Prioritisation ### MoSCoW | Priority | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **Must** | Non-negotiable, do first | | **Should** | Important but not blocking | | **Could** | Nice to have | | **Would / Won't** | Defer to later | The Johari window is also useful for self-awareness and team dynamics: what I know about myself versus what others see. ### Pareto Rank problems by impact and put effort on the vital few causes that drive most of the effect. ## Rolled throughput yield (RTY) RTY is the probability that a unit passes through the **entire** process without a defect at any stage. Multiply the first-pass yield of each stage. Generic loan process example: ```mermaid graph LR A["Enquiry
0.9"] -->|×| B["Application
0.8"] B -->|×| C["Contract
0.7"] C -->|×| D["Payout
0.8"] D --> E["RTY = 0.40"] ``` **RTY = 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.40** Each stage looks fine on its own, between 70% and 90%. End to end, only 40% of units go through clean. The system is weaker than any single step suggests, which is why I look at process efficiency and system efficiency separately. ## Lean > A systematic approach to finding and removing waste (non-value-added activity) through continuous improvement, flowing product only when the customer needs it ("pull"), in pursuit of perfection. ### Lean goals | Goal | In lending terms | |------|------------------| | Zero defects | No sendbacks, no rework, the file moves forward clean | | 100% value add | Every step moves the loan closer to disbursement | | Lot size of one | Process each application as it comes, don't batch | | Customer pull | Work to real demand, not pushed targets | ### Why go Lean - Better customer satisfaction - Higher sales and profit - Long-term health and survival of the company - A lasting competitive edge - Global competition and a constant market focus on quality, cost and delivery (QCD) - Customer expectations keep rising, along with pressure on price ### Five principles of Lean thinking > Do only what creates value the customer is willing to pay for.
