Items 1 to 3 change the data model and should be settled before more screens are built on top of the current shape. The rest can follow.

title: Credit policy for cercit Phase 1
summary: Credit policy for cercit Phase 1 defines hard and soft rules for new car loans to salaried applicants.
body:
# Credit policy — cercit Phase 1

Status: draft for review
Created: 16 Sep 2026
Policy version in code: 2026.08
Related: [[03-Policy-Change-Management]] · [[04-Model-Risk-Management]] · [[07-Policy-Gap-Register]]

---

## Why write this down

The 18 rules in `policy-rule-engine.ts` *are* the credit policy. No document describes them, which means the code is the only statement of what cercit will and will not lend against. That is backwards: the document should be the policy and the code its implementation, so the two can be reconciled and a reviewer can challenge a threshold without reading TypeScript.

This document states the policy as currently implemented, and flags where the implementation disagrees with itself.

## Product scope

| Dimension | Phase 1 |
|---|---|
| Product | New car loans only |
| Segment | Salaried, single applicant |
| Source | Direct leads |
| Excluded | Used vehicles, CV, 3W, top-ups, renewals, restructured, title loans, self-employed, co-applicants |
| Bureau | Mandatory — no file proceeds without one |

Anything outside this needs a policy amendment, not an exception.

## Decision bands

| Band | CIBIL | Outcome | Indicative rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approve | 750–900 | Auto-approve subject to all hard rules passing | 8.99% |
| Maybe | 650–749 | Route to officer review | 9.90% |
| Reject | 300–649 | Auto-decline | Not offered |

Rate is then loaded by employer category — A +0.00%, B +0.40%, C +1.25%. Band caps on LTV, FOIR and tenure interact with category caps; the tighter of the two applies.

## The rule set

Nine hard rules and nine soft. A hard failure declines the file regardless of model grade. A soft failure flags for review and can affect pricing but does not by itself decline.

### Hard rules

| Rule | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `AGE_MIN` | Applicant ≥ 21 | Contractual capacity and income stability |
| `BUREAU_FLOOR` | Score ≥ 650 | Below this, observed default rates do not support the product. Also the backstop for a known model weakness — see below. |
| `FOIR_LIMIT` | Fixed obligations ≤ 50% of income | Repayment capacity ceiling |
| `LTV_LIMIT` | Loan ≤ 120% of ex-showroom | On-road funding ceiling, covering registration and insurance |
| `NO_SEVERE_DPD` | No 90+ DPD or write-off in 12 months | Recent severe delinquency is the strongest single predictor |
| `GOVT_EMPLOYEE_CHECK` | Govt applicants need 3+ years permanent service | Excludes contract and probationary staff whose tenure looks stable but is not |
| `FREE_INCOME_FLOOR` | ≥ 15% of net salary remains after all EMIs including the proposed one | FOIR alone passes thin files at low incomes; this is the absolute floor |
| `TENURE_CAP` | Max 84 months; up to 120 only for a govt employee on a car under Rs 12L | Long tenures on depreciating assets go underwater |
| `LTV_100_SALARIED` | Above 100% of on-road needs verified salary and FOIR within limit; above 90% without verified income fails | Caps unverified-income exposure |

### Soft rules

| Rule | Threshold | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `AGE_MAX` | ≤ 65 at maturity | Review; may shorten tenure |
| `BUREAU_GOOD` | ≥ 700 for preferential terms | Pricing |
| `FOIR_OPTIMAL` | ≤ 40% for best rates | Pricing |
| `NO_RECENT_DPD` | No 30/60 DPD in 6 months | Review flag |
| `LOW_BOUNCES` | No bounces in statement period | Review flag |
| `SALARY_REGULAR` | Salary credits in 5+ of last 6 months | Review flag |
| `EMPLOYER_VERIFIED` | Employer on the verified master | Review flag; drives category |
| `CC_SERVICING` | Card not serviced at minimum-due only | Review flag — revolving behaviour predicts stress |
| `BUREAU_RECALIBRATED` | ≥ 700 for bank-grade terms; 650–699 priced as NBFC | Pricing, post Feb-2026 recalibration (~50 point industry drop) |

## Known inconsistencies

Three, surfaced by writing this down. Each needs a decision, not a code change made quietly.

**FOIR base is ambiguous.** `FOIR_LIMIT` is described in code as "Fixed obligations ≤ 50% of *gross* income". The project specification says FOIR max 50% on *net* salary. These are materially different — a 50% gross FOIR is far more permissive than 50% net. Whichever is intended, both the code comment and the spec must say the same thing, and the `FREE_INCOME_FLOOR` rule (defined on net) should use a consistent base.

**LTV is measured on two different denominators.** `LTV_LIMIT` caps at 120% of *ex-showroom*. `LTV_100_SALARIED` caps at 100% of *on-road*. Both are legitimate measures and they are not comparable. A file can pass one and fail the other in ways that are hard to reason about. The policy should state which is the primary control and what the other is doing.

**Tenure cap interacts with the band cap.** `TENURE_CAP` allows 84 months, while `rate_grid` carries `max_tenure_months` of 96 for the Approve band and 84 for Maybe, and employer categories cap at 84 or 60. Three sources for one number. The rule should state the precedence explicitly: the tightest of rule, band, and category.

## Model interaction

The model advises; policy decides. In practice that means:

- The model produces P(30+DPD), mapped to grades A (<1%), B (<2.5%), C (<6%), D (<15%), E (≥15%)
- A hard rule failure declines the file whatever the grade
- A grade E file passing all hard rules still goes to officer review, not auto-approve

One coupling must be recorded rather than left implicit: the model scores a clean file with a single blemish — bureau 640, nothing else adverse — as grade A, because in the training data such files mostly perform. `BUREAU_FLOOR` is what catches this. That rule is therefore load-bearing on a model weakness, and cannot be relaxed without first retraining or revalidating the model. See [[04-Model-Risk-Management]].

## Deviations and exceptions

A deviation is a documented departure from policy for one case. It is not a policy change.

- Only `credit_manager` and above may approve a deviation, and never on their own case
- Every deviation records the rule deviated from, the reason, the approver, and compensating factors
- Hard rules on `BUREAU_FLOOR`, `NO_SEVERE_DPD` and `FREE_INCOME_FLOOR` should be non-deviable — if they need deviating regularly, the threshold is wrong and belongs in a policy change
- Deviations are reviewed monthly. A rule with a persistently high deviation rate is a standing agenda item for the Policy Manager.

`override_logs` exists in the schema for this. It is not yet wired to a rule-level reason.

## Delegation of authority

To be set. The schema already carries `users.max_sanction_amount` and `daily_case_limit`, and nothing enforces either. Proposed shape:

| Role | Sanction limit | Deviation authority |
|---|---|---|
| Underwriter | Up to their configured limit | None |
| Manager | Higher limit | Soft rules only |
| Credit Head | All | Soft and non-listed hard rules |
| Risk Committee | — | Policy change only |

Enforcement must be server-side — see [[02-Access-Control-and-SoD]].

## Review

Annual, and on any of: an RBI change affecting credit norms, a bureau recalibration, a model version promotion, a material shift in portfolio performance, or three consecutive months of elevated deviation on any rule.

title: Vahan Data API requirements rules and roadmap
summary: Vahan Data API plan outlines requirements, rules, and roadmap for government and private use.
body:
> **Scope:** An end-to-end plan (requirements → design → build → deploy) plus a full financial plan for an **aggregate** Vahan vehicle-registration **Data API**, from two angles: **(A) the Government operating it** (MoRTH/NIC, aiming for self-sufficiency) and **(B) a private company** building a product on top.
> ⚠️ **Read this first.** All forward-looking figures are **illustrative estimates on stated assumptions**, not official budgets, forecasts, or a MoRTH/NIC plan. The only hard facts are cited (e.g. the 2019 policy's ₹111.4 cr / 142 buyers).

## Requirements

### Functional Requirements
*   **Endpoints:** RESTful JSON endpoints delivering authenticated aggregate Vahan vehicle registration metrics.
    *   `GET /api/v1/vehicles/registrations/summary`: National, state, and district-level aggregations grouped by time periods (daily, monthly, yearly).
    *   `GET /api/v1/vehicles/fuel-types`: Breakdown of registrations categorized by fuel type (EV, Petrol, Diesel, CNG, Hybrid).
    *   `GET /api/v1/vehicles/vehicle-classes`: Aggregates by vehicle classification (Two-Wheeler, Passenger Four-Wheeler, Commercial, Transport, Agricultural).
    *   `GET /api/v1/vahan/analytics/trends`: Historical time-series data for trend analysis and forecasting models.
*   **Filters:** Query parameters to refine datasets dynamically:
    *   `state_code`: ISO-3166-2 compliant state identifier.
    *   `district_code`: MoRTH standard district ID.
    *   `from_date` / `to_date`: ISO 8601 date range filters (`YYYY-MM-DD`).
    *   `fuel_category`: Multi-select fuel type filter.
    *   `vehicle_category`: CMVR vehicle class filter.
*   **Formats:** Primary output format is JSON (UTF-8). CSV and Parquet export capabilities for analytical queries exceeding 100,000 records, delivered via async S3-compatible signed URLs.
*   **Dashboards:** Built-in React-based visual analytics portal embedded within the Developer Console showing real-time API call volumes, error rates, popular queries, and dynamic geospatial heatmaps of EV adoption and commercial fleet movements.

### Non-Functional Requirements
*   **Uptime / SLA:** 99.95% availability for production tiers, measured on a monthly basis, excluding planned maintenance windows.
*   **Latency:** P95 response time < 500 milliseconds for aggregated queries; P99 < 1200 milliseconds for complex multi-parameter analytical requests.
*   **Scale:** System architecture designed to handle up to 5,000 requests per second (RPS) at peak loads with horizontal auto-scaling enabled on containerized worker nodes.
*   **Security:** Mandatory TLS 1.3 encryption in transit, AES-256 encryption at rest. OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect (OIDC) protocol implementation integrated with India's national API gateways.

---

## Bill of Materials (BoM)

| Component Category | Component Name / Technology | Indicative Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Infra / Cloud** | MeghRaj (GI Cloud) / NIC National Cloud | Sovereign government cloud hosting for compute, storage, and database tiers. |
| **API Gateway** | API Setu / NAPIX (NIC API eXchange) | Rate limiting, authentication validation, routing, and developer traffic management. |
| **Data Pipeline** | Apache Kafka, Apache Spark, Airflow | Real-time and batch ETL pipelines streaming anonymized aggregates from Vahan DB. |
| **Security** | WAF, HashiCorp Vault, HSM | Web Application Firewall, secrets management, and cryptographic key storage. |
| **Docs & Portal** | Swagger/OpenAPI 3.0, Developer Portal | Interactive API documentation, sandbox environment, and credential self-service. |
| **People / Roles** | DPO, Cloud Architects, SecOps, DBA | Governance, infrastructure maintenance, security monitoring, and database tuning. |
| **IT Vendor** | Empanelled Vendor (TCS/Infosys/Wipro/TechM) | Custom software development, pipeline maintenance, and L2/L3 technical support. |

---

## How the Government Runs It

*   **Delivery Model on API Setu/NAPIX + MeghRaj:** The Vahan Data API infrastructure resides natively inside NIC's MeghRaj cloud environment, utilizing the core routing and consent engines of API Setu and NAPIX. This avoids building redundant gateways and ensures direct integration with national digital public infrastructure (DPI).
*   **NIC Role vs IT-Vendor Role:** 
    *   *NIC (National Informatics Centre):* Acts as the sovereign data owner, system administrator, and security controller. NIC retains root access, oversees master data governance, and manages overarching compliance.
    *   *Empanelled IT Vendors (TCS / Infosys / Wipro / Tech Mahindra):* Deployed via work orders to handle application development, microservices tuning, CI/CD pipeline management, bug fixes, and tier-2/3 technical support under NIC oversight.
*   **GFR-2017 Procurement:** Procurements for vendor resources, specialized software licenses, and hardware expansions are executed strictly in compliance with the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, leveraging competitive bidding via Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portals or limited tender mechanisms for empanelled public-sector IT partners.
*   **Operations & Maintenance (O&M):** Run via a 24x7 Joint Operations Center (JOC) comprising NIC operations teams and vendor embedded engineers, governed by strict SLAs for incident response, patch management, and disaster recovery drills.

---

## System Audits

*   **CERT-In Security Audit:** Mandatory comprehensive vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) conducted prior to initial production launch and repeated annually (or post major architectural changes) by a CERT-In-empanelled auditor.
*   **DPDP Data Audit & DPIA:** Although the Vahan Data API exposes **aggregate-only (non-personal)** data, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and an independent data audit are conducted to verify zero leakage of personally identifiable information (PII) or re-identification risks, satisfying the spirit of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023.
*   **Data-Quality Audits:** Automated daily reconciliation scripts comparing Vahan production database aggregate counts with API output logs to verify mathematical accuracy, missing records, and schema drift.
*   **Audit Cadence:** 
    *   *Security Audits:* Annual (CERT-In empanelled).
    *   *Privacy/Data Audits:* Bi-annual internal review; Annual third-party check.
    *   *Data Quality Checks:* Continuous / Daily automated runs.

---

## Laws, Regulations & Acts Applicable

*   **Motor Vehicles Act & CMVR:** Governs national vehicle registration frameworks, vehicle classes, and statutory transport data parameters.
*   **DPDP Act 2023 + Rules 2025:** Establishes compliance boundaries; while aggregate data is exempt from core processing constraints, strict controls ensure no residual PII is exposed.
*   **IT Act 2000:** Governs electronic records, digital signatures, cyber security infractions, and intermediaries' liabilities.
*   **RTI Act 2005:** Determines parameters for public access to information, balancing open government mandates with commercial confidentiality and state security.
*   **CERT-In Directions (2022):** Mandates incident reporting within 6 hours of a cyber security event and enforces logs retention policies (180 days).
*   **GFR-2017:** Regulates financial management, procurement transparency, asset management, and vendor accountability for public outlays.

---

## Enterprise Enforcement

*   **API Keys & OAuth 2.0:** All incoming consumer requests must authenticate via cryptographic API keys paired with OAuth 2.0 JWT tokens issued upon verified organizational onboarding.
*   **Signed Agreements & T&Cs:** Consumers must execute a binding electronic Service Level Agreement (e-SLA) and Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) forbidding illicit scraping, cross-referencing with other datasets to de-anonymize individuals, or selling raw data payloads.
*   **Rate Limits & Quotas:** Enforced strictly at the API Gateway layer (e.g., Free Tier: 100 req/min; Enterprise Tier: 5,000 req/min), throttling abusive or anomalous traffic spikes instantly.
*   **Audit Logs:** Immutable, append-only access logs streaming to a centralized SIEM tool (integrated with NIC SOC) capturing caller IP, timestamp, endpoint, query parameters, and response status codes.
*   **Penalties:** Violation of terms triggers immediate API key revocation, blacklisting of the entity, forfeiture of security deposits, and potential legal prosecution under the IT Act 2000.
*   **Licensing Tiers:** Segmented into Public/Research (Free, rate-limited), Commercial Enterprise (Paid subscription via BharatKosh/Non-Tax Revenue portal), and Government-to-Government (G2G - Exempt/Unlimited).

---

## Resale-Market Restrictions

*   **Anti-Redistribution / Scraping Clauses:** Legal terms explicitly prohibit wholesale mirroring, secondary redistribution of raw API output dumps, or public scraping of derived endpoints.
*   **Attribution Requirements:** Private applications, research papers, or commercial dashboards utilizing the API must prominently display: *"Data sourced via official Vahan API, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), Govt. of India."*
*   **Sub-Licensing Limits:** Downstream commercial users are barred from embedding Vahan aggregate data into standalone white-label data products intended for re-sale as "raw vehicle data." Data must only be consumed as part of higher-order analytical value-adds (e.g., logistics route optimization, EV charging infrastructure planning).
*   **Policing Mechanisms:** Automated graph analysis on query patterns to spot abnormal extraction routines (e.g., systematic enumeration of all district/date permutations), coupled with manual spot-checks of downstream commercial products by the compliance team.

---

## Long-Run Sustainability & Survival

*   **Funding Model:** A hybrid financial model where basic G2G and academic queries remain subsidized or free, while commercial tiers incur tiered usage fees pooled into a dedicated revolving fund managed by MoRTH/NIC for infrastructure upgrades and engineering talent retention.
*   **Versioning:** Strict semantic versioning (`/api/v1/`, `/api/v2/`) ensuring a mandatory minimum 12-month deprecation notice window for older API iterations, complete with backward-compatibility wrappers where feasible.
*   **Data-Refresh Governance:** Real-time stream processing synchronizing overnight batch dumps and event-driven updates from state-level Vahan registers to guarantee zero data staleness.
*   **Avoiding Obsolescence:** Continuous architectural reviews, transition to cloud-native serverless functions where applicable, and regular developer feedback loops via GitHub Discussions and annual stakeholder roundtables.

---

## Risks & Mitigations

| Risk Category | Risk Description | Impact | Mitigation Strategy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Privacy / DPDP** | Accidental exposure of personal vehicle owner details via complex multi-parameter aggregations. | High | Implement strict post-aggregation query checks (e.g., suppression threshold: query results with fewer than 10 records return null) and regular DPIA audits. |
| **Infrastructure** | Traffic surge or DDoS attack crashing the central API Gateway during peak vehicle registration periods. | High | Deploy Web Application Firewall (WAF), rate-limiting tokens at NAPIX, and leverage MeghRaj auto-scaling worker pools. |
| **Commercial Abuse** | Third-party private products illegally scraping and redistributing bulk aggregate datasets. | Medium | Enforce strict OAuth authentication, behavioral anomaly detection on query frequency, and rapid API-key revocation. |
| **Vendor Lock-in** | Over-reliance on a single empanelled IT vendor for microservice maintenance. | Medium | Mandate open-source core frameworks, containerization (Docker/Kubernetes), complete documentation, and knowledge transfer clauses in GFR contracts. |
| **Data Drift** | Discrepancies between legacy state Vahan databases and centralized aggregate reporting nodes. | Medium | Implement automated daily schema validation, reconciliation data pipelines, and alerting alerts for data engineers. |

---

## Deployment Roadmap

| Phase | Milestone Name | Key Activities | Indicative Duration |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Phase 1** | Requirements & Scoping | Stakeholder consultations, finalization of aggregate schema, legal drafting of T&Cs and DPIA framework. | Weeks 1 – 4 |
| **Phase 2** | Architecture & Design | API design (OpenAPI 3.0), database view optimizations, security architecture mapping on MeghRaj. | Weeks 5 – 8 |
| **Phase 3** | Build & Integration | Core pipeline development by NIC & IT vendor, API Gateway setup on NAPIX, sandbox environment provisioning. | Weeks 9 – 18 |
| **Phase 4** | Security Audits | CERT-In empanelled VAPT, internal privacy audit, remediation of vulnerabilities. | Weeks 19 – 22 |
| **Phase 5** | Pilot Launch | Limited rollout to selected government departments and tier-1 enterprise partners for stress testing. | Weeks 23 – 26 |
| **Phase 6** | General Availability (GA) | Public launch on API Setu, activation of monetization tiers, onboarding of commercial consumers via Developer Portal. | Week 27 |
| **Phase 7** | Scale & Operations | Continuous monitoring, feature expansions, automated schema updates, and bi-annual compliance checks. | Ongoing (Continuous) |

---

## Sources (for the verified anchors)

- MoRTH bulk-data precedent (₹111.4 cr, 142 buyers): [Deccan Herald](https://www.deccanherald.com/india/govt-earned-over-rs-100-crore-by-selling-vehicle-owner-data-to-private-firms-950293.html) · [Internet Freedom Foundation](https://internetfreedom.in/morth-bulk-data-sharing-policy-scrapped/)
- NBFCs registered with RBI (~9,000): [RBI NBFC list / FIDC](https://www.fidcindia.org.in/list-of-nbfcs/)
- General insurers (25): [IRDAI Annual Report 2024-25 highlights](https://algatesinsurance.in/irdai-annual-report-2024-25-highlights/)
- Dealers (~15,000 / ~30,000 outlets): [FADA](https://fada.in/)
- Per-request RC-API market (EKO ~₹3/verification; Surepass, Signzy): [EKO](https://eps.eko.in/products/vehicle-rc-verification-api) · [Surepass](https://surepass.io/vehicle-rc-verification-api/)
- Government API infra (API Setu 8,036 APIs; NAPIX; MeghRaj): [API Setu — NeGD](https://negd.gov.in/our_projects/api-setu/) · [NIC NAPIX](https://www.nic.gov.in/service/napix/)
- Registered vehicles (~354 M, 2022): [CEIC](https://www.ceicdata.com/en/india/number-of-registered-motor-vehicles/registered-motor-vehicles-total)
- DPDP Act 2023 + Rules 2025: [EY — Decoding the DPDP Act](https://www.ey.com/en_in/insights/cybersecurity/decoding-the-digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023)

---
*Companion material: the technical guide & analysis repository (private) — `github.com/cercit/Vahan_2.0` — and the submission proposal `Vahan_Data_Proposal.docx` in this workspace.*

title: Minimum viable product
summary: Minimum viable product is the smallest version that lets a real user complete a real job and yields learning unavailable otherwise.
body:
# MVP: Minimum Viable Product

## At a Glance
- **Core question:** As the first PM at a company with a 0-to-1 product, how do you test viability before spending a year and budget building it? Answer: a ladder — discovery → prototype → MVP → alpha → beta → public launch.
- **MVP definition:** The smallest thing that lets a real user complete a real job and lets you learn something you could not learn any other way. Examples: Zomato’s first MVP was a PDF of restaurant menus; Ola’s was a man at an airport counter phoning drivers; Dropbox’s was a video with no product behind it.
- **Prototype vs MVP:** Prototype is the broader term. Not all prototypes are MVPs, but every MVP is a working, high‑fidelity prototype. Prototype asks “should we build this?” MVP asks “what is the least we can ship to learn?”
- **Alpha vs beta:** Alpha = people you know (family, friends, colleagues) in a controlled setting. Beta = strangers who opted in, still not the general public. The key difference is relationship, not size.
- **Convenience vs comfort:** A comfort product’s disappearance leaves life basically unchanged (Zepto, Blinkit, Instamart). A convenience product’s disappearance drags you back into a genuinely worse process (Ola/Uber puts you back into negotiating with auto drivers). Comfort products must manufacture habit; convenience products inherit pain.
- **Ten MVP types with real examples:**  
  1. Landing Page – Robinhood (waitlist)  
  2. Explainer Video – Dropbox (demo video)  
  3. Concierge – Airbnb (founders hosted guests)  
  4. Wizard of Oz – Zappos (founder bought shoes from stores)  
  5. Piecemeal – Groupon (WordPress + PDFs + email) / Zomato (menu PDF)  
  6. Single‑Feature – Instagram (photo + filter + share)  
  7. Email – Product Hunt (daily list emailed to friends)  
  8. Marketing‑Led – Superhuman (exclusivity queue) / One8 by Virat Kohli (founder as brand)  
  9. Physical – Paper Boat (small‑batch traditional drinks)  
  10. Community‑Led – Notion (indie hackers) / Cult.fit (fitness community)  
- **Failure patterns:** Juicero (over‑engineered), Yik Yak (untested abuse), Stayzilla (wrong market), Hike (ignored user signal), Foodpanda (operations could not scale). Each maps to an avoidable mistake.
- **Four conflict types for product storytelling:** user vs process (Khatabook), user vs competition (Zerodha), user vs deadline (Dunzo/Amazon Prime), user vs technical limits (Razorpay).

## Why this matters
All prior weeks were input work — understanding users, competitors, market sizing. This is the hinge: I put a version of my idea in front of a human and watch what they do. Research tells me what people say; an MVP tells me what people do. In interviews, “how would I validate this?” is the most common follow‑up. A weak answer says “I would build an MVP and get feedback”. A strong answer says “I would run a concierge MVP with twenty users in one office building for two weeks, and my success bar is that at least eight of them complete three or more tasks a week without a remainder”. This gives me the vocabulary, examples, and judgement to give that strong answer. Everything downstream depends on my picking the right MVP now.

The skill of getting something into a user’s hands with almost no resources and reading the result honestly is what founders do on day one and what PMs do every time they receive an unvalidated idea. Ex‑founders often make good PMs; PMs often become founders because of this shared ability.

## Core Concepts

### The 0‑to‑1 problem
I am the first PM at a company with a new, unlaunched product. Founder has an idea, team of ~10. How do I establish whether it will work? The requirement was five executable steps, not a single line. These approaches were produced (summarized):

| Approach | What it is | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Internal dogfooding / alpha | Team uses product | Fast, free, no risk | Team is not real user |
| Sampling | Give free samples, collect feedback | Real users | Feedback is politeness, not demand |
| Controlled beta | Launch to small group, collect feedback | Realistic behaviour, contained blast radius | Only works if group matches persona |
| Competitor research | Study similar products first | Cheap, avoids re‑solving solved problems | Tells you past, not whether your wedge works |
| MVP proper | Build minimum version, launch, polish later | Produces behavioural evidence | Easy to under‑define “minimum” and ship something useless |
| Time‑boxed alpha + beta | Ten‑day trial inside team + outside users | Forces decision date | Ten days may be shorter than natural usage cycle |
| Concept testing with prototypes | Survey using prototypes | Scales to many opinions | Stated intent, not revealed behaviour |
| Pre‑order / waitlist validation | Let customers pre‑book and pay before launch | Money is strongest signal | Requires credible story and real launch date |
| Live usability observation | Watch users interact in real time | Catches what users will never tell you | Small sample, needs working artefact |

I note that the pre‑order and live‑observation answers show the most product judgement because they replace opinion with behaviour. The consolidated lifecycle I follow is: identify problem → validate need → build MVP → test with real customers → collect feedback → measure metric. Note that “build” is step three, not step one.

### Solo‑founder version
Same question but you are a solo entrepreneur with no team, no money, no time. Product: AI‑based daily task tracker via Instagram/WhatsApp/LinkedIn; metric = tasks successfully completed using the app. Class responses:

- Borrow an existing community (e.g., local gym/yoga centre) offering free access in exchange for use.  
- Friends/family with a prototype.
- Paid ads + personalized reels for niche, then beta version.  
- Landing page + short demo videos on LinkedIn/Instagram, manual testing, tight circle of close friends/founder peers for beta, watch key metrics.  
- Social‑media influencers in productivity niche.  
- Sabziwalas and milkwalas who already send bills over WhatsApp (upgrading an existing habit).  
- Free college access, feedback via MS Forms.  
- Seven‑day productivity challenge (event with natural end date).  
- Partner with a few startups to get teams, not individuals.

Teaching point: with no resources, the question shifts from “what should I build?” to “where does a group of people with this exact pain already gather, and what can I hand them tomorrow?”

### Acquisition‑trigger exercise
For each product you use, recall the first time you tried it and the honest reason why. Table:

| Product | First try reason | Underlying driver |
|---|---|---|
| Google Maps | Word of mouth, pre‑installed, opened when lost | Utility, on‑need basis |
| PhonePe / Google Pay | Cashback, scratch cards, referrals, friend asking for money/loan | Incentive to try, utility to stay |
| Uber / Ola | Emergency, auto driver refused ride, could not negotiate, fixed price | Utility |
| Zomato / Swiggy | Laziness, not wanting to find restaurant, ease of use | Convenience |
| Microsoft Excel | Office work, data management, company demanded it | Utility, near‑compulsory |
| Google Drive | Came with Gmail, phone storage full | Utility |
| Zepto / Blinkit / Instamart | Speed, saving time, not wanting to step out | **Comfort** |

Two lessons:
1. The trigger that gets someone in the door is often not the reason they stay. Cashback/scratch cards got a country onto UPI apps; utility kept them. You need both acquisition hook and utility, and you must know which is which.
2. Almost nothing on that list was acquired through advertising. It was word of mouth, pre‑installation, a friend’s request, employer demand, or genuine need. When planning MVP distribution, plan for those mechanisms, not for a media budget you lack.

### Convenience vs comfort
One‑line test: **Comfort is when the product goes away but your life still remains the same.**

- If Ola/Uber disappeared, you go back to standing on a road, being refused by auto drivers, negotiating fare, having no idea what ride should cost → old process was genuinely bad → **convenience**.
- If Zepto/Blinkit/Instamart disappeared, you walk to the corner kirana store, mildly annoying, life not materially worse → **comfort**.

Implications for a PM:
1. **Product vision:** For comfort products you cannot rely on underlying pain; you must build the habit yourself and defend it constantly.
2. **Unit economics:** Comfort products usually compete on speed and price, which is expensive. Quick‑commerce pattern: new users get 5‑7‑minute deliveries + free goodies; after 3‑4 months of 2‑3 orders/week, promise drifts to 10‑12‑15 min. Early speed is a customer acquisition cost, not a service standard.
3. **Fragility:** Comfort product loses to whoever is slightly faster or cheaper because switching costs the user nothing. Convenience product is protected by the memory of how bad the alternative was.

Note: comfort is not a lesser category; quick commerce is enormous. Comfort products are harder — they must manufacture demand rather than absorb it; price that difficulty into your plan.

### Launch ladder: discovery → alpha → beta → public
Steps written on the board:
1. **Discovery** – Ask users, discover needs (surveys, interviews, focus groups). Output: persona, pain points.
2. **Alpha** – Take to friends and family (people you know personally or who work with you). Output: bugs, usability fixes. They are patient but not honest about desire.
3. **Beta** – Take to unknown people in a controlled environment (opted‑in strangers). Commercial example: Play Store beta programme. Output: edge cases, scale data.
4. **Public launch** – Everyone. Output: growth, retention, revenue.

Critical distinction: **relationship**. Alpha users know you; beta users do not. That single change makes beta feedback trustworthy in a way alpha feedback never is.

### Beta programmes: live industry standard
I opened Play Store, searched Uber, scrolled to bottom, and saw “Join the beta program”. What I get:
- App will crash, have bugs (that’s the deal).
- New features not in normal app, sometimes months early.
- Direct access to development and product team (usually an email address to write to).
- Some programmes run a bug bounty (payment for finding defects), usually reserved for security risks that could cost real revenue.
- Occasionally becomes a hiring path (you’re already working with the team).

Privacy: data‑sharing implications are disclosed up front; read documentation before accepting. Not “like donating your blood” — it’s a standardised industry mechanism.

Prompt I used (worth saving):
“I want to try some of the latest B2C beta products. Can you tell me in India which companies offer access to join the beta products, and also give me the link to join those programs. Focus on consumer tech products only.”  
Follow‑up: “Are there consumer products like Meesho, Swiggy, Zomato, Urban Company and others also offering the same?”  
I change “consumer tech” to B2B, edtech, healthtech, or fintech to target my own industry. Programmes surfaced: Google Search Labs, Google Gemini, Amazon Alexa India Hindi beta, WhatsApp beta, Samsung, OpenAI, Revolut India. Blinkit’s beta can already be full, which shows competitors join each other’s beta programmes; it’s normal and sensible for a PM to know where the industry is heading.

Reasons for joining a beta: earn bounty money, try unreleased features, learn what companies think before applying, get in touch with core/PM teams, find loopholes to propose new ones, as a competitor know what’s coming next. Joining one (Truecaller beta, Gemini Spark beta) and writing a short outline a month later is a ready‑made portfolio piece.

### Prototype vs MVP
The natural question: which do we build first, and which is broader?
- **Prototype** is the broader term. Not all prototypes are MVPs, but all MVPs are prototypes — specifically, high‑fidelity working prototypes of your product.
- MVP is a subset of prototype. By definition, an MVP is nothing more exotic than a working prototype.

Full comparison:

| Aspect | Prototype | MVP |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Validate idea or design direction | Test core value with minimal features |
| Who uses it | Internal teams, limited stakeholders | Early adopters, real test users |
| Development level | Low or medium fidelity — click‑through, mock UI | Fully functional, but limited in scope |
| Features included | Only visuals or basic flow, no real functionality | Only must‑have core features |
| Working? | May or may not actually work | Must work |
| Action completion | User can complete *partial* actions | User must be able to complete the *full* action |
| Revenue | May or may not show how money is made | Must clearly establish how business earns revenue |
| Testing focus | UX flow, concept feedback | Product‑market fit, real usage, willingness to pay |
| Output / goal | Decide whether to build it at all | Learn what users want most, iterate fast |
| Time in lifecycle | Earliest design stage | After prototype, before alpha |

Practical lines:
- “Prototype you can use with internal testers or limited stakeholders. MVP is what is taken to the users. Otherwise the user will not be able to get the value out of your product, and they will not be willing to pay for it.”
- “MVP is just the bare bones, the most basic part that is needed to run your application.”
- I note that a prototype can also show how a new feature would be added to an existing product — not only for new products.
- I confirm that prototype and proof of concept can be used interchangeably in normal PM conversation; Figma and similar wireframing tools are standard for making one (next week).

### Fidelity: low, medium, high
Fidelity = how much detail is captured.
- **Low fidelity** – pen‑and‑paper sketch; no colours, no working clicks, just boxes and arrows showing where a user goes. Example: nine grey wireframe phone screens (scan screen, results list, detail view, comments, search, keyboard entry, events and exhibitions, saved items, profile with settings) joined by blue arrows showing every navigation link. No colour, no branding, no real content — just structure and flow.
- **Medium fidelity** – clickable, greyscale or lightly styled, real structure, placeholder content.
- **High fidelity** – all colours, buttons, and some animations captured; close enough to the real thing that a user reacts to it as a product rather than a drawing.

Rule of thumb: **your fidelity should match the question you are asking**. If the question is “does this flow make sense?”, a paper sketch answers it for free. If the question is “will people pay for this?”, you need something high fidelity and working — i.e., an MVP.

### What an MVP must contain (and what it must not)
Working definition of “minimum”:
> **The most basic functionality that can completely deliver the user value**, such that the user can finish the job they came to do.

My dos and don’ts: build functionality to complete the user story, rather than leaving the user incomplete. A half‑finished journey teaches me nothing because the user’s drop‑off tells me about my gap, not about their desire.

Three tests for any proposed MVP:
1. **Can one real user complete one real job end‑to‑end?** If not, it’s a prototype, not an MVP.
2. **Do you know what number will move if it works?** In the task‑tracker example, the number was explicitly stated: tasks successfully completed using the app. Launching without knowing your measure is one of the five “don’ts”.
3. **Is it clear how the business would eventually make money?** Firm rule: an MVP should establish the revenue logic even if it does not collect revenue yet. Zomato’s ₹20 delivery charge is the model.

### Keeping operations light
Repeated pattern across success stories:
- Ola did not buy cars; partnered with existing drivers, took commission.
- Amazon did not build warehouses first; packed books itself, used postal service.
- Airbnb did not build property inventory; listed founders’ own apartment, used Facebook Marketplace groups.
- Zomato did not build restaurant integrations; photographed menus, made PDF.

Principle: **keep your operations light until you have scaled to the point where you genuinely need a technology product**. Humans deliver the service first; you learn the process by doing it manually; you get better at it; then you build product around what you learned. Automating a process you do not yet understand is the most expensive mistake for a startup.

Counterweight: a good MVP alone will not take you anywhere. Ola’s airport‑counter idea was not original (Meru Cabs already doing it). Ola won because it replaced the manual MVP with better technology and better operations, and scaled across India. Meru did not, and left the market. Your MVP buys you the right to build the real thing; it is not the real thing.

### Vibe coding as an MVP tool
I learned that this term was introduced because it changes what a non‑engineer PM can produce. **Vibe coding** means asking AI to build the website, application, or mobile product for me by describing what I want. The ISB story below shows what one person built with it in a single placement cycle. For now: the cost of a working MVP has fallen far enough that “I could not build it” is no longer a defensible reason to ship only a slide deck.

## Frameworks & Models

### 1. The launch ladder (discovery → prototype → MVP → alpha → beta → GA)
- **What it is:** sequence of gates a product passes through from idea to public launch, each answering one question.
- **When to use it:** any time you are asked “how would you take this to market?” or “how would you validate this?” It is the backbone of a structured interview answer.

| Stage | Question it answers | Who is involved | What you produce |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discovery | What is the real problem? | Target users, non‑users | Interview notes, survey data, empathy map, persona |
| Prototype | Should we build this at all? | Internal team, a few stakeholders | Sketch or Figma click‑through |
| MVP | What is the least we can launch to learn? | Early adopters, real users | A working, minimal product with a metric |
| Alpha | Is it working well enough internally? | People you know — team, friends, family | Bug list, usability fixes |
| Beta | Is it ready for the real world? | Opted‑in strangers, not the general public | Edge cases, scale and performance data |
| Public launch | Can we serve everyone? | Everyone | Growth, retention, revenue |

**Worked mini‑example — AI task tracker:**  
Discovery: interview twelve working professionals about how they plan a day.  
Prototype: five‑screen Figma flow of the WhatsApp conversation.  
MVP: WhatsApp number where *you* manually send the morning prompt and three nudges, for twenty people from one gym.  
Alpha: your own colleagues, week one.  
Beta: WhatsApp group of fifty strangers from that gym’s member list, week three.  
Metric throughout: tasks completed per user per week.

### 2. Prototype vs MVP vs Alpha vs Beta — the four mnemonics
- **Prototype:** “Should we build this?” — idea validation  
- **MVP:** “What’s the minimum we can launch to learn?” — value testing  
- **Alpha:** “Is it working well enough internally?” — tech and usability check  
- **Beta:** “Is it ready for the real world?” — scale and polish check  

### 3. Alpha launch vs beta launch
| Aspect | Alpha launch | Beta launch |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Test functionality in early, controlled environment | Gather feedback from real users before full release |
| User involvement | Internal team or selected friendly users | Broader external users, still not the general public |
| Development level | Early, functional, may be unstable | Near‑final, stable, may still have bugs |
| Features included | Most key features, not necessarily polished | Almost complete, missing only polish and final touches |
| Testing focus | Bug detection, performance, usability | Edge cases, performance, scale readiness |
| Output / goal | Fix major flaws before wider testing | Validate stability and readiness for full launch |
| Time in lifecycle | Before beta | Just before full public launch |

**Worked mini‑example:** launching a college parcel‑collection app.  
Alpha = you, three friends, two security guards in one hostel block for a week; watching for crashes and confusion.  
Beta = every student in two hostels who signs up via WhatsApp group; watching for what happens at 7 pm when forty parcels arrive at once.

### 4. The ten types of MVP
- **When to use it:** the moment you know what you are uncertain about. Each type answers a different uncertainty — demand, desirability, willingness to pay, usability, operational feasibility.

| Type | How it works | Real example | When to use it | What you should be doing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Landing Page MVP | Single page explaining product; collect emails/sign‑ups | Robinhood — waitlist page validating interest in commission‑free trading | Need to know if anyone cares, and you have nothing built | One clear value proposition, one CTA, measure sign‑up rate against visits |
| Explainer Video MVP | Show product vision in video before building it | Dropbox — 2‑3 min demo video, 75,000+ sign‑ups overnight | Product technically hard to build, must justify build | Keep short, show value moment, track sign‑ups and drop‑off |
| Concierge MVP | Deliver service manually; user knows it is manual | Airbnb — founders personally hosted first three guests | Need to learn service deeply before designing it | Do work by hand, sit with user, write down every pain point |
| Wizard of Oz MVP | User believes it is automated; humans behind curtain | Zappos — founder photographed shoes in local stores, bought and shipped each order himself | Want realistic demand data without building backend | Fake automation convincingly, measure real conversion |
| Piecemeal MVP | Stitch existing tools together to simulate product | Groupon — WordPress, PDFs, email; Zomato — menu PDF over WhatsApp | Need something functional this week with no engineering | Notion, Google Forms, WhatsApp, Sheets, Zapier |
| Single‑Feature MVP | Ship exactly one feature and see if anyone cares | Instagram — photo, filter, share, nothing else | Clear hypothesis about one core behaviour | Pick one user problem and solve it better than anyone |
| Email MVP | Send personalised email with value proposition instead of building | Product Hunt — Ryan Hoover emailed friends daily list of cool products before site existed | Audience small, reachable, specific | Email tight target list, measure clicks and replies |
| Marketing‑Led MVP | Run campaign to validate need before product ready | Superhuman — manufactured FOMO with exclusivity and onboarding queue; One8 by Virat Kohli — founder as walking advertisement | Category crowded, desire is constraint, not capability | Build positioning and early‑access sign‑ups; be own brand ambassador |
| Physical MVP | Small batch of real physical product | Paper Boat — limited local production of traditional Indian drinks | Form factor, taste, packaging, or feel is thing being tested | Small batch, D2C or local channels, watch repeat purchase |
| Community‑Led MVP | Engage community and co‑build with them | Notion — evolved with indie hackers and product communities; Cult.fit and Hyrox in India | Identity and belonging are part of value | Start in niche community — Reddit, Discord, WhatsApp group — and build in the open |

**Common mistake:** confusing concierge and Wizard of Oz. From outside they look identical; the difference is what the **user believes**.  
- Concierge: user knows a person is helping them (Airbnb founders opened their own front door).  
- Wizard of Oz: user thinks the system is automated (Zappos customers believed they were buying from a warehouse).  
Use concierge when you want to learn from a conversation. Use Wizard of Oz when you want clean behavioural data uncontaminated by the user knowing they are being helped by a founder.

### 5. MVP dos and don’ts
| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Focus on solving **one core problem for one target persona** | Don't try to build every feature you imagine from day one |
| Validate with **real user feedback early and often** | Don't ignore user input or treat your assumptions as facts |
| Use **low‑cost, low‑code, or no‑code tools** to move fast | Don't spend months or large budgets before validating the idea |
| Build **just enough functionality to complete the user story** | Don't aim for a perfect, polished product in the first version |
| **Define and track success metrics** — retention, sign‑ups, adoption, engagement | Don't launch without knowing what you are testing or measuring |

My added emphasis on the “don’ts”: if I take months and a large budget before I validate, a competitor will take the market while I am still polishing. Confusion point is real — Just Dial’s problem was that a user landing on it could not tell what it was for.

### 6. The four conflict types (product storytelling frame)
- **When to use it:** when you have to explain in thirty seconds why your product should exist.

| Conflict type | Pain point | Example from deck | Story angle |
|---|---|---|---|
| User vs Process | Inefficient workflows, complex interfaces | Khatabook — small shopkeepers kept manual ledgers that were error‑prone and slow; Khatabook digitised bookkeeping in a simple mobile app | “From 20 minutes per transaction to instant records — without learning Excel.” |
| User vs Competition | Feature gaps, switching costs | Zerodha — traders stuck with traditional brokers charging high commissions on clunky platforms; Zerodha offered zero‑brokerage direct investing with a modern interface | “Trade without paying more for what you don't need.” |
| User vs Deadline | Deadlines, scaling, time pressure | Dunzo / Amazon Prime — urban users needed errands done in under an hour: groceries, packages, medicine; instant pick‑up and delivery via large rider network | “What if you could get back an hour of your day, every day?” |
| User vs Technical limits | Integration issues, technical limitations | Razorpay — Indian businesses struggled to integrate UPI, cards, and wallets across different providers; one unified gateway removed the friction | “Multiple systems slow you down — one clean integration removes all of it.” |

More examples:
- **Zerodha vs Groww** is a user‑vs‑competition story told from the other side. Zerodha’s minimalist, no‑frills interface was its virtue at MVP stage. Groww arrived with a better experience and took the market. Zerodha is now second‑largest, not first. Lesson: minimalism is a starting position, not a permanent strategy; better user experience beats incumbency.
- **Paytm vs PhonePe** is a friction story. Paytm required KYC and a Paytm Payments Bank account before you could send money. PhonePe integrated UPI directly and let you transact immediately. Removing friction is a valid MVP wedge on its own.

### 7. The MVP failure taxonomy
- **When to use it:** as a risk checklist against your own plan.

| Failure mode | What goes wrong | Case | Check to run |
|---|---|---|---|
| Over‑engineering | Build sophisticated tech for problem that does not need it | Juicero — Wi‑Fi‑enabled press whose packets could be squeezed by hand | Ask: what is the dumbest version that delivers the same value? |
| Wrong target segment | MVP fine; market has no need | Stayzilla — homestays for Tier 2/3 cities where hotels were already cheap and half empty | Ask: is there actual scarcity or pain in this segment, or am I assuming? |
| Untested negative use cases | Test happy path only; abuse kills you | Yik Yak, Koo in India — went viral, never tested moderation at scale | Ask: what is the worst thing a bad actor can do with this? |
| Ignoring the signal users gave you | Users tell you what they love; you build something else | Hike — users came for stickers; it added fraud detection, group messaging, file sharing | Ask: what is the one thing my users keep coming back for, and am I doubling down on it? |
| Operations that cannot scale | Demand grows, operating model breaks | Foodpanda — early lead in Tier‑1 food delivery, could not batch multiple orders to one rider | Ask: what breaks at 10× volume, and what does each unit cost me? |
| Cluttered value proposition | User lands and cannot tell what product is for | Just Dial; also Facebook Deals — users could not distinguish from Marketplace and died in four months | Ask: can a stranger say what this does in one sentence after five seconds? |
| Failure to keep up | Product does not evolve with how people work | Orkut, Yahoo — outpaced by email‑based collaboration and better experiences | Ask: what has changed in my users' lives since we designed this? |

## Examples & Case Studies 

### Global success stories
1. **Dropbox — explainer video MVP**  
   - Format: 2‑3 min demo video; no shippable product behind it.  
   - Result: 75,000+ sign‑ups overnight before hard engineering.  
   - Lesson: test idea before building infrastructure.  
   - Extension: now standard at largest tech companies (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google I/O, Microsoft Build, Apple WWDC show demos months before launch). Also parallels social proof in education (past student landing a 15 LPA role from same cohort).

2. **Airbnb — concierge MVP**  
   - Format: simple website with photos of founders’ own apartment.  
   - India translation: listing my own place during a high‑demand event (G20 summit in Delhi, World Cup final near Narendra Modi Stadium, Ram Mandir opening in Ayodhya).
   - Lesson: solve a real, time‑sensitive problem with scrappy, testable version; market timing + manual execution validated concept.  
   - Later positioning shift: reframed from price competition with hotels to “why stay in a white‑walled hotel bedroom when you could stay with locals and get the local experience?”

3. **Zappos — Wizard of Oz MVP**  
   - Format: manual, deliberately non‑scalable backend. Founder photographed shoes in local stores, listed them on site; when ordered, he went to store, bought pair, shipped himself. Customers thought they were buying from an online shoe retailer.  
   - Lesson: prove demand first, even if operations are entirely manual; focus on user behaviour, not scalability, at ppm.  
   - Modern parallel: founder‑as‑brand‑ambassador marketing (Virat Kohli’s One8 shoes, founder wearing branded t‑shirt through airports). You are not buying media; you are being the media.

4. **Amazon — niche‑first MVP**  
   - Format: online bookstore with manual fulfilment.  
   - Lesson: focus on a niche, master logistics manually, grow only after validating trust and delivery.  
   - AWS coda: Amazon Web Services began as internal tool to scale storage for Amazon’s own employees; someone realised cloud integration was good enough to sell; today AWS contributes more revenue and profit than e‑commerce business. Internal tools are a legitimate, under‑used source of MVPs.

5. **Facebook — closed‑network MVP**  
   - Format: campus‑only social network, TheFacebook, gated by .edu email addresses.  
   - Lesson: use your network; launch to a tight, well‑defined user group with high trust factor; exclusivity creates desire.  
   - Live Indian version at ISB placements: student built WhatsApp‑based OTP forwarding system for security guards to receive deliveries; guard’s app generated a new OTP sent to student; guard hands parcel only when student presents second OTP. Access restricted to ISB email IDs, profiles per batch — exactly Facebook’s .edu gate. This is a textbook MVP: obvious observable problem, closed high‑trust user group, near‑zero build cost via vibe coding, live with real users.

### Indian success stories
6. **Zomato — piecemeal MVP (PDF)**  
   - Format: PDF food directory of restaurant menus; no app, no delivery, no reviews.  
   - Deepinder Goyal noticed lunch hour convergence causing huge queues; responded by photographing menus, compiling into PDF, sending over WhatsApp/Slack/Teams/email before lunch; pre‑booked orders so food arrived at desk or ready to collect without queueing. Early web version called Foodiebay, focused only on menu discovery.  
   - Commercial validation: once service working, they said “if you want this delivered to your office, we will charge ₹20 extra”. People paid → proved willingness to pay → built the app.  
   - Lesson: start with what people need right now (menus), solve that well, layer other services later (delivery, reviews, loyalty).  
   - My answer to prototype vs MVP question: the PDF *was* the artefact; it was sent, people used, people paid → makes it an MVP, not merely a prototype.

7. **Ola — manual‑dispatch MVP**  
   - Format: phone booking, basic website, manual driver coordination.  
   - Started at busiest airports (Delhi, Bangalore), staff at counter asked arriving passengers destination, offered fixed price; drivers waited outside; calls routed to founder team in Bangalore who matched requests against driver phone list and rang them individually. No app, no automation, no GPS, no tracking.  
   - Core behaviour tested: do people want a predictable cab without wasting time at airport, without negotiating price? Once proven, they built app — first version had rides only, no AC option, no cab categories, flat vehicles at flat prices.  
   - I did not start with own fleet; partnered with existing drivers/operators on commission — outsourced‑operations pattern repeated across cases.
   - Uncomfortable counterpoint raised: idea not original (Meru Cabs already doing it). Ola won because it executed better and scaled nationally on back of technology and operations. My conclusion: if my MVP is good but I cannot replace it with scalable product and scalable operations, I become Meru and someone else takes the market. Building an MVP does not, by itself, take me anywhere.
   - Lesson: validate whether core behaviour — ride booking — is desirable before investing in a technology‑heavy platform.

8. **Razorpay — developer‑pain MVP**  
   - Format: simplified API with three‑step integration aimed at startups.  
   - Incumbents (PayU, Citrus Payments, etc.; PayPal never really penetrated India) onboarded merchants by: obtain banking licence, get GST approval, file regulatory documents, then have engineer sit with your engineer to write twenty‑thirty lines of code, then test — days to weeks before first rupee.  
   - Razorpay’s insight: any business needing a payment gateway will pay commission; what they will not tolerate is waiting. For a snacks brand grown big enough to collect payments online, do you want to spend four‑five days integrating a gateway, or start transacting this afternoon?  
   - Offered three steps and roughly a single line of code, integrable by engineer or non‑engineer, live in hours rather than weeks, no waiting on approvals. No dashboards, no analytics — just a clean way to collect payments.  
   - Lesson: focus MVP on solving one key developer pain, especially in regulated, red‑tape‑heavy space.

### Other examples
- **Microsoft Teams**: launched as desperate measure when COVID hit; improved continuously; now largest player in segment despite Slack and Zoom head start. Corporate MVPs are real; speed beat polish.  
- **Amazon AWS**: covered above.  
- **NotebookLM**: built as prototype to test RAG — upload document, summarise with AI, generate other formats including audio podcast; became one of most‑used products of its kind; prototypes sometimes escape the lab.  
- **Urban Company**: started in services fixing/replacing RO water‑purifier filters; doing work manually taught them filter supply chain and that customers face filter change every two‑three months; now launched own Native purifier with value proposition “no filter change for at least two years”. Service first, learn demand, then productise.  
- **Cult.fit and Hyrox** as community‑led MVPs; positioning line: “I'm not gym‑going, I cult‑go”.  
- **Zerodha vs Groww**: Zerodha kept deliberately minimal experience; Groww arrived with better experience and took share; Zerodha now second‑largest. Lesson: minimalism is starting position; better UX beats incumbency.  
- **Paytm vs PhonePe**: Paytm insisted on KYC and Paytm Payments Bank account before money could move; PhonePe integrated UPI and removed step; removing friction is a strategy.  
- **Zepto, Blinkit, Instamart**: new users get 5‑7‑minute deliveries plus free goodies and sample packs; regular users, three‑four months in, quietly get 10‑12‑15 min. Drift is deliberate; once habit formed, deadline promise no longer what retains you.

### Failed MVPs
- **Juicero** — Wi‑Fi‑enabled juice machine. Razor‑and‑blades model: sell machine cheap, make money on proprietary juice packets that only fit that machine. Investors funded heavily; ran ~1.5 years. YouTube demo showed packets could be squeezed by hand → MVP over‑engineered; customers found out packets could be squeezed by hand. Lesson: engineering solution built for problem that did not need engineering is not an MVP, whatever else it is.  
- **Yik Yak** (and Koo in India) — anonymous college chat app. MVP went viral; never tested moderation at scale; once moderators and law‑enforcement caught up, users left and product died. Lesson: you tested that people want it; you did not test what people would do with it. Negative use cases are part of MVP, not post‑launch concern.  
- **Facebook Deals** — local deal offers. Facebook Marketplace already existed; users could not tell difference between the two. Deck’s verdict: lacked merchant interest and user adoption; killed in four months. Lesson: internal clarity is not user clarity; if a user cannot articulate why this exists and the other thing does not do it, you have a positioning failure, not a feature gap.  
- **Stayzilla** — homestay platform like Airbnb, India. Wanted to make Tier 2/3 cities next Airbnb hotspots. Hotels in those cities already cheap, occupancy already low → no scarcity, no price gouging, no unmet demand. Add trust and safety concern of staying in stranger’s home in smaller city → value proposition disappears. Deck adds: MVP did not validate host‑side experience in Tier 2/3, mismatch in user expectations. Contrast with Airbnb: Airbnb targeted saturated markets where hotels were fully booked and unavailable; Stayzilla targeted markets where hotels were empty. Same MVP, opposite outcome because of segment. My take: if I have a good MVP but I take it to the wrong users, it will most likely fail.
- **Hike** — app with Indian sticker culture. Everyone who used Hike used it for stickers. Signal: users told Hike exactly what they valued. Instead of consolidating on it and becoming leader in that niche, Hike expanded into fraud detection, group messaging, file sharing — areas where it had no competency and where WhatsApp already dominant. Deck verdict: feature‑rich, but failed to test retention loops and could not compete with WhatsApp. My take: when I release an MVP and my customers have given me approval for something, I try to make *that* big. Why do I want to try something where my competencies do not lie?
- **Foodpanda** — food delivery MVP in Tier‑1 cities. Early advantage over Swiggy and Zomato; leading food‑delivery player in Tier‑1 cities. Failed on operations: could not scale, specifically could not assign multiple orders to a single rider — batching problem that determines whether food delivery is profitable at all. Deck verdict: focused on growth over unit metrics; MVP never stress‑tested logistics and vendor coordination. Lesson: in operations‑heavy business, MVP has to test operating model, not just demand.  
- **Just Dial, Orkut, Yahoo** — mentioned in passing. Just Dial’s problem: clutter — user arrives and cannot work out what they are there for. Orkut failed to keep up with shift toward email‑based collaboration and products built around it. Both are versions of same trap: product stopped answering a clearly‑stated question for the user.
