## Key Takeaways
1. **“Build first, polish later”** is right only if “first” means the smallest thing that delivers complete value. User must be able to complete the full action.  
2. **Not all prototypes are MVPs, but all MVPs are prototypes.** Prototype is the broader category; MVP is a working, high‑fidelity member of it.  
3. **Keep operations as light as possible, and outsource the MVP wherever you can.** Ola partnered with drivers; Amazon used post office; Airbnb used Facebook groups. Humans deliver service manually first; you learn the process; only then do you build product around it.  
4. **A good MVP does not win the market. Scaling it does.** If you cannot follow your MVP with a scalable product and scalable operations, someone else will take the market you proved existed.  
5. **Take the MVP to the right segment.** Repeated across Stayzilla vs Airbnb contrast: same product succeeds in market with scarcity, fails in market without it. Segment choice is part of MVP, not separate exercise.  
6. **When users tell you what they love, double down on it.** Hike lesson: customers approved stickers → make stickers enormous. Do not diversify into competencies you do not have.  
7. **Never launch without knowing what you will measure.** Listed among the five “don’ts”; returned to when framing task‑tracker exercise where metric was stated before question: number of tasks successfully completed using the app.  
8. **Convenience and comfort are different businesses.** Given its own definition line; tested against six products; fastest way to understand how defensible your product actually is.  
9. **Join a beta programme this week.** Open the Play Store, find the beta programmes for apps I use, join one, and write up the experience a month later. Beta participation should be a habit, not a one‑off.
10. **Type your own answers.** Twice declined to accept answers obviously pasted from ChatGPT, and said so openly. Point was not about tooling — course teaches AI prompting every week — but that thinking muscle only develops if you use it.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
- **Confusing “minimum” with “incomplete.”** An MVP with a broken or missing final step teaches you nothing because the user’s drop‑off is caused by your gap, not their lack of interest. Build the full user story, narrowly.  
- **Building the technology before validating the behaviour.** Ola’s founders picked up phones for months; Zomato photographed menus. If first instinct is “we need an app”, ask what the equivalent of the PDF is for your product.  
- **Treating friends and family as evidence.** Alpha users useful for catching crashes and confusion; useless for measuring desire because they want you to succeed. Do not report alpha feedback as validation.  
- **Confusing a survey response with a purchase.** “Would you use this?” is answered by almost everyone with a polite yes. Pre‑booking, paying, or repeatedly using are the only reliable signals. Class’s strongest suggestion was the pre‑book test for exactly this reason.  
- **Picking the MVP type before naming the uncertainty.** Every type in catalogue answers a different question. If you cannot state in one sentence what you are unsure about, you cannot choose sensibly, and you will default to whatever is easiest to build.  
- **Testing only the happy path.** Yik Yak and Koo went viral and died on abuse. Ask what a hostile or careless user can do with your product before you widen the group.  
- **Launching into a market with no scarcity.** Stayzilla’s failure. Before you take an MVP to a segment, verify there is genuine unmet demand there. Empty hotels mean no problem to solve.  
- **Chasing every feature request while ignoring the one thing users love.** Hike’s failure. Retention comes from doubling down, not from breadth.  
- **Ignoring unit economics because growth looks good.** Foodpanda’s failure. If you cannot state what one order or one user costs you and what breaks at ten times the volume, your MVP has not tested the business.  
- **Confusing “we are minimal” with “we are done.”** Zerodha’s minimalism was an MVP virtue that became a vulnerability when Groww arrived with a better experience. Minimalism is a starting position with an expiry date.  
- **Assuming an MVP means a poor experience.** It means a narrow experience. Razorpay’s MVP had no dashboards and no analytics, but the one thing it did — integrate in three steps — was better than anything else on the market.  
- **Skipping the revenue logic.** An MVP should make clear how the business would eventually earn money, even if it does not collect a rupee yet. Zomato’s ₹20 delivery charge was the whole point of the exercise, not an afterthought.

## Interview & Portfolio Angle

### How to talk about this in an interview
MVP questions come in three shapes:  
1. “How would you validate this idea?”  
2. “You have three weeks and no engineers, what do you ship?”  
3. “Tell me about an MVP you admire and why.”  
All three test whether you can trade certainty for speed deliberately, and whether you know what you are buying with that trade.

**Structure that works:**  
1. **State the riskiest assumption first.** Example: “The thing most likely to be wrong here is that busy professionals will respond to an AI nudge rather than ignore it.”  
2. **Choose an MVP type and justify the choice against that assumption.** Example: “Because my uncertainty is about behaviour rather than about whether I can build it, I would run a Wizard of Oz MVP over WhatsApp before writing any code.”  
3. **Define the population and the size.** Example: “Twenty members of one gym, for two weeks.”  
4. **Name the metric and the bar.** Example: “Tasks completed per user per week. My bar is that at least eight of twenty users complete three or more tasks a week in week two without me chasing them.”  
5. **State what each outcome makes you do next.** Example: “If it clears the bar, I build the automation. If half clear it, I interview the other half before building anything. If nobody does, the nudge is not the product and I go back to discovery.”  

That last step separates a senior‑sounding answer from a junior one. Anyone can propose a test; deciding in advance what each result will make you do is the actual PM skill.

I sprinkle in vocabulary where it fits naturally — concierge versus Wizard of Oz, alpha versus beta, fidelity — but I do not perform it. One well‑chosen term beats five.

### Sample questions and shape of a strong answer
**Q1. “What is the difference between a prototype and an MVP?”**  
*Strong answer:* lead with hierarchy, not a list of differences. “Prototype is the broader term — every MVP is a working, high‑fidelity prototype, but most prototypes never become MVPs. The functional difference is completion and evidence: with a prototype a user can complete part of a flow and give me an opinion on the concept; with an MVP a user completes the whole job, in the real world, and gives me behaviour. A prototype answers ‘should we build this?’ An MVP answers ‘what is the least we can launch to learn?’ A prototype might be a paper sketch. An MVP has to work, and it should make clear how the business eventually earns money.” Then give one example of each from a product you know.

**Q2. “You are a solo founder with no budget. How do you get your first hundred users?”**  
*Strong answer:* I refuse the generic. I do not say “social media and word of mouth”. I name a place where my persona already gathers and is already performing a version of the behaviour. sabziwalas and milkwalas who already send bills over WhatsApp — the channel and habit already exist, so the product upgrades rather than creates. I follow with mechanism (free access, a seven‑day challenge, partnership with a gym or college), then the metric I would watch, then the honest failure condition. I mention that I would run this as a concierge or piecemeal MVP so the first version costs me time rather than money.

**Q3. “Tell me about an MVP that failed and what you would have done differently.”**  
*Strong answer:* pick one where failure has a clean, teachable cause. Stayzilla is excellent because contrast with Airbnb is sharp: Airbnb targeted markets where hotels were sold out and prices had tripled; Stayzilla targeted Tier 2/3 cities where hotels were cheap and half empty. Product was not wrong, segment was. What I would have done differently: before building supply, I would have run a landing‑page or email MVP in three candidate cities and measured booking intent per city, and I would have validated the host side first, since supply was the harder half. Hike is another strong choice because it shows you can read a retention signal.

### What belongs in your portfolio
1. **Acquisition‑trigger teardown** (exercise explicitly asked for). Take six to eight products you use, and for each one document honestly: what made you try it the first time, what made you keep using it, and whether it is a convenience product or a comfort product by the “if it disappeared, would my life change?” test. Then close with a paragraph on what this tells you about how you would launch your own product. It is personal, specific, cannot be generated by anyone else, and demonstrates a way of thinking rather than a memorised framework. Good for LinkedIn post as well as portfolio page.  
2. **MVP plan for the idea you have been developing through the course.** One page: the riskiest assumption, the MVP type chosen and why, the exact user group, what you will build and what you will deliberately not build, the metric and the pass bar, and the decision you will take at each outcome. This page becomes the front of your PRD in Week 6.  
3. **If I took the beta challenge**, a short write‑up of a beta programme I joined: what I got early, what was broken, what I reported, and one product decision I would have made differently as the PM of that product. Almost no candidate walks into an interview with that.

## Practice Tasks
**T06.1 — The acquisition‑trigger and comfort audit.**  
Pick eight products you personally use. For each, write three lines: the first time you used it and why, why you still use it, and whether it is convenience or comfort by the disappearance test. Then write a closing paragraph on which of your eight are genuinely defensible and why.  
*Done when:* you have a single page with eight products, each classified, and a closing paragraph that names at least one product you would consider fragile and explains why.

**T06.2 — Choose and defend an MVP type for your course idea.**  
Take the product idea you have been working with since Week 2. Write your single riskiest assumption in one sentence. Then pick exactly one of the ten MVP types from the catalogue and justify the choice in a short paragraph. Write down what you will build, what you are deliberately excluding, and the one metric you will watch.  
*Done when:* one page containing a stated assumption, a named MVP type with justification, an explicit exclusion list of at least three features you are not building, and a metric with a numeric pass bar.

**T06.3 — Design a concierge MVP you could run this week for free.**  
Using the same idea, design a version where *you* do all the work manually. Who are the ten to twenty users, and where do they already gather? What exactly will you do by hand each day? What will you record about each interaction? How long will you run it before deciding?  
*Done when:* you have a daily operating script (what you do, in order, each day), a named user group with a plan for reaching them, a feedback capture format, and an end date.

**T06.4 — MVP failure post‑mortem.**  
Choose one failed product from the list — Juicero, Yik Yak, Koo, Facebook Deals, Stayzilla, Hike, or Foodpanda — and write a one‑page post‑mortem. Cover: what the MVP was, what it validated correctly, what it never tested, and the two specific decisions I would have made differently, in order.
*Done when:* the page names the failure mode from the taxonomy, and your two alternative decisions are concrete actions rather than principles (“run a landing‑page test in three cities before hiring supply staff”, not “understand the market better”).

**T06.5 — Join a beta programme and report back.**  
Use the prompt: “I want to try some of the latest B2C beta products. Can you tell me in India which companies offer access to join the beta products, and also give me the link to join those programs. Focus on consumer tech products only.” I pick one, I read the data‑sharing terms before I accept, and I enrol. I use it for at least two weeks. If I had enrolled on the call, this would be the deliverable I would present in a month.
*Done when:* you have a short write‑up covering the programme you joined, one feature you saw before the public did, one bug or rough edge you found, whether you reported it and what happened, and one decision you would have made differently as that product’s PM.

**T06.6 — Rewrite your product pitch using a conflict type.**  
Take your idea and write four one‑line story angles, one for each conflict type: user vs process, user vs competition, user vs deadline, user vs technical limits. Then choose the one that is truest for your product and expand it into a three‑sentence pitch modelled on the Khatabook line: “From 20 minutes per transaction to instant records — without learning Excel.”  
*Done when:* you have all four one‑liners written, one selected with a reason, and a three‑sentence pitch that names the old pain, the new state, and what the user no longer has to do.

**T06.7 (stretch) — Sketch the low‑fidelity flow.**  
On paper or in any free tool, sketch the five to nine screens your MVP needs, and draw arrows for every navigation path between them. No colour, no branding, no real copy. This is deliberate preparation for the Figma and wireframing week.  
*Done when:* every screen has at least one inbound and one outbound arrow, and there is no screen a user can reach with no way back.

## Glossary
- **Alpha group / alpha launch** — Testing with people you personally know: team members, friends, family. Controlled environment, tolerant users, early and possibly unstable build. Answers “is it working well enough internally?”  
- **Beta group / beta launch** — Testing with opted‑in strangers who are not yet the general public. Near‑final build. Answers “is it ready for the real world?”  
- **Beta programme** — A company's public mechanism for enrolling outside users into pre‑release builds, e.g., the “Join the beta program” link at the bottom of a Google Play listing.  
- **Bug bounty** — Payment for finding defects in a product, usually reserved for security risks that could cost the company real revenue rather than for every bug.  
- **Comfort product** — A product whose disappearance would leave your life essentially unchanged, only slightly less easy. Zepto, Blinkit, Instamart.  
- **Community‑Led MVP** — Building with and inside a niche community, so identity and belonging carry the product. Notion with indie hackers; Cult.fit.  
- **Concierge MVP** — You deliver the service manually and the user knows it is manual. Airbnb's founders hosting their first guests.  
- **Conflict type** — The narrative frame for a product story: user vs process, user vs competition, user vs deadline, or user vs technical limits.  
- **Convenience product** — A product that formalised a genuinely painful process, so its disappearance would return you to something materially worse. Uber and Ola versus roadside fare negotiation.  
- **Dogfooding** — Using your own product internally before exposing it to users.  
- **Email MVP** — Delivering the value proposition by personal email instead of building a product. Product Hunt began this way.  
- **Explainer Video MVP** — A video demonstrating the product's value before the product exists. Dropbox.  
- **Fidelity** — How much detail a prototype captures. Low fidelity captures structure only; high fidelity captures colours, buttons, and some animation.  
- **High‑fidelity prototype** — A prototype with real colours, buttons, and motion, close enough to the real thing that users react to it as a product.  
- **Landing Page MVP** — A single page describing the product, used to collect sign‑ups or interest. Robinhood's waitlist.  
- **Low‑fidelity prototype** — A sketch‑level prototype, including pen and paper, that shows flow and structure without visual detail.  
- **Marketing‑Led MVP** — Validating demand through a campaign, positioning, or the founder's own visibility before the product is ready. Superhuman; One8 by Virat Kohli.  
- **MoSCoW** — A prioritisation framework (must have, should have, could have, would have) mentioned as part of feature prioritisation.
- **MVP (Minimum Viable Product)** — The smallest working version of a product that lets a real user complete a real job end to end, generates learning, and makes the revenue logic clear. In phrasing, a working prototype.
- **Physical MVP** — A small batch of a real physical product made to test form, packaging, or usability. Paper Boat.  
- **Piecemeal MVP** — Stitching existing tools together to simulate a product. Groupon on WordPress, PDFs, and email; Zomato's menu PDF.  
- **Product‑market fit** — Evidence that a defined group of users genuinely want your product, usually shown by real usage and willingness to pay.  
- **Product muscle** — the phrase for the instinct that lets me spot who my real users are and where they already are, without being told.
- **Proof of concept** — Used interchangeably with prototype in normal PM conversation; a demonstration that an idea can work.  
- **Prototype** — Any early representation of a product used to validate the idea or the design direction. The broader category that contains MVPs.  
- **Razor and blades model** — Selling the base product cheaply and making money on the consumables that only work with it. Juicero's machine and juice packets; the iPhone and its accessories.  
- **RAG (retrieval‑augmented generation)** — The technique NotebookLM was originally built to test: an AI system that answers using documents you supply.  
- **Single‑Feature MVP** — Shipping exactly one feature to test one behaviour. Instagram's photo, filter, share.  
- **SKU** — A distinct sellable item. Amazon chose books partly because the SKU count is effectively unlimited.  
- **Unit economics** — What one order, user, or transaction costs and earns. Foodpanda's failure was a unit‑economics failure disguised as a growth story.  
- **Vibe coding** — Building a website, app, or product by describing it to AI rather than writing the code yourself.  
- **Waitlist** — A list of people who have registered interest before launch; the primary output of a landing‑page or explainer‑video MVP.  
- **Wizard of Oz MVP** — The user believes the product is automated while humans perform the work behind the scenes. Zappos.  
- **0‑to‑1 product** — A new product that has not yet been launched.

## Source Files
| File | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `Classtranscript.txt` | Full auto‑generated transcript of the two‑hour (Academic 7 — Case Study: The MVP, 3 Aug 2026, 8‑10 PM IST). Contains the two opening scenario exercises with answers, the convenience vs comfort discussion, the Play Store beta walkthrough, the prototype vs MVP debate, every case study told in full, the Dropbox video, the failed‑MVP discussion, the MVP type summary, the resource recommendations, and the closing schedule announcement moving theory to Monday and Friday with TA on Thursday. |

title: Cercit policy framework overview
summary: The cercit policy framework outlines four components, ownership, and change management to govern AI-assisted lending decisions.
body:
# cercit policy framework — overview

Status: draft for review
Owner: Sameer Mittimani
Created: 16 Sep 2026
Scope: cercit Phase 1 — new car loans, salaried, single applicant, direct leads

Related: [[01-Role-Policy-Manager]] · [[02-Access-Control-and-SoD]] · [[03-Policy-Change-Management]] · [[04-Model-Risk-Management]] · [[05-Credit-Policy]] · [[06-KYC-Policy]] · [[07-Policy-Gap-Register]]

---

## Why this exists

cercit is built on one principle: AI assists, policy decides. That makes the policy the regulated artifact, not the model. If the rule set is the thing that actually approves or declines a loan, then how rules get changed matters more than how the model scores.

Right now the system has 18 policy rules, a rate grid, and an XGBoost model — and no governed way to change any of them. `togglePolicyRule()` writes straight to `policy_rules.is_active` with no approval and no audit trail. A person who can open the Policy Rules screen can switch off the CIBIL floor, and nothing in the system records that it happened or who did it.

This framework closes that, and sets up the wider policy suite a lender is expected to hold.

## The four components, and what governs each

cercit separates four things that are often conflated. Each attracts a different policy owner.

| Component | Question it answers | Governing policy | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Document AI | What does the document say? | Document Verification & Authenticity; Outsourcing (AWS is material outsourcing); Records Retention | Operations / CIO |
| Data & Feature Engine | What does the borrower's behaviour look like? | Income Assessment; Account Aggregator Consent; Bureau Usage | Credit Head |
| ML Risk Model | How risky is this pattern historically? | [[04-Model-Risk-Management]] | Chief Risk Officer |
| Policy & Decision Engine | Does this qualify under approved policy? | [[05-Credit-Policy]]; Delegation of Authority; Deviation & Exception | Credit Head, changes routed through Policy Manager |

Keeping these apart is what lets you answer an auditor's question. "The model said grade A but you declined" is only defensible if the policy that overrode it is versioned, approved, and pinned to that decision.

## Module to policy map

Mapped against what is actually built, not a generic lender.

| cercit module | Where it lives | Policies required | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apply flow, eligibility check | `/apply`, `/check-eligibility` | KYC/CDD, Data Protection & Privacy, Consent Management, Fair Practices Code | Must |
| Document upload & extraction | `aws/` Lambdas, `document-orchestrator.ts` | Document Verification & Authenticity, Outsourcing/Vendor, Data Localisation, Records Retention | Must |
| Bureau pull & parsing | `ccr-parser.ts`, `bureau_reports` | Credit Bureau Usage (CIC Act — purpose limitation, consent, no bulk pulls), Bureau Recalibration handling | Must |
| Bank statement / AA | `bank-statement-parser.ts`, `cashflow-analyzer.ts` | Account Aggregator Consent, Income Assessment, Transaction Categorisation standards | Must |
| ML risk model | `risk-score-model.ts`, `public/models/*.onnx` | [[04-Model-Risk-Management]] | Must |
| Policy rule engine | `policy-rule-engine.ts`, `policy_rules` | [[05-Credit-Policy]], [[03-Policy-Change-Management]], Deviation & Exception | Must |
| Rate grid / pricing | `rate_grid`, `employer_category_pricing` | Pricing Policy, Fair Practices Code (APR and charge disclosure) | Must |
| Officer decision, override | `fn_officer_decision`, `override_logs` | Delegation of Authority, Deviation & Exception, Segregation of Duties | Must |
| Approval & sanction letters | `/applications/$id/approval`, `/sanction` | Fair Practices Code, Sanction Letter standards, Adverse Action / reason communication | Must |
| Audit log | `audit_events`, `/audit-log` | Audit Trail, Records Retention, IT & Information Security | Must |
| Users & roles | `users`, `auth.ts` | [[02-Access-Control-and-SoD]], Know Your Employee | Must |
| Dashboard / MIS | `/dashboard` | Risk Reporting & MIS | Should |
| Employer master | `/employers` | Employer Categorisation Policy | Should |
| Grievance | not built | Grievance Redressal | Must before live |
| Collections | not built (out of Phase 1) | Collections & Recovery, Repossession | Won't — Phase 1 |

## MoSCoW for Phase 1

Phase 1 is a portfolio-grade build on synthetic data, not a licensed lender. That changes what is genuinely required *now* versus what has to exist before a single real customer is onboarded. Both columns matter — the second is what makes the build credible as a product artifact.

| Policy | Needed for Phase 1 build | Needed before real customers | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit Policy & Underwriting | Must | Must | Already implicit in 18 rules; needs writing down |
| Policy Change Management | Must | Must | The live gap — see [[07-Policy-Gap-Register]] |
| Access Control & SoD | Must | Must | Role permissions are client-side only today |
| Model Risk Management | Must | Must | Model is live with no validation record |
| KYC/AML/CFT | Should | Must | Synthetic data now, but the flow shape must be right |
| Data Protection & Privacy | Should | Must | PAN/mobile encryption written, not yet applied |
| Fair Practices Code | Should | Must | Letters already disclose rate and charges |
| Grievance Redressal | Could | Must | Not built |
| Pricing | Should | Must | Rate grid exists, policy does not |
| Outsourcing / Vendor | Could | Must | AWS + Supabase are material outsourcing |
| Fraud Risk Management | Could | Must | `fraud_signals` table exists, unused |
| IT & Cybersecurity | Could | Must | |
| BCP / DR | Won't | Must | |
| Liquidity, Capital Adequacy, ALCO | Won't | Must (as a licensed entity) | Balance-sheet policies, not system policies — out of scope for the build |
| CSR / ESG | Won't | Could | |

The bottom three rows are worth stating explicitly: they are real obligations for an NBFC but they have no representation in this system and never will. A build like cercit should not pretend to cover them.

## Ownership and review calendar

| Policy | Owner role | Approver | Review |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit Policy & rule thresholds | Policy Manager (author) | Credit Head / Risk Committee | Annual + on trigger |
| Rate grid / pricing | Policy Manager (author) | Credit Head + CFO | Quarterly |
| Model Risk | Model owner | CRO / Risk Committee | Annual + on drift breach |
| KYC/AML | Compliance Officer (MLRO) | Board | Annual |
| Access & SoD | Admin | Compliance | Semi-annual access review |
| Data Protection | DPO / Legal | Board | Annual |
| Fair Practices Code | Business Head | Board | Bi-annual |

Ad-hoc review triggers, any policy: a regulatory change, a material incident (fraud, breach, mass decline), a model drift breach, a new product or segment, or an audit finding.

## The one structural decision

Everything else follows from this: **a Policy Manager must be able to author a policy change but never to activate one alone.**

Giving one role unilateral write access to the rule engine creates a larger blast radius than any underwriter has. An underwriter can mis-decide one case. A policy change mis-applied silently re-decides every case after it. So the role gets authoring rights plus a mandatory second approver, effective dating, and a full version history — see [[03-Policy-Change-Management]].

## Open questions

1. Does the Policy Manager sit under Credit or under Risk? Under Risk gives better independence from the sales-side pressure to loosen rules; under Credit gives faster turnaround. Recommendation: Risk, with a service-level commitment on turnaround so Credit does not lose speed.
2. Who is the second approver when the change is small (a fee, a display label) versus material (a bureau cut-off)? A single approval path for both will get bypassed. See the change-tiering proposal in [[03-Policy-Change-Management]].
3. Should a model version promotion follow the same workflow as a rule change? They have different risk shapes but the same need for a sign-off record.

title: Lending and compliance glossary
summary: Lending and compliance glossary defines terms such as AUA/KUA, blind index, cooling-off period, and notes cercit's existing versus planned features.
body:
# Lending and compliance glossary

> Drafted by Hermes (free model) on 17 Sep 2026, then corrected by Claude the same night. The draft had these errors, fixed below: AUA/KUA, blind index, cooling-off period, CTR, KIN, LSP, OVD, PSI, RLS, UCIC and effective dating were defined wrongly, and several entries said cercit already does things it does not (multi-bureau pulls, V-CIP, NACH, hypothecation registration, PSI inspections). Statements about cercit now describe what exists or say "planned". Numbers marked (verify) still need checking against the primary source.

**Account Aggregator (AA)** — An RBI-licensed intermediary that moves a borrower's financial data, such as bank statements, from the bank to the lender with the borrower's consent. cercit plans to use it instead of uploaded statements.

**Adverse action** — Declining or worsening the terms of a loan. Lenders must tell the borrower the main reasons for a rejection in writing.

**APR (annual percentage rate)** — The all-in yearly cost of a loan: interest plus processing fees and other charges. It must be shown in the Key Fact Statement.

**AUA / KUA** — Authentication User Agency and KYC User Agency: the UIDAI licences an entity needs to run Aadhaar authentication and Aadhaar e-KYC. Lenders usually access these through a licensed provider.

**Blind index** — A keyed hash of an encrypted value, used to search for it or enforce uniqueness without decrypting it. cercit's migration 012 uses one so PAN stays unique after encryption.

**CDD (customer due diligence)** — Identifying and verifying the customer and understanding the relationship before lending.

**CIC (credit information company)** — A licensed credit bureau: TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, CRIF High Mark or Equifax. cercit currently parses an uploaded CIBIL report.

**CKYCR** — The Central KYC Records Registry run by CERSAI. Lenders search it first, download an existing record with consent, and upload new records.

**Cooling-off period** — A window after a digital loan is taken in which the borrower can exit by repaying principal and proportionate APR without penalty. Minimum 3 days for loans of 7 days' tenure or more, 1 day for shorter loans.

**Crypto-erasure** — Destroying the key that encrypts data so the data can never be read again. An accepted purge method under NIST SP 800-88.

**CTR (cash transaction report)** — A report to FIU-IND of cash transactions above ₹10 lakh in a month, including connected transactions.

**Delegation of authority** — Who may approve what: loan amounts, deviations and policy changes by role.

**Deviation** — An approved, recorded departure from credit policy for one case. Not the same as a policy change.

**DLG (default loss guarantee)** — A partner's contractual cover for part of the lender's losses on a portfolio. Capped at 5% of the portfolio under RBI rules.

**DPD (days past due)** — How many days a payment is overdue.

**DPDP Act** — The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: consent, purpose limitation, storage limitation and data principal rights for personal data.

**EDD (enhanced due diligence)** — Extra checks for high-risk customers, such as source of funds and senior approval.

**Effective dating** — Giving a policy value a start date (and later an end date), so changes are scheduled and past decisions can be matched to the rules in force at the time.

**FIU-IND** — The Financial Intelligence Unit of India, which receives STRs and CTRs.

**FOIR (fixed obligations to income ratio)** — Monthly EMIs, including the proposed one, divided by monthly income. cercit's base (gross or net) is still to be decided.

**Form 60** — A declaration filed by a person who does not have a PAN.

**Free income ratio** — The share of net income left after all EMIs. cercit declines below 15%.

**Hypothecation** — A charge over a movable asset such as a car, without the lender taking possession. It is recorded on the vehicle's registration. cercit does not yet check or register it.

**KFS (Key Fact Statement)** — A standard summary of loan terms, APR and charges given to the borrower before the agreement is signed.

**KIN** — The 14-digit KYC Identification Number issued by CKYCR.

**LSP (lending service provider)** — A company that acts for a regulated lender in sourcing, underwriting support or collections, under the digital lending directions.

**LTV (loan-to-value)** — The loan amount divided by the vehicle's value. cercit currently measures it on two different bases, which is an open decision.

**Maker-checker** — One person prepares a change, a different person approves it.

**Model drift** — A model's inputs or accuracy moving away from what it was trained on.

**NACH** — National Automated Clearing House, used for recurring EMI debits under a mandate. Planned, not built.

**NPA (non-performing asset)** — A loan with payment overdue for more than 90 days.

**OVD (officially valid document)** — An identity or address document accepted by RBI for KYC: passport, driving licence, Aadhaar proof of possession, voter ID, NREGA job card, NPR letter.

**PEP (politically exposed person)** — Someone with a prominent public function, or their close family or associates. Treated as high risk.

**Penal charges** — A charge for a default or breach of terms. RBI requires these to be charges, not added to the interest rate, and not compounded.

**PMLA** — The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002: identification, record-keeping and reporting duties. Records kept at least 5 years after the relationship ends.

**PSI (population stability index)** — A measure of how much a model's input distribution has shifted since training. Above 0.2 usually means investigate.

**Re-KYC** — Periodic update of a customer's KYC: every 2, 8 or 10 years for high, medium or low risk.

**RLS (row-level security)** — A Postgres feature that decides, row by row, which records a database user may read or change.

**Segregation of duties** — Splitting related tasks across people so no one can complete a risky action alone.

**SMA (special mention account)** — A loan overdue but not yet an NPA: SMA-0 up to 30 days, SMA-1 31–60, SMA-2 61–90.

**STP (straight-through processing)** — An application decided without a person touching it. Not enabled in cercit Phase 1.

**STR (suspicious transaction report)** — A report to FIU-IND of a suspicious transaction, filed within 7 working days of forming the suspicion (verify).

**UCIC (unique customer identification code)** — One customer ID across all of a lender's products, to stop the same person appearing as several customers.

**V-CIP (video customer identification process)** — RBI-permitted video KYC run by the lender's own staff, with liveness and geotagging. Planned, not built.

**Vahan** — The national vehicle registration database, which records hypothecation. Planned integration.

title: Policy change management SOP for cercit credit appraisal
summary: The SOP outlines how policy changes for the cercit AI credit appraisal system are drafted, simulated, approved, activated, monitored, and rolled back.
body:
# DRAFT — SOP for policy change management

> Generated by Hermes (free model) on 17 Sep 2026 00:09. Not verified. Claude must check facts and numbers before this is used.

Standard Operating Procedure: Policy Change Management — Cercit Credit Appraisal

Purpose
This procedure governs how policy rules, thresholds, and model settings for the cercit AI credit appraisal system are changed, approved, activated, monitored, and rolled back. It ensures every change is tiered correctly, simulated, approved, versioned, and pinned to credit decisions so that any past decision can be reconstructed.

Roles
Policy Manager: drafts versions, runs impact simulation (last 1,000 applications for tier; 40 test fixtures available in scripts/run-test-cases.ts), assigns tier, submits for approval, logs cosmetic changes.
Credit Head: approves standard changes (2 working days notice); approves emergency tightening; notes material changes; approves rollbacks.
Risk Committee: notes all material changes; ratifies emergency tightening within 5 working days or it lapses; receives annual report.
Admin: ensures database constraints (`approved_by <> authored_by`; exactly one ACTIVE version per product); manages `policy_versions` status lifecycle.

Standard change procedure
1. Policy Manager drafts a new `policy_versions` record (status DRAFT, tier STANDARD) with rationale and `policy_version` set.
2. Policy Manager runs impact simulation against the last 1,000 applications; records `simulation_id`.
3. Confirm zero decision flips. If any flip, escalate to material procedure.
4. Submit for approval; `approved_by` must differ from `authored_by`.
5. Credit Head reviews and approves or rejects; 2 working days notice from approval to effect.
6. Set `status = APPROVED`, then schedule `effective_from` (next business day at earliest).
7. At effective date, activate (`ACTIVE`); previous version set to `SUPERSEDED`.
8. Update `credit_decisions` and `recommendations` to pin `policy_version_id`; store `model_version` from `MODEL_VERSION`.
9. Monitor 30 days; if behaviour diverges materially from simulation, initiate rollback or corrective change.
10. Once stable, close the change record (`status` retained for audit).

Material change procedure
1. Policy Manager drafts version (`tier = MATERIAL`) with mandatory `rationale` and `regulatory_ref` if applicable.
2. Run impact simulation vs last 1,000 applications; capture flip count by decision band, employer category, CIBIL band, estimated approval rate and rate effect.
3. Confirm any decision flip — if zero, reclassify as standard.
4. Submit for approval; `simulation_id` linked.
5. Credit Head approves; Risk Committee notes (does not approve separately, but must note).
6. 5 working days notice; `effective_from` set to next business day at earliest.
7. At effective date, activate; previous version marked `SUPERSEDED`.
8. Pin `policy_version_id` to decisions; record `model_version`.
9. Post-change monitoring for 30 days: actual mix, deviation rate, approval rate, early delinquency.
10. If actual diverges materially from simulation, treat as a finding and initiate rollback or corrective change; close only when stable.

Emergency tightening procedure
1. Only for tightening (stricter rule, activation of a rule, tighter cap), never loosening.
2. Credit Head activates with written reason; `tier` noted as emergency.
3. Effective immediately; `status` moves to active; previous version superseded.
4. Log immediately; report at next Risk Committee meeting regardless.
5. Risk Committee must ratify within 5 working days, else it lapses automatically (`ROLLED_BACK`).
6. Monitor 30 days; rollback if needed follows the same approval path unless within the ratification window (reverting the emergency triggers rollback directly).

Rollback procedure
1. Rollback activates a prior `SUPERSEDED` version, not an in-place edit.
2. For standard rollback: follows material approval path (Credit Head; Risk Committee notes if it was a material version).
3. For emergency rollback within ratification window: direct rollback permitted.
4. The rolled-back version becomes `ACTIVE`; the newer version is marked `SUPERSEDED`.
5. Any decisions already made stay pinned to the version that applied (`policy_version_id` is never rewritten).
6. Log rollback event; include in annual report.

Records to keep
- Every `policy_versions` record indefinitely (DRAFT, PENDING_APPROVAL, APPROVED, ACTIVE, SUPERSEDED, REJECTED, ROLLED_BACK).
- Change records, rationale, simulation output, and approvals: 10 years.
- Audit events: submit, approve, reject, activate, supersede, rollback.
- Annual report to Risk Committee: changes by tier, emergency changes and their ratification, rollbacks, rules with persistently high deviation rates.

Checklist before approving
1. The tier is correct — simulation against last 1,000 applications shows zero flips (standard) or any flips (material).
2. `rationale` is filled and readable.
3. `regulatory_ref` is present if a regulatory instruction forced the change.
4. `simulation_id` points to a completed impact run.
5. `approved_by` differs from `authored_by` (database-enforced).
6. `effective_from` is a future next-business-day timestamp (or immediate for emergency tightening).
7. Notice period met: 2 working days (standard) or 5 working days (material).
8. Only one `ACTIVE` version will exist per product after activation.
9. Previous version will be marked `SUPERSEDED`, not deleted.
10. `credit_decisions` and `recommendations` will be pinned to the new `policy_version_id` at decision time.
11. `model_version` (from `MODEL_VERSION`) is stored with the decision.
12. Emergency change is tightening only; loosening takes full path.
13. For emergency: written reason recorded; Risk Committee ratification due within 5 working days.
14. Rollback does not alter previously pinned decision versions.
15. 30-day post-change monitoring is scheduled before closing the change record.

title: Value stream mapping
summary: Value stream mapping separates touch time from queue time using observed timestamps, illustrated with a loan disbursement example.
body:
Mapping a process end to end so that **touch time** and **queue time** are visible separately. It is
the Measure-phase tool that shows where lead time actually goes.

## Worked example: a loan disbursement stream

Measure four things for each step: touch time, queue or wait time, rework rate, and work in progress
(the backlog by ageing).

In a lending disbursement, the pattern I expect is a small amount of real hands-on work sitting inside
days of elapsed time. The usual causes are work split across teams and systems, repeated validation,
missing documents and payment exceptions. That gap between work time and waiting time is the case
for Lean in a lending process.

## Process boxes in the disbursement stream

Pre-checklist → Agreement → Validation → Instruction → Payout → Reconcile / notify

## Data collection sheet

For each process box, record **actual** values:

| Field | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Volume / day | Throughput |
| Touch time | Hands-on work |
| Queue time | Waiting before the box |
| FPY / rework | First-pass yield |
| Owner / system | Who and where |

## The rule that matters most

> **Do not estimate queue time from SLA alone.** Observe timestamps, ageing and actual handoffs.

This is the instruction most likely to be impossible to follow — the timestamps may not exist in the
system for every handoff. Where nothing logs a handoff, that absence is itself a finding.

## Future state — controlled straight-through flow

The illustrative target design:

1. Digital readiness check — prevent incomplete cases entering
2. Single case file + e-sign — one source of truth
3. Rules-based validation — auto-clear the standard cases
4. Risk lane for exceptions — specialist review only where needed
5. Payout API + confirmation — status and UTR captured
6. Auto-reconcile + notify — close the loop same day

Targets: same-day or defined promise · higher first-pass yield · live ageing and exception
visibility · controls risk-based and auditable.

## Kaizen plan

The future state becomes owned actions: problem → countermeasure → owner → date. Without the owner
and the date it is a wish, not a plan.

Related: [[8-Wastes]] · [[DMAIC-Roadmap]] · [[Gemba-Plant-Visit]] · [[Six-Sigma-INDEX]]

title: Post-WWII silver coinage changes in India
summary: After WWII, India replaced silver coins with nickel and cupro-nickel issues, culminating in the 1950 Republic series.
body:
## 1. Economic and geopolitical reasons for phasing out silver (post-WWII)

- **Bullion value overtook face value.** Wartime demand pushed silver's market price up until the metal in a silver rupee was worth more than one rupee. By Gresham's law, people hoarded and melted silver coins, draining them from circulation. Removing precious metal was the only way to keep coins in the economy.
- **Progressive debasement was already under way.** The standard silver rupee (.917 fine) had been cut in **1940** to a *quaternary* alloy of **50% silver, 40% copper, 5% nickel, 5% zinc**. When even 50% silver became too valuable, silver was dropped entirely.
- **1946–47 switch to base metal.** Higher denominations (1 Rupee, ½ Rupee, ¼ Rupee) went to **pure nickel**; lower denominations (annas) used **cupro-nickel (~75% copper / 25% nickel)**. Nickel was chosen for hardness, wear resistance, and being ferromagnetic (an easy authenticity check).
- **Geopolitics.** India had lent large quantities of silver to the war effort (including US Lend-Lease silver shipped to India); post-war India needed to conserve foreign-exchange and bullion reserves and, after 1947, to assert monetary sovereignty. *(I won't quote an exact Lend-Lease tonnage — figures I can't verify precisely.)*

## 2. The 1947 "Tiger" One Rupee — technical breakdown (KM# 559)

- **Composition:** ~100% **nickel** (ferromagnetic). *Not* cupro-nickel.
- **Weight:** ~**11.9 g** (some catalogues list 11.8 g).
- **Diameter:** **28 mm**; thickness ~2.48 mm.
- **Edge:** **security edge** (milled).
- **Obverse:** crowned bust of **George VI** facing left, legend "GEORGE VI KING EMPEROR".
- **Reverse:** a **Bengal tiger**, "ONE RUPEE" and the date 1947, with the denomination in English, Devanagari and Urdu.
- **Mint marks:** struck only in 1947 at **Bombay** — identified by a **small diamond below the date** — and **Lahore** — **no mark**. (Bombay mintage ~118 M; Lahore ~42 M.) It was the last rupee of British India.

## 3. Demonetisation of older British Indian currency (incl. Victoria-era annas)

- The legal machinery was the **Indian Coinage Act, 1906** (amended by ordinance through the 1940s), letting the government declare series non-tender after set dates while allowing treasury exchange for a grace period.
- **Silver** was withdrawn in stages as the coinage was debased (1940 onward) and hoarding accelerated; older high-fineness silver (Victoria/Edward/George V) was steadily called in for its bullion.
- **Victoria-era base-metal annas and fractions** (¼ anna, ½ pice, 1/12 anna, and the later cupro-nickel one-anna) were worn, low-value pieces withdrawn gradually through routine treasury/bank recalls rather than one dramatic decree. *I can't give reliable exact dates or notification numbers for a "Victoria anna" demonetisation — I won't invent them.*
- **The real, verifiable endpoint for the anna itself:** the anna/pice system was abolished by **decimalisation** — the **Indian Coinage Act, 1955**, effective **1 April 1957** (the "naya paisa" system). Pre-decimal annas ceased to be legal tender in the years following. That is the defensible anchor date.

## 4. The 1950 Republic of India series — designs and release

- **Official release: 15 August 1950** (the pre-decimal "Anna series", the Republic's first coins).
- **Denominations:** 1 Pice, ½ Anna, 1 Anna, 2 Annas, ¼ Rupee, ½ Rupee, 1 Rupee. Metals: rupee fractions in **nickel**, annas in **cupro-nickel**, the pice in **bronze**. Shapes: 1 Anna scalloped, ½ Anna and 2 Annas square with rounded corners, the rest round.
- **Obverse (uniform):** the **Lion Capital of Ashoka** (Sarnath) at centre, with the legend **"GOVERNMENT OF INDIA"** and the date. The motto *Satyameva Jayate* was **not** part of the 1950 issue (added to coinage later).
- **Reverse (motif by group):**
  - **1, ½, ¼ Rupee** — denomination and date flanked by **ears of corn / grain sheaves** (agricultural self-sufficiency).
  - **2 Annas, 1 Anna, ½ Anna** — a **humped (Zebu/Nandi) bull**.
  - **1 Pice** — a **galloping horse**.
  Legends give the value in English and Devanagari.

title: Cercit lending platform blueprint
summary: The cercit lending platform blueprint outlines policies, admin parameters, impact analysis, and a phased build plan to turn cercit into an end-to-end lending system.
body:
Policies, admin parameter register, impact analysis and build plan for turning cercit into an end-to-end lending platform. 17 Sep 2026 Turning cercit into a lending platform Foundation live All foundation migrations run on Supabase, the rules engine is deployed on AWS, and the code is pushed. 13 migrations run on the live database 120 database checks passing 26 weeks, one module at a time 118 small tasks, each develop → integrate → go 229 admin fields, current / proposed / go-live Where the build stands. What "the rules are in the database" buys you Until today the credit rules lived in the browser, where anyone could read them and no record said which rules produced a given decision. Now a rule set is a version: it is written, proposed, approved by a second person, and starts on a date. The old version is closed at the exact moment the new one starts, so a decision made last month can still be read against the rules that were in force last month. How "change as a feature" actually works Five mechanisms. Together they mean a regulation change or a new provider is a configuration change with an approval, not a software release. 1. Parameters are data with a schema. Every row in Admin Parameter Register becomes a record that knows its type, unit, allowed range, owner role, approver role, whether it is locked, and which regulation it traces to. The admin screen is generated from that schema, so adding a parameter does not need a new screen. 2. Everything is effective-dated. A value has a from-date and a to-date. Changes are scheduled, not applied on click. Every decision records which version it used. 3. Rules are decision tables, not code. The 18 rules become rows: parameter, operator, threshold, severity, reason code, version. A server-side engine evaluates them. Thresholds never appear in source code. 4. Providers sit behind adapters. A KYC provider, bureau or AA connector implements one interface. Switching vendor is a dropdown on the activation tab. 5. Features ship dark. New capability is released switched off and turned on per tenant, product, branch or percentage, through Off → Sandbox → Pilot → Live. A sixth, worth building later: a regulatory watch. New RBI and UIDAI circulars are pulled and summarised, and each one that touches a parameter opens a change request for the Policy Manager. That is a good use of AI — see Future Proofing Decision Pack . What selling this requires A company buying cercit will check these before it looks at the features. They should sit in the admin area — a separate console that officers never see — but not all under the admin role . If the system administrator who creates users can also edit the bureau floor, one person can create an account, give it policy rights, change a rule, and approve it. Every control in Policy Change Management falls over. So the console is one place, and inside it each section has an owner role. The admin role owns people, organisation, integrations and flags. Policy sections are owned by the Policy Manager and approved by the Credit Head. What the admin role can do Create, edit, suspend and reactivate users Create custom roles by picking permissions from a fixed catalogue Assign roles, branches, products and sanction limits to users Run access reviews and see who holds what Activate or deactivate integrations and feature flags (with approval, below) Manage organisation settings: branches, calendar, languages Read the audit trail What the admin role cannot do Change any credit, pricing, KYC-risk or model parameter Decide, override or view a loan application Reveal full customer PII Approve their own role change, or change their own permissions Create a permission that is not in the catalogue Edit or delete audit records Permission catalogue Permissions are defined in code and versioned with the application. Admins compose roles from them; they cannot invent new ones. This is what keeps custom roles safe — a new role can only ever be a combination of known, reviewed capabilities. Grouped by area, roughly 45 permissions: Area Permissions Applications app.view.own , app.view.team , app.view.all , app.create , app.evaluate , app.decide , app.override , app.reassign Customer data pii.view.masked , pii.reveal , kyc.verify , kyc.edd.approve Policy policy.view , policy.author , policy.simulate , policy.approve , policy.emergency Pricing pricing.view , pricing.author , pricing.approve Models model.view , model.propose , model.approve Compliance aml.review , aml.file_str , grievance.handle , retention.manage , consent.view People user.view , user.manage , role.manage , role.approve , access.review Platform integration.manage , integration.approve , flag.manage , org.manage Oversight audit.view , report.view , report.export Scoping — role is not enough A commercial lender needs more than "is a credit officer". Access is the role plus attributes: Attribute Example Product Can decide new car, not CV Branch / region Chennai region only Amount Up to ₹10 lakh Channel Direct and dealer, not DSA Time Access expires on a date (contract staff, auditors) This is attribute-based access control layered on roles. It matters for selling the product: every lender's delegation-of-authority matrix is different, and hardcoding four roles will not survive the first customer. Role creation with maker-checker Admin drafts a role or a role change The system checks the conflicting-pair list and blocks toxic combinations outright A second approver (another admin or compliance) approves The change takes effect, and everyone holding the role is listed in the approval record An admin cannot approve a change that grants a permission to a role they hold. Joiners, movers, leavers Event Rule Joiner Account created from HR request, lowest role by default, MFA set up before first access Mover Old role removed on the same day the new one is granted — no accumulation Leaver Disabled same day; sessions killed; access to open cases reassigned Long leave Suspended after 45 days dormant Contract / auditor Access with an expiry date, never open-ended Break-glass access For a production incident where normal roles are not enough. A named break-glass account, disabled by default, enabled only by two people together, time-boxed to four hours, every action logged, and reviewed by compliance within one working day. Console layout Eleven sections. Each opens to a short list, not a wall of fields. # Section Contains (from Admin Parameter Register ) Owner edits Approver Visible to 1 People & access B admin admin (second) / compliance admin, compliance, auditor 2 Organisation A admin compliance admin, compliance 3 Products & credit policy C, D, E, F, G, H, J policy_manager credit_head governance roles 4 Pricing I policy_manager credit_head + finance governance roles 5 KYC & AML — the activation tab L, M, N compliance (KYC risk), admin (provider switch) compliance head compliance, admin, credit_head 6 Customer protection O compliance business head governance roles 7 Data & privacy P, T DPO / compliance DPO compliance, auditor 8 Models K model owner credit_head + CRO governance roles 9 Integrations S, Q admin compliance for anything touching KYC or bureau admin, compliance 10 Change control U — pending approvals, calendar, history, simulations — — every governance role 11 Feature flags V admin credit_head for decision-affecting flags admin, credit_head "Governance roles" means admin, policy_manager, credit_head, compliance and auditor. Officers and managers see none of this — they see the resulting policy as read-only text on the case screen. Each field in every section shows the same four things you asked for: current value, proposed value, proposed go-live date, status (draft / pending / approved / scheduled / live). The KYC activation tab The idea is sound and worth building exactly as you described: the admin turns methods on, and the provider plumbing sits behind the switch. Every KYC method is a card: Card field What it holds Status Off → Sandbox → Pilot → Live → Retired Provider Dropdown of providers that have an adapter built Credentials A pointer to the secrets store, never the key itself Limits e.g. Aadhaar OTP ₹60,000/year cap, 12-month full-CDD deadline Pilot scope Branches, products or a % of traffic Fallback What happens if this provider fails: next method, queue, manual Health Success rate, average latency, last error — last 24 hours Test connection Runs a sandbox call Go-live approval Compliance must approve Sandbox → Pilot and Pilot → Live Cards on the tab: in-person KYC, Aadhaar OTP e-KYC, Aadhaar face auth, V-CIP, CKYCR search/download/upload, DigiLocker, PAN verification, mobile OTP, sanctions & PEP screening, live photo capture. Some settings on these cards are locked and shown with a padlock rather than a toggle — V-CIP by the lender's own staff, Aadhaar stored as last-four only, biometrics never stored, risk category never shown to the customer. They are displayed so the admin can see the rule exists, but there is no way to switch them off from the console. That is deliberate. The same lifecycle for everything switchable KYC methods, bureau providers, the AA connector, document AI, auto-approval, new products — all follow Off → Sandbox → Pilot → Live → Retired. One pattern, learned once, audited once. It is also what makes "change as a feature" real: new capability ships dark and is switched on by configuration, not by a release. Review Access review quarterly. That makes the policy the regulated artifact, not the model. If the rule set is the thing that actually approves or declines a loan, then how rules get changed matters more than how the model scores. Right now the system has 18 policy rules, a rate grid, and an XGBoost model — and no governed way to change any of them. togglePolicyRule() writes straight to policy_rules.is_active with no approval and no audit trail. A person who can open the Policy Rules screen can switch off the CIBIL floor, and nothing in the system records that it happened or who did it. This framework closes that, and sets up the wider policy suite a lender is expected to hold. The four components, and what governs each cercit separates four things that are often conflated. Each attracts a different policy owner. Component Question it answers Governing policy Owner Document AI What does the document say? Document Verification & Authenticity; Outsourcing (AWS is material outsourcing); Records Retention Operations / CIO Data & Feature Engine What does the borrower's behaviour look like? Income Assessment; Account Aggregator Consent; Bureau Usage Credit Head ML Risk Model How risky is this pattern historically? Model Risk Management Chief Risk Officer Policy & Decision Engine Does this qualify under approved policy? Credit Policy ; Delegation of Authority; Deviation & Exception Credit Head, changes routed through Policy Manager Keeping these apart is what lets you answer an auditor's question. "The model said grade A but you declined" is only defensible if the policy that overrode it is versioned, approved, and pinned to that decision. Ownership and review calendar Policy Owner role Approver Review Credit Policy & rule thresholds Policy Manager (author) Credit Head / Risk Committee Annual + on trigger Rate grid / pricing Policy Manager (author) Credit Head + CFO Quarterly Model Risk Model owner CRO / Risk Committee Annual + on drift breach KYC/AML Compliance Officer (MLRO) Board Annual Access & SoD Admin Compliance Semi-annual access review Data Protection DPO / Legal Board Annual Fair Practices Code Business Head Board Bi-annual Ad-hoc review triggers, any policy: a regulatory change, a material incident (fraud, breach, mass decline), a model drift breach, a new product or segment, or an audit finding. The one structural decision Everything else follows from this: a Policy Manager must be able to author a policy change but never to activate one alone. Giving one role unilateral write access to the rule engine creates a larger blast radius than any underwriter has. An underwriter can mis-decide one case. A policy change mis-applied silently re-decides every case after it. So the role gets authoring rights plus a mandatory second approver, effective dating, and a full version history — see Policy Change Management . Open questions Does the Policy Manager sit under Credit or under Risk? Under Risk gives better independence from the sales-side pressure to loosen rules; under Credit gives faster turnaround. Recommendation: Risk, with a service-level commitment on turnaround so Credit does not lose speed. Cannot decision a loan application. No approve, reject, refer, or override on any individual case. No role check, no second approval, no audit event, no record of the previous value, no effective date. The Policy Rules screen calls it directly from a switch control. The consequences, in order of severity: A credit rule can be disabled by anyone who reaches the screen, and nothing records it. There is no way to answer "what rule set was in force when this loan was decided?" — policy_version is a string on the rule row, and rules mutate in place. A decision made in August cannot be reconstructed after a September change. There is no rollback. The prior threshold is simply gone. is_active is the only thing the UI changes, but the same table holds threshold_value and severity_on_fail — an UPDATE could change a cut-off with the same lack of ceremony. Point 2 is the one that would fail an audit. Everything else is recoverable; an unreconstructible decision is not. Change tiering A single approval path for every change gets bypassed, because most changes are trivial and the ceremony feels absurd. Three tiers, distinguished by whether the change can alter an outcome. Tier What it covers Approver Notice Material Anything that can flip a decision: rule threshold, severity, activating or deactivating a rule, rate grid rates, LTV/FOIR/tenure caps, band boundaries, model promotion Credit Head + Risk Committee noting 5 working days; effective from next business day at earliest Standard New reason code wording, display order, rule description, employer category label, non-pricing fee text Credit Head 2 working days Cosmetic Typo, label, help text, sort order — provably cannot affect an outcome Policy Manager self-serve, logged Immediate The test for material versus standard: run the change through impact simulation. If zero of the last 1,000 applications change decision, it is standard. If any change, it is material. That makes the tier a fact rather than an opinion. Emergency tightening is a fourth path, below. Lifecycle flowchart TD A[Change requested] --> B[Policy Manager drafts version] B --> C[Impact simulation vs last 1000 applications] C --> D{Any decision flips?} D -- No --> E[Tier: Standard] D -- Yes --> F[Tier: Material] E --> G[Submit for approval] F --> G G --> H{Approver review} H -- Reject --> I[Back to draft with comments] I --> B H -- Approve --> J[Scheduled with effective date] J --> K[Activate at effective date] K --> L[Previous version marked superseded] L --> M[Post-change monitoring 30 days] M --> N{Behaving as modelled?} N -- No --> O[Rollback or corrective change] N -- Yes --> P[Close change record] The two states that do not exist today and matter most are scheduled and superseded . Scheduled lets a change be approved now and take effect on a date, which is how you avoid mid-day rule switches. Superseded keeps the old version readable forever instead of overwriting it. Version model The proposal, described rather than coded — implementation is a separate decision. A policy_versions record carries the state, not the individual rules. Rules belong to a version. policy_versions version_id e.g. 2026.09.01 status DRAFT | PENDING_APPROVAL | APPROVED | ACTIVE | SUPERSEDED | REJECTED | ROLLED_BACK tier MATERIAL | STANDARD | COSMETIC authored_by -> users (must hold policy_author) submitted_at approved_by -> users (must hold policy_approve, must differ from authored_by) approved_at effective_from timestamptz effective_to timestamptz, null while active rationale text, mandatory regulatory_ref text, nullable — the circular or direction that forced it simulation_id -> the impact run that supported approval Two constraints carry the control: approved_by <> authored_by , enforced by the database, not by the UI exactly one version may hold status = ACTIVE per product at any timestamp And the rule rows become version-scoped: a rule change writes a new rule row against a new version rather than updating the existing row. The current policy_rules table already has policy_version ; what is missing is that it is not a foreign key to anything and rules are edited in place. Pinning decisions to policy The audit-critical piece. Every credit decision must record the exact policy version that produced it. credit_decisions and recommendations should carry policy_version_id written at decision time. policy_results already stores per-rule outcomes per application, which is most of the way there — but without a version pin, a rule that later changes its threshold makes the stored result uninterpretable. You can see that FOIR_CAP failed; you cannot see what the cap was that day. Same for the model: store model_version alongside. MODEL_VERSION is already a constant in onnx-inference.ts ; it just is not persisted with the decision. Impact simulation Before approval, a change is run against recent applications in a sandbox, producing: Count and percentage of decisions that flip, in each direction The flip breakdown by decision band — approve to reject is a very different event from maybe to approve Affected volume by employer category and by CIBIL band Estimated effect on approval rate and on weighted average rate This is the artifact the approver actually reads. "Tighten FOIR from 50 to 45" means nothing on its own; "would have declined 34 of the last 1,000, of which 29 were Category C" is a decision. The infrastructure is largely there — scripts/run-test-cases.ts already runs 40 scenarios through the policy engine. Simulation is that, pointed at historical applications instead of fixtures. Emergency changes Only for tightening, never for loosening. A rule can be made stricter, or switched on, without the full notice period when there is an active fraud pattern or a regulatory instruction with immediate effect. Activated by Credit Head with a written reason Effective immediately Ratified by the Risk Committee within 5 working days, or it lapses automatically Logged and reported at the next committee meeting regardless of outcome Loosening always takes the full path. The asymmetry is deliberate: an over-tight rule declines good business, which is visible and recoverable; an over-loose rule writes bad loans, which surfaces months later. Rollback Because versions are immutable and superseded ones are retained, rollback is activating a prior version rather than reversing an edit. It follows the same approval path as a material change, except when reverting an emergency change within its ratification window. Anything already decided under the rolled-back version stays decided under it. Rollback is never retrospective — the pinned version on each decision is the record of what actually applied. Post-change monitoring For 30 days after a material change: Actual decision mix against what the simulation predicted Deviation and override rate on the affected rules — a spike means the threshold is wrong, not that officers are misbehaving Approval rate, and early delinquency once the vintage is old enough to read A change whose actual behaviour diverges materially from its simulation is a finding about the simulation, and should be raised as one.
