Today that is one model, plus several rule-based calculators that are deliberately excluded because they are deterministic arithmetic, not inference. Component In scope Why cercit-risk-v1 XGBoost classifier Yes Probabilistic, trained, drifts risk-score-model.ts grade bands Yes Maps model output to a decision-relevant grade policy-rule-engine.ts No Deterministic rules — governed by Policy Change Management FOIR, LTV, EMI calculators No Fixed formulas bureau-score-interpreter.ts Borderline Rule-based today; in scope if it becomes fitted Model inventory Field Current value Model ID cercit-risk-v1 Type XGBoost binary classifier Target 30+ DPD within 12 months Features 18 Training data 10,000 synthetic profiles generated from industry benchmarks AUC-ROC 0.91 PR-AUC 0.61 Brier 0.023 Base rates in training bad30 4.0%, default90 1.1% Serving ONNX via onnxruntime-web , wasm, in the browser Output use P(30+DPD) mapped to grades A–E; advisory to the officer Owner Unassigned — gap Validation None performed — gap Approval to deploy None recorded — gap Tiering Tier the model by consequence, and let the tier drive how much governance it attracts. Tier Definition This model Critical Auto-decisions without human review Phase 2 target High Materially shapes a human decision, or sets price Current — Phase 1 Low Informational, no decision influence cercit is Phase 1: the officer decides and the model advises. That is High, not Critical. But the gap between the two is one product decision — the moment auto-approval turns on, this becomes Critical and needs independent validation before, not after. Findings on the current model Four, from reading the implementation. The first two are governance; the last two are design choices that are defensible but must be written down rather than discovered. The model file is publicly served. public/models/cercit-risk-v1.onnx ships as a static asset, so anyone who loads the site can download the trained model. Two consequences: the model is extractable IP, and more importantly it is probeable — a broker can run it offline and find the exact feature combination that lands grade A, then shape applications to hit it. For a Phase 1 demo on synthetic data this is acceptable and worth noting. Before real lending, scoring moves server-side. Inference runs on the client. The score is computed in the borrower-facing or officer-facing browser. Anything computed client-side can be manipulated client-side. If a score computed in the browser is ever written back and stored as the official risk score, the trust boundary is broken — the server would be accepting a number it did not compute. This needs checking before launch, and server-side scoring is the fix. Contributions are counterfactual, not SHAP. risk-score-model.ts produces per-feature deltas by swapping a feature to its training mean and re-running inference. That is a reasonable, cheap approximation and it is honest — but it is not Shapley, and the UI should not imply it is. True SHAP importances exist only as global values in the meta JSON. If an officer or a regulator is told "this is why the model scored the file", the method has to be stated accurately. The known limitation is a policy dependency, not a defect. A clean file with one blemish — bureau 640, nothing else wrong — still scores grade A, because in the training data such files mostly perform. The policy engine catches it with a hard floor at 650. This is the intended division of labour, and it means the model's weakness is load-bearing on a specific rule. If BUREAU_FLOOR is ever relaxed, this limitation becomes live exposure. That coupling should be recorded against both the model and the rule. Development standards Training data lineage documented: source, generation method, date, row count, base rates. For synthetic data, the benchmark assumptions have to be written down and attributed — they currently live in car-loan-industry-knowledge and scripts/generate-training-data.ts and nowhere else. Feature definitions with the exact transformation, and an explicit check that no feature is a proxy for a protected attribute Train/test split and its rationale; no leakage from target into features Reproducible: seed, versions, and a regenerable pipeline Model card per version covering intended use, out-of-scope use, performance by segment, and known failure modes Synthetic training data deserves its own caution. A model fitted to data generated from assumptions will reproduce those assumptions with high confidence and no external validation. AUC 0.91 against synthetic holdout says the model learned the generator, not that it predicts real defaults. That distinction must be stated wherever the metric is quoted, including in portfolio material. Validation Independent of the developer. For a team too small for a separate function, an external reviewer or a structured self-challenge with documented dissent. Before any version goes live: Conceptual soundness — do the features make credit sense, and is the target definition right Performance on a holdout the developer did not see Performance by segment: employer category, CIBIL band, ticket size, geography. A model that is strong overall and weak on Category C is a model that misprices a specific population. Stability — PSI on features between training and recent applications Calibration, not just discrimination. Grade bands are cut on absolute probability thresholds (A < 1%, B < 2.5%), so a mis-calibrated model puts files in the wrong band even with a good AUC. Brier 0.023 is a start; a reliability curve is the actual test. Benchmark against the rules-only baseline. computeRiskScoreLegacy still exists and is the natural challenger — if the model does not beat it, it is complexity without return. Bias testing across age, gender, and geography, given DPDP and fairness expectations Approval and deployment Model promotion follows the material-change path in Policy Change Management : Model owner proposes with the model card and validation report Impact simulation against recent applications — decision flips in each direction Credit Head plus CRO approve; Risk Committee notes Effective date scheduled; model_version pinned to every decision from that point Prior version retained and re-activatable No model version reaches production without a recorded approver, the same rule as policy. Ongoing monitoring Check Frequency Trigger Score distribution vs training Monthly Mean shift beyond tolerance Feature PSI Monthly PSI > 0.2 on any feature Grade band mix Monthly Material shift in band proportions Calibration — predicted vs actual bad rate by band Quarterly, once vintages mature Actual outside predicted band range Discrimination — AUC on realised outcomes Semi-annual Drop below an agreed floor Override rate against model grade Monthly Officers systematically disagreeing is a signal about the model Segment performance Semi-annual Any segment materially worse Two of these cannot run yet and should be stated as such: calibration and realised AUC need actual repayment outcomes, which a synthetic-data Phase 1 does not have. Until real vintages exist, the model is unvalidated against reality regardless of its holdout metrics. Retirement A version is retired when a successor is approved, when monitoring breaches persist without remediation, or when the portfolio it was fitted on no longer resembles the book. Retired versions stay archived and readable — decisions made under them must remain reconstructible. Gaps to close, in order Assign a model owner — nobody is accountable today Record a deployment approval for cercit-risk-v1 , retrospectively if need be Write the model card, including the synthetic-data caveat Pin model_version to stored decisions Move scoring server-side before any real customer data Stand up drift monitoring Independent validation before Phase 2 auto-decisioning 05-Credit-Policy.md Credit policy draft for review Created: 16 Sep 2026 Policy version in code: 2026.08 Related: Policy Change Management · Model Risk Management · Policy Gap Register Why write this down The 18 rules in policy-rule-engine.ts are the credit policy. No document describes them, which means the code is the only statement of what cercit will and will not lend against. That is backwards: the document should be the policy and the code its implementation, so the two can be reconciled and a reviewer can challenge a threshold without reading TypeScript. This document states the policy as currently implemented, and flags where the implementation disagrees with itself. Product scope Dimension Phase 1 Product New car loans only Segment Salaried, single applicant Source Direct leads Excluded Used vehicles, CV, 3W, top-ups, renewals, restructured, title loans, self-employed, co-applicants Bureau Mandatory — no file proceeds without one Anything outside this needs a policy amendment, not an exception. Decision bands Band CIBIL Outcome Indicative rate Approve 750–900 Auto-approve subject to all hard rules passing 8.99% Maybe 650–749 Route to officer review 9.90% Reject 300–649 Auto-decline Not offered Rate is then loaded by employer category — A +0.00%, B +0.40%, C +1.25%. Band caps on LTV, FOIR and tenure interact with category caps; the tighter of the two applies. The rule set Nine hard rules and nine soft. A hard failure declines the file regardless of model grade. A soft failure flags for review and can affect pricing but does not by itself decline. Hard rules Rule Threshold Rationale AGE_MIN Applicant ≥ 21 Contractual capacity and income stability BUREAU_FLOOR Score ≥ 650 Below this, observed default rates do not support the product. Also the backstop for a known model weakness — see below. FOIR_LIMIT Fixed obligations ≤ 50% of income Repayment capacity ceiling LTV_LIMIT Loan ≤ 120% of ex-showroom On-road funding ceiling, covering registration and insurance NO_SEVERE_DPD No 90+ DPD or write-off in 12 months Recent severe delinquency is the strongest single predictor GOVT_EMPLOYEE_CHECK Govt applicants need 3+ years permanent service Excludes contract and probationary staff whose tenure looks stable but is not FREE_INCOME_FLOOR ≥ 15% of net salary remains after all EMIs including the proposed one FOIR alone passes thin files at low incomes; this is the absolute floor TENURE_CAP Max 84 months; up to 120 only for a govt employee on a car under Rs 12L Long tenures on depreciating assets go underwater LTV_100_SALARIED Above 100% of on-road needs verified salary and FOIR within limit; above 90% without verified income fails Caps unverified-income exposure Soft rules Rule Threshold Effect AGE_MAX ≤ 65 at maturity Review; may shorten tenure BUREAU_GOOD ≥ 700 for preferential terms Pricing FOIR_OPTIMAL ≤ 40% for best rates Pricing NO_RECENT_DPD No 30/60 DPD in 6 months Review flag LOW_BOUNCES No bounces in statement period Review flag SALARY_REGULAR Salary credits in 5+ of last 6 months Review flag EMPLOYER_VERIFIED Employer on the verified master Review flag; drives category CC_SERVICING Card not serviced at minimum-due only Review flag — revolving behaviour predicts stress BUREAU_RECALIBRATED ≥ 700 for bank-grade terms; 650–699 priced as NBFC Pricing, post Feb-2026 recalibration (~50 point industry drop) Known inconsistencies Three, surfaced by writing this down. Each needs a decision, not a code change made quietly. FOIR base is ambiguous. FOIR_LIMIT is described in code as "Fixed obligations ≤ 50% of gross income". The project specification says FOIR max 50% on net salary. These are materially different — a 50% gross FOIR is far more permissive than 50% net. Whichever is intended, both the code comment and the spec must say the same thing, and the FREE_INCOME_FLOOR rule (defined on net) should use a consistent base. LTV is measured on two different denominators. LTV_LIMIT caps at 120% of ex-showroom . LTV_100_SALARIED caps at 100% of on-road . Both are legitimate measures and they are not comparable. A file can pass one and fail the other in ways that are hard to reason about. The policy should state which is the primary control and what the other is doing. Tenure cap interacts with the band cap. TENURE_CAP allows 84 months, while rate_grid carries max_tenure_months of 96 for the Approve band and 84 for Maybe, and employer categories cap at 84 or 60. Three sources for one number. The rule should state the precedence explicitly: the tightest of rule, band, and category. Model interaction The model advises; policy decides. In practice that means: The model produces P(30+DPD), mapped to grades A (<1%), B (<2.5%), C (<6%), D (<15%), E (≥15%) A hard rule failure declines the file whatever the grade A grade E file passing all hard rules still goes to officer review, not auto-approve One coupling must be recorded rather than left implicit: the model scores a clean file with a single blemish — bureau 640, nothing else adverse — as grade A, because in the training data such files mostly perform. BUREAU_FLOOR is what catches this. That rule is therefore load-bearing on a model weakness, and cannot be relaxed without first retraining or revalidating the model. See Model Risk Management . Deviations and exceptions A deviation is a documented departure from policy for one case. It is not a policy change. Only credit_manager and above may approve a deviation, and never on their own case Every deviation records the rule deviated from, the reason, the approver, and compensating factors Hard rules on BUREAU_FLOOR , NO_SEVERE_DPD and FREE_INCOME_FLOOR should be non-deviable — if they need deviating regularly, the threshold is wrong and belongs in a policy change Deviations are reviewed monthly. A rule with a persistently high deviation rate is a standing agenda item for the Policy Manager. override_logs exists in the schema for this. It is not yet wired to a rule-level reason. Delegation of authority To be set. The schema already carries users.max_sanction_amount and daily_case_limit , and nothing enforces either. Proposed shape: Role Sanction limit Deviation authority Underwriter Up to their configured limit None Manager Higher limit Soft rules only Credit Head All Soft and non-listed hard rules Risk Committee — Policy change only Enforcement must be server-side — see Access Control and SoD . Review Annual, and on any of: an RBI change affecting credit norms, a bureau recalibration, a model version promotion, a material shift in portfolio performance, or three consecutive months of elevated deviation on any rule. 06-KYC-Policy.md KYC policy draft for review Created: 16 Sep 2026 Source research: Downloads/KYC Policy.md (Sameer, Sep 2026) Related: Policy Framework Overview · Access Control and SoD · Policy Gap Register Standing caveat cercit runs on synthetic data and is not a licensed lender. Nothing here is being applied to a real customer. The point of writing it now is that the shape of the onboarding flow has to be right — retrofitting KYC into a flow designed without it is the expensive path, and the data model decisions being made now (what gets stored, masked, retained) are hard to reverse later. Where the build already diverges from what a real deployment needs, that is called out rather than papered over. Regulatory basis RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016, as updated), PMLA 2002 and Rules, Aadhaar Act 2016 and UIDAI regulations, IT Act 2000 s.43A and s.72A, DPDP Act 2023. RBI requires a Board-approved KYC policy built on four elements: Customer Acceptance Policy, Risk Management, Customer Identification Procedure, and ongoing monitoring. Scope for Phase 1 Individual salaried borrowers, single applicant, Indian resident, new car loan. Not covered: NRI, non-individuals, joint applicants, minors, PEPs as a served segment (they are an EDD trigger, not a product). Customer acceptance No anonymous or fictitious-name relationships No onboarding where identity cannot be verified against an OVD No onboarding where the applicant appears on a sanctions or watchlist Sole proprietors and self-employed are out of Phase 1 scope entirely Identification — what is required Item Requirement In cercit today Identity + address One OVD: passport, driving licence, Aadhaar (proof of possession), voter ID, NREGA job card, NPR letter Apply form collects Aadhaar and PAN Address, if OVD lacks current Deemed OVD — utility bill, property tax receipt, pension order, employer accommodation letter. Current proof within 3 months Address fields collected; no document-level proof flow Tax ID PAN, or Form 60 where unavailable PAN collected and validated by pan-validator.ts Live photograph Required in the customer file Not implemented Contact Mobile and email, mobile OTP-verified Collected; OTP verification not implemented Consent Explicit, before any Aadhaar or CKYCR use Not implemented Income documents are not a KYC requirement — they come from the credit policy. Worth keeping separate so the two do not get conflated in the document checklist. Onboarding methods Three are permitted. Phase 1 should pick one and design for the others. In-person. Originals verified, copies captured, live photo and signature taken. Fully compliant, slowest. Aadhaar e-KYC. OTP or biometric against UIDAI, with consent. Returns demographic data only. Non-face-to-face, so RBI treats the resulting account as higher risk until address is positively verified. Only masked Aadhaar may be retained. Video KYC (V-CIP). Live geo-tagged video call, PAN and OVD shown on camera, liveness check through interactive questions, session recorded and retained. Treated on par with in-person once all criteria are met. Recommendation for cercit: design the data model for V-CIP and Aadhaar e-KYC, since a digital-first car loan will not send people to branches. But the flow must record which method was used per customer, because the risk treatment differs. That field does not exist today. Risk categorisation Every customer gets a rating, and the rating drives re-KYC frequency and the depth of due diligence. Rating Examples Re-KYC Low Salaried, verified employer, local address, Aadhaar-verified 10 years Medium Address mismatch, employer unverified, non-face-to-face onboarding 8 years High PEP or related, adverse media, sanctions near-match, unusual transaction patterns, cash-intensive profile 2 years Non-face-to-face onboarding is high-risk by default until address is positively verified. Additional controls RBI expects there: one-to-one mobile binding so no alternate number can be linked post-CIP, and first credit from a known source. Enhanced due diligence Triggered by high risk. Measures: source of funds and wealth verification, senior management approval before onboarding, mandatory PAN verification, and closer transaction monitoring. Every EDD case and its outcome is documented and auditable. Data handling — the part that binds the build This is where KYC policy and the data model meet, and where decisions made now are costly to undo. Aadhaar is never stored in full. Not the number, not an unmasked image, not in logs. Only the last four digits, or an irreversible hash. The schema gets this right — customers.aadhaar_last_four VARCHAR(4) and no full-Aadhaar column. Biometrics are never stored. UIDAI prohibits it. If biometric authentication is used, only the authentication result may be retained. PAN is masked in storage and display. Migration 012 encrypts PAN at rest and serves a masked form; full value is available only through fn_customer_pii , which checks the caller is an active officer and writes a PII_REVEAL audit event. That is the right shape. It is written and not yet applied. Document images are access-controlled and hashed. Store one copy, keep a hash for tamper detection, watermark "for KYC use only". Not implemented. Encryption. TLS 1.2+ in transit, AES-256 at rest, keys in a managed store with rotation. Migration 012 uses pgcrypto with the key in a locked-down app_secrets table — workable, though a managed key service is better before real data. Retention Data Period Basis KYC identification records 5 years after relationship ends RBI / PMLA Transaction records 5 years from transaction RBI / PMLA Video KYC recordings 5 years after closure RBI MD Audit and access logs 5 years Reconstruction E-KYC tokens, UIDAI responses Discard on completion UIDAI — never persist Anonymised analytics Indefinite Outside DPDP if irreversible Where tax law requires longer (often 8 years for financial records), the longer period wins. DPDP requires erasure once the purpose is served and no law mandates retention, so a retention schedule with enforced purge is required — not just a stated period. Legal holds suspend purge and are reviewed periodically so nothing is held indefinitely by default. None of this is implemented. There is no retention field, no purge job, and no legal-hold concept in the schema. Re-KYC Triggered by schedule (per risk rating above) or by event: address change, risk re-rating, adverse media, unusual activity, or a minor turning adult. If nothing has changed, a self-declaration suffices. If address changed, fresh proof is required. Re-rating upward requires fresh OVD for identity and address. Gaps for Phase 1, in priority order No consent capture anywhere in the apply flow — this is foundational for both Aadhaar use and DPDP No onboarding-method field, so risk treatment cannot differ by method No customer risk rating, and therefore no re-KYC schedule No mobile OTP verification No live photograph capture No document hash or tamper detection No retention schedule, purge job, or legal hold PII encryption written but not applied No sanctions or watchlist screening No CKYCR integration — worth designing for, since it removes most of the document collection burden Items 1 to 3 change the data model and should be settled before more screens are built on top of the current shape. The rest can follow. 07-Policy-Gap-Register.md Gap register Policy and control gap register live register Created: 16 Sep 2026 Related: Policy Framework Overview · Role Policy Manager · Access Control and SoD · Policy Change Management · Model Risk Management · Credit Policy · KYC Policy Every item here was found by reading the cercit code and schema, not from a generic checklist. Severity is judged against Phase 1 (synthetic data, portfolio build) and separately against a real deployment, because they differ sharply. Severity key P1 — blocks credible Phase 1 completion; the control gap is visible in the product itself P2 — must exist before any real customer data P3 — needed for a licensed operation, not for the build Register # Gap Where P1/P2/P3 Fix 1 Policy rules writable with no approval or audit. togglePolicyRule() does a direct UPDATE on is_active api.ts , policy-rules.tsx:115 P1 Route all policy writes through the workflow in Policy Change Management ; revoke direct UPDATE from authenticated 2 No policy version pinned to decisions — past decisions cannot be reconstructed after a rule changes credit_decisions , recommendations P1 Add policy_version_id and model_version , written at decision time 3 Rules are edited in place; no history, no rollback policy_rules P1 Version-scoped rule rows; superseded versions retained 4 No policy_manager or credit_head role exists users.role , auth.ts P1 Add both, with the permission split in Access Control and SoD 5 Role permissions are client-side only; nothing enforces them server-side auth.ts ROLE_PERMISSIONS P1 Enforce in RLS and SECURITY DEFINER functions. fn_customer_pii is the pattern 6 RLS written but never applied — every table open to the anon key sql/009_rls_policies.sql P1 Run it 7 Sanction limits not enforced. max_sanction_amount exists and nothing reads it users , fn_officer_decision P1 Check in the decision RPC 8 Model deployed with no owner, no validation record, no approval cercit-risk-v1 P1 Assign owner, write the model card, record approval retrospectively 9 [email removed] bypasses authentication even when Supabase is configured login.tsx P1 Product decision — documented backdoor or remove 10 No deviation register at rule level; override_logs not wired to a rule reason override_logs P2 Capture rule deviated from, reason, approver, compensating factors 11 Model file publicly downloadable and inference runs client-side — model is extractable and probeable public/models/*.onnx P2 Move scoring server-side before real data 12 No consent capture anywhere in the apply flow /apply P2 Foundational for Aadhaar use and DPDP 13 No customer risk rating, so no re-KYC schedule can exist customers P2 Add rating and next-review date 14 No onboarding-method field; risk treatment cannot differ by method customers P2 Add method; drive risk rating from it 15 PII encryption written but not applied sql/012 , sql/013 P2 Run after review 16 No retention schedule, purge job, or legal-hold concept schema-wide P2 Retention fields plus an enforced purge 17 No sanctions or watchlist screening — P2 Required before any real onboarding 18 No mobile OTP verification, no live photograph /apply P2 Both are RBI CIP expectations 19 No document hash or tamper detection documents P2 Store a hash per file 20 No MFA on any account, including privileged roles auth P2 Enable for policy_manager , credit_head , admin at minimum 21 No periodic access review — P2 Quarterly recertification; conflicting-pair report 22 fraud_signals table exists but is unused; no fraud risk policy fraud_signals P2 Wire or remove — an empty control table reads as a control that exists 23 No grievance redressal mechanism not built P2 RBI FPC requirement 24 No drift monitoring on the model — P2 PSI, score distribution, calibration once vintages exist 25 Pricing policy undocumented though the rate grid exists rate_grid P2 Write it; tie changes to the material-change path 26 Two sources of truth for pricing — engine.ts uses a 5-band mock matrix, DB has 3 bands engine.ts , rate_grid P1 Reconcile; one of them is wrong 27 FOIR base ambiguous — code says gross, spec says net policy-rule-engine.ts P1 Decide and align both 28 LTV measured on two denominators — 120% ex-showroom vs 100% on-road LTV_LIMIT , LTV_100_SALARIED P2 State which is primary 29 Tenure cap has three sources — rule 84, band 96, category 84/60 rule engine, rate_grid , employer_category_pricing P2 State precedence: tightest wins 30 Model's known weakness is load-bearing on BUREAU_FLOOR , recorded nowhere — P2 Record the coupling against both 31 Outsourcing policy absent though AWS and Supabase are material outsourcing — P3 Register, due diligence, exit plan 32 No BCP/DR, IT/IS, or fraud policy documents — P3 Required for a licensed entity 33 Synthetic-data caveat not stated wherever AUC 0.91 is quoted docs, LinkedIn, review report P2 The metric measures fit to a generator, not prediction of real defaults Themes The control gaps cluster in one place. Items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 are all the same underlying problem: the system has no concept of authority . It knows who a user is, and it knows what they did, but it has no server-side notion of what they are allowed to do or what approval a change required. That is the Phase 1 work. Reconstructibility is the audit-critical one. Item 2 is the single gap most likely to fail a review. Everything else is a control that can be added; an unreconstructible decision is permanently unrecoverable. Any application decided before version pinning exists has no defensible record of what rules produced it. Three internal inconsistencies were found by writing the policy down — items 26, 27, 29. None was visible from the code alone; each surfaced from comparing the implementation against a plain-language statement of intent. That is the argument for the document existing. Sequence Items 26, 27 — resolve the contradictions before building governance on top of them Items 6, 5, 7 — apply RLS, enforce roles and limits server-side Items 4, 1, 3, 2 — the roles, then the change workflow, then versioning, then decision pinning Item 8 — model governance record Item 9 — decide on the demo backdoor Everything P2, before any real customer Found during the build (17 Sep 2026) Found while writing and testing foundation migrations 015–020 on a local Postgres. "Fixed" means fixed in code on local main ; it takes effect when the migration is run in Supabase. # Gap Where Status 34 fn_officer_decision was explicitly granted to anon — anyone holding the public anon key could record approve/reject decisions without logging in sql/007 Fixed in 018 (needs app.decide ; anon cannot execute) 35 Every SECURITY DEFINER function was executable by PUBLIC by default, including fn_list_applications , which returns every applicant's name and email sql/004 , 006 Fixed in 018/019 (permission check + execute revoked); internal pipeline steps closed to the API 36 Decision audit events and override logs recorded (SELECT id FROM users LIMIT 1) as the actor — the first user in the table, not the person who acted sql/007 Fixed in 018 37 fn_submit_full_application accepts the CIBIL score as a caller-supplied parameter (default 750), so the assessment trusts a number the browser sends sql/006 Open — Underwriting UW3 (score must come from the bureau report) 38 Most SECURITY DEFINER functions in 004/006 have no pinned search_path sql/004 , 006 Partly fixed (submission, decision, list, PII); rest retired with the engine move (FD4) 39 Migration 012 would have failed on Supabase twice: on the required mobile column, and because pgcrypto lives in the extensions schema there sql/012 Fixed before anyone ran it 40 When the database refuses a request, getApplications silently shows mock applications src/lib/api.ts Open — replaced as each module moves off mock data 41 src/lib/supabase-rpc.ts calls eight functions that do not exist; nothing imports it src/lib Open — FD6.1 cleanup 42 togglePolicyRule reported success even when row-level security changed nothing src/lib/api.ts Fixed (counts returned rows) Status updates to earlier items: #1 (policy rules writable) — 020 written, run when ready (it disables the Policy Rules switches until Credit control replaces them). #2, #3 (no versioning) — tables and guards in 016/017; decisions start recording the version in CC5. #5 (no server-side role checks) — 018. #6 (RLS not applied) — still open until 009 is run (FD3). #43 PII key handling (17 Sep 2026, open). The key created by migration 012 was read back and pasted into the assistant chat window during the first run. Test data only, no customer records, so no real exposure. Before any real data is loaded: generate a fresh key, re-encrypt the stored values in one transaction, and keep the spare copy in a password manager. Rule for the build: secrets are never pasted into chat, email, or any file inside the public repository. 00-REVIEW-NOTES.md Hermes drafts — review Run overnight 16–17 Sep 2026 through hermes -z (free model). Seven drafts, about seven minutes of model time in total. Claude did a first-pass check the same night; the verdicts below are from that check, not a full review. Draft Size First-pass verdict What to do H1 Admin Field Tooltips 229 tooltips Usable. Covers every field in the register, no invented numbers Light edit during T1.12 H2 Lending Glossary 45 terms Was wrong, now corrected. Hermes misdefined 11 terms (AUA/KUA, KIN, RLS, PSI, blind index, cooling-off, CTR, LSP, OVD, UCIC, effective dating) and claimed cercit already does things it does not. Claude rewrote it Use the corrected version; check the one remaining verify H3 SOP Policy Change ~6 KB Mostly faithful. One inversion: says the Credit Head "notes" material changes — the policy says the Credit Head approves and the Risk Committee notes Fix that line, then review in T1.6 H5 RBAC Test Cases 30 negative + 10 positive Good. Stays close to the access-control policy. N11/N12 overlap; N26 is not testable as written Merge N11/N12, rewrite N26, then build as T1.19 H6 Admin Console User Stories 29 stories Thin. Asked for 35–45 with 3–5 criteria each; got 29 with one compressed Given/When/Then each. The "mover" story is mislabelled as a suspension Expand acceptance criteria before loading into Jira H7 SOP KYC ~4.6 KB Faithful. Every number matches the KYC policy (3 months, 2/8/10 years) Review during T2.4 H8 P1 Policy Drafts 4 policies Usable. One invented number: "post-release verification within 24 hours" in the release-control policy — not from any source Decide the number or remove it; review in T1.21 Pattern worth noting Where Hermes was handed a source document (H3, H5, H7), it stayed close to it. Where it was asked to write from general knowledge (H2), it produced confident, wrong definitions. That matches your routing guide: give free models the facts, let them do the writing, and have Claude check anything they state on their own.

title: Guide to the new Vahan public report portal
summary: Guide to the new Vahan public report portal explains menus, filters, glossary, and quirks for accessing India's vehicle‑registration data.
body:
> **A plain-language community guide to India's new Vahan vehicle-registration data portal — its menus, every report filter, a glossary of all values, and the known quirks to watch for.**

---

## ⚠️ The old dashboard is going away

The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH) has published this notice on the old Vahan dashboard:

> 📢 **The new Public Dashboard is now available. Vahan4Dashboard will be discontinued after 15 August 2026.** Please use the new dashboard for the latest data and features. For any issues, contact **[email removed]**.

If you have bookmarks, scripts, or reports that rely on the old page, you need to move to the new portal. This guide is here to make that switch painless.

| | Old (retiring) | New (use this) |
|---|---|---|
| **Report builder** | [vahan4dashboard reportview](https://vahan.parivahan.gov.in/vahan4dashboard/vahan/view/reportview.xhtml) | [Vahan Public Report](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/vahanpublicreport?lang=en) |
| **Visual dashboard** | (same old app) | [Vahan Public Dashboard](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/publicdashboard/vahan?lang=en) |
| **Status** | Discontinued after **15 Aug 2026** | Live now |

---

## What this guide is

The new **Vahan Public Report** page lets anyone pull India's vehicle-registration statistics (from 1970 onward) filtered by state, RTO, maker, vehicle class, fuel, emission norm, and more. But the page is dense, some option names are cryptic, and a few controls only appear after the page loads.

This guide inventories **every menu and filter value** on the new portal and explains each in business-friendly terms, so you can find and understand the data without guesswork.

**It is an unofficial, community-maintained reference** — not affiliated with MoRTH or NIC. Data source and copyright belong to MoRTH/NIC (see [Attribution](#attribution--disclaimer)).

## Who it's for
Analysts, journalists, researchers, auto-industry and finance professionals, and anyone who used the old Vahan dashboard and needs to find their way around the new one.

---

## 📖 Contents

1. **[What's changing](docs/[[01-Whats-Changing|01-whats-changing]].md)** — old vs new, the timeline, and where each thing moved.
2. **[Portal map](docs/[[02-Portal-Map|02-portal-map]].md)** — sitemap, header/footer menus, and the report-builder controls.
3. **[Report filters reference](docs/[[03-Report-Filters|03-report-filters]].md)** — every filter and its full list of options, verbatim.
4. **[Glossary](docs/[[04-Glossary|04-glossary]].md)** — what each value actually means, in plain language.
5. **[Known issues & caveats](docs/[[05-Known-Issues|05-known-issues]].md)** — dead links, quirks, spelling oddities, and data-coverage limits.
6. **[Technical changes](docs/[[06-Technical-Changes|06-technical-changes]].md)** — what changed old→new, what gets easier or harder, and the impact on scraping & enterprise use.
7. **[Paid API scenario](docs/[[07-Paid-API-Scenario|07-paid-api-scenario]].md)** — an illustrative look at what an official paid data API could earn and who'd buy it.
8. **[Financial study](docs/[[08-Financial-Study|08-financial-study]].md)** — illustrative end-to-end costs (state collection → central ops → API build/run) vs. per-request revenue, payback, and break-even.

---

## 🚀 Quick start: pull your first report

1. Open the **[Vahan Public Report](https://analytics.parivahan.gov.in/analytics/vahanpublicreport?lang=en)** page.
2. In **Report Filters**, set at minimum: **Year Type** (Calendar or Financial), **Year**, and a **State** (this loads the RTO list).
3. Add any other filters you need — Maker, Class, Fuel, Emission, etc.
4. Choose your **Y-Axis** (rows) and **X-Axis** (columns) to shape the output table.
5. Enter the **CAPTCHA** and click **Apply**. The results grid loads below.

> **Tip:** You can only select a **1-year span** at a time. Figures count **registrations at RTOs, not manufacturer sales** — see the [glossary](docs/[[04-Glossary|04-glossary]].md#key-terms).

---

## Attribution & disclaimer

- **Data & portal:** © Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH), Government of India; portal designed and developed by the National Informatics Centre (NIC). MoRTH's copyright policy permits free reproduction with accurate, non-misleading use and source acknowledgement.
- **This guide** is an independent compilation of publicly available information, captured from the live portal on **6 August 2026**. It is **not** an official government document.
- **Accuracy:** option lists change whenever MoRTH updates the portal (a new fuel, a new emission norm, a new state joining Vahan 4). Some values (marked in the docs) load via JavaScript and are **medium-confidence** — confirm them live before relying on them. See [Known issues](docs/[[05-Known-Issues|05-known-issues]].md).
- **Official contact:** Team Transport Analytics, NIC — `parivahan[dot]analytics[at]nic[dot]in`. For dashboard migration issues: **[email removed]**.

## License
Documentation licensed under **[CC BY 4.0](LICENSE)** — reuse freely with attribution.

## Contributing
Spotted a changed value or a new filter? See **[docs/[[05-Known-Issues|05-known-issues]].md](docs/$3.md#help-keep-this-current)** and open an issue or pull request.

*Last reviewed: 6 August 2026.*

title: Vahan auto intelligence pipeline
summary: Vahan auto intelligence pipeline scrapes state registration data, cleans it, verifies against government totals, and outputs a PDF report and LinkedIn prompt.
body:
One command scrapes India's Vahan vehicle-registration dashboard, cleans the data,
verifies it against the government's own totals, and produces a PDF report plus a
ready-to-paste LinkedIn prompt.

```
python vahan_make.py
```

---

## The pipeline (what happens when you run it)

| Stage | What it does | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Questions | Asks ICE/EV and the target year (previous year added automatically) | — |
| 2. Scraper | Downloads 36 states × 2 years + 2 "All India" check files, 12 browser tabs at once | 74 `.xls` files in `Downloads\Vahan_State_OEMs\<date>\` |
| 3. Cleaner | Merges all state files, maps OEM/state names | `Cleaned_OEM_Master_<date>.xlsx` |
| 4. Security check | Sum of 36 states vs official All-India file, month by month | ✅/❌ per month; `Verification_FAILED_<date>.xlsx` if mismatch |
| 5. Reports | Asks report month once, builds both outputs | `Auto_Intelligence_<month>.pdf` + `LinkedIn_Prompt_<month>.txt` |

## The files

| File | Role | Can run alone? |
|---|---|---|
| `vahan_make.py` | The whole pipeline (imports the other two) | Yes — this is the main one |
| `Linkdn_4.py` | PDF report generator | Yes (asks for Excel path + month) |
| `generate_prompt_1.py` | LinkedIn prompt generator | Yes (asks for Excel path + month) |

---

## Wait times — the rhythm that works (learned the hard way)

The Vahan site is a slow government site where **every click triggers a hidden
background reload**. The script must pause after each action or clicks land on a
page that isn't ready. Removing these waits made the run faster but **broke the
data silently** — jobs failed or downloaded half-loaded tables.

| Action | Wait | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Open the page | 3 s | Let the page settle |
| Pick the state | 3 s | Site reloads the office list in background |
| Other 4 filter picks | 1 s each | Small settle time |
| Refresh button 1 | **5 s** | Loads the vehicle-type checkboxes |
| Each vehicle tick | 0.5 s | Small settle time |
| Refresh button 2 | **5 s** | Loads the data table — the critical one |
| Before download | 2 s | Table finishes rendering |

**Lesson: faster ≠ better.** The download is a *photo of whatever the table shows
at that moment*. Nothing errors if the photo is taken too early — the numbers are
just quietly wrong. ~24 s of waiting per state is the price of correct data.

## The MARUTI bug — why totals were wrong (biggest lesson)

The cleaner finds month columns by asking *"does this cell start with JAN, FEB,
MAR…?"* — and **MARUTI starts with MAR**. In small states, where Maruti appears
within the first 15 rows, the scanner mistook the maker list for headers and
silently dropped every maker above it.

- **16 of 72 files** were damaged (Andaman, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Sikkim,
  Tripura, Manipur, Nagaland, Bihar-2026, DNH&DD…) — Bihar 2026 alone lost 43,215 units
- **77,751 units recovered** after the fix (grand total 7,415,412 → 7,493,163)
- Big states escaped by luck: their maker lists are long, so Maruti sits below row 15

**Fix:** a month header must be a *bare* month name ("JAN", or "JAN(2026)") — never
a word that merely begins with one.

**Lesson:** when totals look wrong, suspect the *data cleaning* as much as the
scraping. And an independent cross-check (below) catches what eyeballing can't.

## The All-India security check

Every run downloads two extra files with the state dropdown set to
**"All Vahan4 Running States (36/36)"** — the government's own all-India total,
fetched with identical filters. After cleaning, the script compares:

```
sum of 36 individual state files  vs  official All-India file, per month
```

- All months match → `✅ CHECK PASSED`
- Any mismatch → `❌ CHECK FAILED` + `Verification_FAILED_<date>.xlsx` naming the
  exact months and differences

This check was tested by planting a deliberate 5-unit error — it caught it and
named the month. Notably, **before** the MARUTI fix the check couldn't catch
anything, because the same bug corrupted both sides of the comparison equally.

**Lesson:** verify against an *independent* source, not against your own math.

## Smaller fixes worth remembering

| Fix | Symptom it prevented |
|---|---|
| Force UTF-8 output at startup (all 3 scripts) | Crash on ✓/✅ symbols in Windows consoles — killed the pipeline *after* the PDF but *before* the prompt |
| Read files as Excel first, web-page second | Vahan's `.xls` files are really `.xlsx` — the old order failed 72 times per run before falling back |
| PDF "India Total" rows (heatmap + state table) | Top-15 states cover only ~90% of India; the total row makes missing data visible |
| LinkedIn prompt reuses last year's real number | Old formula divided by zero if a market fell exactly 100% |
| Checkbox failures print a warning | Used to fail silently → wrong vehicle types included with no trace |

## Reading the run — messages and what they mean

| Message | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `[n/74] ✅ Downloaded: <state>` | Job done — final count should be 74 | None |
| `⚠️ Warning: couldn't select checkbox` | Vehicle filter didn't apply → that state too high | Re-run that day |
| `❌ Permanent Failure for: <state>` | 3 tries failed → state missing → total too low | Re-run that day |
| `[!] REJECTED <file>` | Downloaded file was junk | Re-run that day |
| `⚠️ N OEMs … NOT in your hardcoded list` | New maker names appeared | Open `Action_Required_New_OEMs_<date>.xlsx`, add them to `OEM_MAPPING` |
| `❌ CHECK FAILED` | State sums ≠ official All-India total | Open `Verification_FAILED_<date>.xlsx`, re-run the listed months' states |

## Timing expectations

- One state job ≈ 45–55 s (waits + site loading) · 74 jobs ÷ 12 tabs ≈ **5–6 min** per full run
- Every retry adds its full job time again — a slow site day can double the run
- Bank analogy: 74 customers, 12 counter windows, one (government) clerk serving
  all windows — more windows ≠ proportionally faster

---

*Compiled from the debugging sessions of July 2026 — every lesson here was paid
for with a real bug.*

title: Choosing a green belt project
summary: Choosing a Green Belt project involves scoring ideas against four tests to ensure a measurable Y, identifiable X's, a real gap, and accessible data.
body:
A Green Belt programme is a deployment, not a course. It ends with a chartered project that runs for months, so the choice of project decides most of the outcome.

## What a project needs

I score every idea against four tests:

1. **A measurable Y.** One number that defines success.
2. **Identifiable X's.** Plausible drivers I can list and then test.
3. **A real, live gap.** DMAIC closes gaps. A problem that's already solved doesn't qualify.
4. **Data I can already reach.** If the baseline needs a system that doesn't exist yet, the project stalls in Measure.

## Size decides whether it finishes

"Select project" is its own DMAIC step because the method falls apart when the project is too big. **I pick the smallest project that still qualifies, not the most impressive one.** I find out the minimum scope that counts for certification and build to that line, not past it.

The project sits on top of the day job for months, so a small, finishable scope matters twice over.

## Kinds of project and how they score

| Type | Example Y | Example X's | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data quality at source | First-pass yield of a recurring data extract, usable without a re-request | Field coverage at source, spec clarity, ownership of the extract | Strong. Fixing it removes recurring rework for everyone downstream. Size it by hours lost across all consumers, not one person's. |
| Market share loss | Share % in a defined segment and region | Enquiry reach, conversion, product mix, coverage, turnaround | Analytically clean, since share = reach × conversion is already a Y = f(X). It tends to add analysis more than it removes rework. |
| Cycle time | End-to-end lead time and first-pass yield | Document completeness, queue depth, handoff count, exception rate, third-party response time | A common choice, so I'd narrow it to one segment or region to make it distinct. |
| Something already automated | Reporting cycle time | None left to test | Evidence, not a project. DMAIC needs a live gap. Useful to show credibility when a team picks a lead. |

**Framing a benefit.** "Saves me two to three days" is weak. "The output reaches decision-makers two to three days earlier every month" is a cycle-time cut with a business consequence, and that's the language a steering group responds to.

The project that removes recurring work from people's weeks usually beats the one that produces the most interesting analysis.

## Certification: ask who certifies it

A few days of training isn't a Green Belt anywhere. Certification almost always needs the finished project, sometimes an exam too. Who issues it matters more than anything else, and nobody volunteers the answer, so I ask:

- **Internal certificate:** counts inside the company, little outside.
- **The training consultant's certificate:** modest outside recognition.
- **An accredited body (ASQ, IASSC):** this one travels.

Related: [[DMAIC-Roadmap]] · [[Value-Stream-Mapping]]

title: Vahan Data API financial model
summary: Vahan Data API financial model outlines cost-revenue projections for government and private perspectives.
body:
> **Scope:** An end-to-end plan (requirements → design → build → deploy) plus a full financial plan for an **aggregate** Vahan vehicle-registration **Data API**, from two angles: **(A) the Government operating it** (MoRTH/NIC, aiming for self-sufficiency) and **(B) a private company** building a product on top.
> ⚠️ **Read this first.** All forward-looking figures are **illustrative estimates on stated assumptions**, not official budgets, forecasts, or a MoRTH/NIC plan. The only hard facts are cited (e.g. the 2019 policy's ₹111.4 cr / 142 buyers).

## Financial model

This section evaluates the financial viability of operating the Vahan Aggregate API from two distinct institutional viewpoints: **Perspective A (Government Operation)** aiming for self-sufficiency and cost-recovery, and **Perspective B (Private Reseller)** building a high-margin value-added SaaS product on top of raw or open government data feeds (Surepass-style).

---

### PERSPECTIVE A: Government Operating Model (MoRTH / NIC)
*Objective: Achieve complete operational self-sufficiency, covering central Vahan hosting overheads and API maintenance costs via enterprise tier licensing.*

#### Break-Even & Self-Sufficiency Analysis (Perspective A)

### PERSPECTIVE B: Private Company Reselling Value-Added Products (Surepass-Style)
*Objective: Build an agile, high-margin B2B SaaS data layer by licensing public/semi-public aggregate datasets, packaging them with advanced visualization dashboards, predictive analytics models, and developer-friendly SDKs.*
