title: Model risk management for cercit-risk-v1
summary: Model risk management for cercit-risk-v1 outlines scope, gaps, and required actions before deploying the XGBoost credit model.
body:
# Model risk management

Status: draft for review
Created: 16 Sep 2026
Applies to: `cercit-risk-v1` (XGBoost, ONNX) and any successor
Related: [[00-Policy-Framework-Overview]] · [[03-Policy-Change-Management]] · [[05-Credit-Policy]]

---

## Scope

Any analytical model whose output influences a credit decision, price, or limit. Today that is one model, plus several rule-based calculators that are deliberately excluded because they are deterministic arithmetic, not inference.

| Component | In scope | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `cercit-risk-v1` XGBoost classifier | Yes | Probabilistic, trained, drifts |
| `risk-score-model.ts` grade bands | Yes | Maps model output to a decision-relevant grade |
| `policy-rule-engine.ts` | No | Deterministic rules — governed by [[03-Policy-Change-Management]] |
| FOIR, LTV, EMI calculators | No | Fixed formulas |
| `bureau-score-interpreter.ts` | Borderline | Rule-based today; in scope if it becomes fitted |

## Model inventory

| Field | Current value |
|---|---|
| Model ID | `cercit-risk-v1` |
| Type | XGBoost binary classifier |
| Target | 30+ DPD within 12 months |
| Features | 18 |
| Training data | 10,000 synthetic profiles generated from industry benchmarks |
| AUC-ROC | 0.91 |
| PR-AUC | 0.61 |
| Brier | 0.023 |
| Base rates in training | bad30 4.0%, default90 1.1% |
| Serving | ONNX via `onnxruntime-web`, wasm, in the browser |
| Output use | P(30+DPD) mapped to grades A–E; advisory to the officer |
| Owner | Unassigned — **gap** |
| Validation | None performed — **gap** |
| Approval to deploy | None recorded — **gap** |

## Tiering

Tier the model by consequence, and let the tier drive how much governance it attracts.

| Tier | Definition | This model |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Auto-decisions without human review | Phase 2 target |
| High | Materially shapes a human decision, or sets price | **Current — Phase 1** |
| Low | Informational, no decision influence | |

cercit is Phase 1: the officer decides and the model advises. That is High, not Critical. But the gap between the two is one product decision — the moment auto-approval turns on, this becomes Critical and needs independent validation before, not after.

## Findings on the current model

Four, from reading the implementation. The first two are governance; the last two are design choices that are defensible but must be written down rather than discovered.

**The model file is publicly served.** `public/models/cercit-risk-v1.onnx` ships as a static asset, so anyone who loads the site can download the trained model. Two consequences: the model is extractable IP, and more importantly it is probeable — a broker can run it offline and find the exact feature combination that lands grade A, then shape applications to hit it. For a Phase 1 demo on synthetic data this is acceptable and worth noting. Before real lending, scoring moves server-side.

**Inference runs on the client.** The score is computed in the borrower-facing or officer-facing browser. Anything computed client-side can be manipulated client-side. If a score computed in the browser is ever written back and stored as the official risk score, the trust boundary is broken — the server would be accepting a number it did not compute. This needs checking before launch, and server-side scoring is the fix.

**Contributions are counterfactual, not SHAP.** `risk-score-model.ts` produces per-feature deltas by swapping a feature to its training mean and re-running inference. That is a reasonable, cheap approximation and it is honest — but it is not Shapley, and the UI should not imply it is. True SHAP importances exist only as global values in the meta JSON. If an officer or a regulator is told "this is why the model scored the file", the method has to be stated accurately.

**The known limitation is a policy dependency, not a defect.** A clean file with one blemish — bureau 640, nothing else wrong — still scores grade A, because in the training data such files mostly perform. The policy engine catches it with a hard floor at 650. This is the intended division of labour, and it means the model's weakness is load-bearing on a specific rule. If `BUREAU_FLOOR` is ever relaxed, this limitation becomes live exposure. That coupling should be recorded against both the model and the rule.

## Development standards

- Training data lineage documented: source, generation method, date, row count, base rates. For synthetic data, the benchmark assumptions have to be written down and attributed — they currently live in `car-loan-industry-knowledge` and `scripts/generate-training-data.ts` and nowhere else.
- Feature definitions with the exact transformation, and an explicit check that no feature is a proxy for a protected attribute
- Train/test split and its rationale; no leakage from target into features
- Reproducible: seed, versions, and a regenerable pipeline
- Model card per version covering intended use, out-of-scope use, performance by segment, and known failure modes

Synthetic training data deserves its own caution. A model fitted to data generated from assumptions will reproduce those assumptions with high confidence and no external validation. AUC 0.91 against synthetic holdout says the model learned the generator, not that it predicts real defaults. That distinction must be stated wherever the metric is quoted, including in portfolio material.

## Validation

Independent of the developer. For a team too small for a separate function, an external reviewer or a structured self-challenge with documented dissent.

Before any version goes live:

- Conceptual soundness — do the features make credit sense, and is the target definition right
- Performance on a holdout the developer did not see
- Performance by segment: employer category, CIBIL band, ticket size, geography. A model that is strong overall and weak on Category C is a model that misprices a specific population.
- Stability — PSI on features between training and recent applications
- Calibration, not just discrimination. Grade bands are cut on absolute probability thresholds (A < 1%, B < 2.5%), so a mis-calibrated model puts files in the wrong band even with a good AUC. Brier 0.023 is a start; a reliability curve is the actual test.
- Benchmark against the rules-only baseline. `computeRiskScoreLegacy` still exists and is the natural challenger — if the model does not beat it, it is complexity without return.
- Bias testing across age, gender, and geography, given DPDP and fairness expectations

## Approval and deployment

Model promotion follows the material-change path in [[03-Policy-Change-Management]]:

1. Model owner proposes with the model card and validation report
2. Impact simulation against recent applications — decision flips in each direction
3. Credit Head plus CRO approve; Risk Committee notes
4. Effective date scheduled; `model_version` pinned to every decision from that point
5. Prior version retained and re-activatable

No model version reaches production without a recorded approver, the same rule as policy.

## Ongoing monitoring

| Check | Frequency | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Score distribution vs training | Monthly | Mean shift beyond tolerance |
| Feature PSI | Monthly | PSI > 0.2 on any feature |
| Grade band mix | Monthly | Material shift in band proportions |
| Calibration — predicted vs actual bad rate by band | Quarterly, once vintages mature | Actual outside predicted band range |
| Discrimination — AUC on realised outcomes | Semi-annual | Drop below an agreed floor |
| Override rate against model grade | Monthly | Officers systematically disagreeing is a signal about the model |
| Segment performance | Semi-annual | Any segment materially worse |

Two of these cannot run yet and should be stated as such: calibration and realised AUC need actual repayment outcomes, which a synthetic-data Phase 1 does not have. Until real vintages exist, the model is unvalidated against reality regardless of its holdout metrics.

## Retirement

A version is retired when a successor is approved, when monitoring breaches persist without remediation, or when the portfolio it was fitted on no longer resembles the book. Retired versions stay archived and readable — decisions made under them must remain reconstructible.

## Gaps to close, in order

1. Assign a model owner — nobody is accountable today
2. Record a deployment approval for `cercit-risk-v1`, retrospectively if need be
3. Write the model card, including the synthetic-data caveat
4. Pin `model_version` to stored decisions
5. Move scoring server-side before any real customer data
6. Stand up drift monitoring
7. Independent validation before Phase 2 auto-decisioning

title: Lessons learned building SamsMind in four days
summary: Lessons learned building SamsMind include deciding privacy model first, using closed AI categories, tuning link thresholds on real data, and separating approvals from data.
body:
I built my second brain end to end in four days, following the Second Self course: capture, AI filing, linking, a map, and an ask box that answers from my notes. These are the lessons worth keeping, written so I can reuse them on cercit, the IJP case and future projects.

## Product and PM lessons

**Decide the privacy model before writing code.** The original plan said "local AI only" for everything. That would have meant a slow model sorting my notes badly. Splitting notes into three levels (blocked, personal, shareable) let the free cloud model handle Masai and cercit notes while personal ones never leave the laptop. One early decision removed a whole class of later arguments.

**Give the AI a closed list, not an open question.** "Pick one of my 18 areas" works far better than "invent a category". The same idea applies to any classification product: constrain the output and the quality goes up.

**Copy the course where it helps, deviate where it hurts, and write down why.** I followed the course on auto-filing and auto-linking, which is less manual work. I deviated on the public repo and Streamlit hosting, which would have put my notes on the internet. A table of "course vs mine, and why" made those choices easy to defend instead of looking like gaps.

**Users don't read the UI the way the builder does.** My Ask box worked, but I couldn't tell which box asks and which box searches, and the browser's autocomplete dropdown looked like something I had to pick from. Labels like "Ask anything, then press Enter" fixed it. Test with the real user, not with the person who built it.

**Let the user change the rules.** The course design refuses to answer when the notes don't cover a question. I wanted "ask anything". The fix wasn't a debate: answer from my notes first with sources, and put general knowledge in a clearly marked "Not from your notes:" paragraph. Honesty came from the labelling, not the restriction.

**Tune numbers on real data.** The course's link threshold of 0.75 gave only 14 links on my notes. Looking at the actual pairs showed everything down to 0.65 was clearly related, so 0.65 became the default. A dry run before committing to a number paid off.

**Ship in weekly slices, each one usable.** Every week ended with something I could run: capture, then filing, then the map, then ask. Each week's output fed the next.

## Privacy and safety lessons

- **Fail closed.** A missing or wrong privacy level means personal. Unknown means "don't send".
- **Approval lives outside the data.** Public approvals sit in their own file, so the raw captures never change.
- **Check the thing you publish, not the thing you meant to publish.** The validator scans the actual bundle, and `mind public validate` refuses a bundle that changed after it was checked. On its first run it caught a path. It was a false alarm (an example path from a public web page), which taught me to make the rules specific (real personal folders) rather than loose.
- **Clean data before AI sees it.** The Vault import removed names, phone numbers, keys and employer details, and rewrote class notes as my own knowledge before anything was captured. Files with work logic, diaries and meeting notes stayed out completely.
- **Booby-trapped links are a real risk on a public page.** Rendered notes now only keep normal web links.

## How the AI parts actually work (in plain words)

- **Embeddings:** text becomes a list of 384 numbers that stands for its meaning. Similar meanings give similar numbers, measured with cosine similarity.
- **A small local model doesn't know jargon.** It didn't recognise "FOIR", so asking "What is FOIR?" found nothing. Adding keyword search on the question's important words fixed it. Meaning-search plus keyword-search beats either one alone.
- **Send the relevant part of a long note, not the start.** The FOIR formula sat deep inside long notes. Picking the paragraphs that mention the question's words fixed the answer.
- **RAG with citations:** find notes, send only those to the model, make it cite `[note-id]`, and remove any citation of a note it was never given. That stops invented sources.
- **Free models change.** `inkling:free` stopped working for API calls ("only available on agentic harnesses"). Nemotron 3 Super worked. Keep the model name in `.env` so switching takes one line.
- **Writing rules can be enforced, not just requested.** Summaries and answers that use banned words (crucial, delve…) or open with "The note…" are rewritten once automatically.

## Windows and tooling gotchas

- OneDrive locks folders, so deleting and recreating a folder fails. Empty it instead.
- SQLite's `with` block doesn't close the file on Windows, so it stays locked. Close it explicitly.
- Windows consoles default to cp1252, which crashes on ₹ or —. Force UTF-8 output.
- Keep the Python environment outside OneDrive, or OneDrive tries to sync a gigabyte of torch.
- Install torch's CPU build. The GPU build is huge and not needed here.
- Commands only work from the right folder (`.\mind` failed from `C:\Windows\system32`). Adding the folder to PATH fixes it for good.

## Working with AI agents: what went wrong and what caught it

- **A test deleted real data.** The first CLI tests cleared the real capture archive and wiped two test captures. Fix: every test now uses a temporary folder. Rule: tests must never touch real data.
- **Escaping bugs from generated code.** Several times, writing code through shell commands turned `\n` or `\b` into real newlines or hidden characters. One hidden character made a style rule silently match nothing, and the redo found zero notes. Writing code as files, not shell one-liners, avoided it. A test that checks the rule actually fires would have caught it at once.
- **Two sessions doing the same job overwrote each other.** Parallel rewrite workers from another session clobbered finished notes. One owner per job.
- **Big multi-agent audits hit the account's session limit.** The first audit ran only 3 of 82 reviewers, and the second about half. Smaller fleets, or running after the limit resets, would have finished cleanly.
- **Independent checks are worth it.** Three skeptics per finding cleanly separated real gaps (missing requirements, a stale README) from claims that didn't hold up (the "uncommitted change" was already committed).

## Numbers at the end

- 120 notes captured.
- 97 filed across all four PARA buckets, with 23 personal notes waiting for a local model.
- 37 links.
- 96 tests.
- 10 notes approved for the public site, which is built and checked but not published.

## Still open

- Approve more notes so the public map has links, then decide whether to publish.
- Set up a local model (Ollama) so the 23 personal notes get sorted and can be used in answers.
- Optional: capture and process buttons on the map page (the course's Streamlit sidebar).
- Finish the audit dimensions that didn't run (privacy, bugs, data quality).

title: Platform architecture for cercit lending platform
summary: Platform architecture describes moving business logic from the browser to backend services for cercit's lending platform.
body:
# Platform architecture — from cercit to an end-to-end lending platform Status: draft for decision Created: 17 Sep 2026 Related: [[09-Admin-Console-and-IAM-Policy]] · [[11-Impact-Analysis]] · [[12-Future-Proofing-Decision-Pack]] --- ## Your question: is the webpage just the front end? Your mental model is the right target. It is not how cercit works today. A webpage should be a window: it shows data and sends the user's actions somewhere else. Decisions, data and models should live behind it, where the user cannot see or change them. In cercit right now, three pieces of real business logic run inside the browser: | Logic | File | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | The 18 credit rules | `src/lib/policy-rule-engine.ts` | Anyone can open the browser's developer tools and read or alter them before a result is shown | | Pricing | `src/lib/engine.ts` | Uses a 5-band mock matrix that disagrees with the database | | The ML risk model | `src/lib/risk-score-model.ts` + `public/models/cercit-risk-v1.onnx` | The trained model is downloadable, and the score is computed on the user's machine | And there is a second copy of the policy engine on the server — `fn_run_policy_engine` in `sql/004_functions.sql`. Two engines for one policy means they will drift apart, and nobody will know which one decided a given loan. The backend pieces that do sit where they should: Supabase Postgres (tables, decision and assessment functions, RLS policies not yet applied) and six AWS Lambda document extractors (built, not deployed). One more finding: `bank-statement-parser`, `cashflow-analyzer`, `salary-slip-parser`, `document-classifier`, `cam-data-assembler`, `scheme-eligibility`, `employer-verifier` and `ccr-parser` sit in `src/lib` with nothing importing them. They duplicate what the Lambdas do. Dead code that looks like a feature is a problem during due diligence — a buyer will ask what it does. So, corrected: **in the target design, the webpage has no business logic. In cercit today, it has the most important business logic.** Moving it out is the first architecture job. ## The lending lifecycle a commercial platform has to cover cercit today covers roughly steps 3 to 8, and only for the officer's view. ```mermaid flowchart LR L[1 Lead] --> K[2 Onboarding & KYC] K --> A[3 Application] A --> D[4 Documents] D --> G[5 Data gathering
bureau, AA, employer, Vahan] G --> S[6 Assessment
rules, model, pricing] S --> X[7 Decision
officer or STP] X --> KF[8 Sanction & KFS] KF --> E[9 Agreement
e-sign, e-stamp] E --> P[10 Pre-disbursal checks
insurance, NACH, RC] P --> DB[11 Disbursal to dealer] DB --> SV[12 Servicing
EMI, charges, prepayment] SV --> C[13 Collections] SV --> CL[14 Closure
NOC, hypothecation removal] CL --> R[15 Retention & purge] ``` Running across all fifteen: identity and access, configuration and policy, audit, consent, notifications, fraud and AML monitoring, grievance, regulatory reporting (CIC, FIU-IND, RBI returns), and a data platform. ## Should these be built separately? Yes. cercit is currently one React app doing five jobs: public website, customer application, officer console, admin screens, and decision engine. That is fine for a prototype and wrong for a product. Recommended split: | # | Module | Build or buy | Why separate | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Decisioning engine** — rules, model scoring, pricing, CAM | Build. This is the IP | Different change cadence, heavy audit, must be server-side | | 2 | **Configuration & policy service** — parameter register, versions, maker-checker, flags | Build | Every other module reads from it; "change as a feature" lives here | | 3 | **Identity & access** | Buy/adopt (Supabase Auth now; Keycloak or a managed IdP later) | Security-critical; lenders will demand SSO | | 4 | **Origination workflow (LOS)** — application, case queue, tasks | Build, thin | The glue between customer and decision | | 5 | **KYC & onboarding hub** | Build the hub, buy the providers | Providers change; the hub's interface should not | | 6 | **Document AI** | Build (Lambdas exist) | Scales separately, GPU/OCR costs | | 7 | **Data connectors** — bureau, AA, Vahan, PAN | Build adapters, buy data | Each provider fails differently | | 8 | **Documentation** — KFS, sanction, agreement, e-sign, e-stamp | Build templates, buy e-sign/e-stamp | Legal templates versioned like policy | | 9 | **Loan management (LMS)** — schedules, EMI, charges, prepayment, closure | Buy or partner first | Large, accounting-heavy, well served by existing Indian vendors | | 10 | **Collections** | Later; buy or partner | Out of Phase 1 | | 11 | **Fraud & AML monitoring** | Build rules, buy screening lists | Different users (compliance), different data | | 12 | **Grievance & customer service** | Build thin or use a CRM | Regulatory SLAs | | 13 | **Co-lending & partnerships** | Later | Only if a bank partner is signed | | 14 | **Data & reporting platform** | Build | MIS, model monitoring, regulator returns | | 15 | **Front ends** — customer app, staff console, admin console, dealer portal | Build, shared design system | Different users, different security | Modules 1, 2, 3 and 15 are the minimum split to do next. The rest can stay as folders inside one backend (a "modular monolith") until volume justifies breaking them out — see [[12-Future-Proofing-Decision-Pack]]. ## How "change as a feature" actually works Five mechanisms. Together they mean a regulation change or a new provider is a configuration change with an approval, not a software release. **1. Parameters are data with a schema.** Every row in [[08-Admin-Parameter-Register]] becomes a record that knows its type, unit, allowed range, owner role, approver role, whether it is locked, and which regulation it traces to. The admin screen is generated from that schema, so adding a parameter does not need a new screen. **2. Everything is effective-dated.** A value has a from-date and a to-date. Changes are scheduled, not applied on click. Every decision records which version it used. **3. Rules are decision tables, not code.** The 18 rules become rows: parameter, operator, threshold, severity, reason code, version. A server-side engine evaluates them. Thresholds never appear in source code. **4. Providers sit behind adapters.** A KYC provider, bureau or AA connector implements one interface. Switching vendor is a dropdown on the activation tab. **5. Features ship dark.** New capability is released switched off and turned on per tenant, product, branch or percentage, through Off → Sandbox → Pilot → Live. A sixth, worth building later: a regulatory watch. New RBI and UIDAI circulars are pulled and summarised, and each one that touches a parameter opens a change request for the Policy Manager. That is a good use of AI — see [[12-Future-Proofing-Decision-Pack]]. ## What selling this requires A company buying cercit will check these before it looks at the features. | Area | Requirement | cercit today | |---|---|---| | Tenancy | Each lender's data and policy isolated — `tenant_id` everywhere plus RLS, or a dedicated deployment | Single tenant | | Data residency | All data in India | Not pinned | | SSO | Lender staff log in with their own identity provider (SAML/OIDC) | Email + password | | Security assurance | ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, annual VAPT by a CERT-In empanelled auditor | None | | RBI outsourcing fit | Right to audit, business continuity, exit plan, data handback on termination | None | | DPDP | Data processing agreement; the lender is the fiduciary, you are the processor | None | | Availability | Stated uptime, RTO and RPO, tested DR | Not defined | | Integration | Documented APIs, webhooks, sandbox environment | Internal only | | Configurability | Lender sets its own policy, pricing, roles, workflow, branding | Hardcoded | | Audit | Immutable trail, exportable for the lender's auditors | Table exists, writable | | Commercials | Usage metering (per application / per decision), billing | None | | Support | Release notes, change notice to lenders, support SLAs | None | One regulatory point to settle with a lawyer: if cercit ever talks to borrowers on a lender's behalf, it may be a Lending Service Provider under the digital lending directions, which brings its own obligations. Sold purely as software run by the lender's staff, it is a technology vendor under outsourcing rules instead. The product boundary decides which. ## Target shape ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Front[Front ends — no business logic] CW[Customer web/app] SC[Staff console] AC[Admin console] DP[Dealer portal] end GW[API gateway
auth, rate limits, tenant] Front --> GW subgraph Core[Core services] IAM[Identity & access] CFG[Config & policy service] LOS[Origination workflow] DEC[Decisioning
rules + model + pricing] KYC[KYC hub] DOC[Document AI] CON[Data connectors] DOCS[Documentation & e-sign] end GW --> Core DEC --> CFG LOS --> DEC LOS --> KYC LOS --> DOC LOS --> CON subgraph Later[Later / partner] LMS[LMS] COL[Collections] AML[Fraud & AML] CLA[Co-lending] end Core --> EV[(Event log & audit)] EV --> DATA[Data platform
MIS, monitoring, returns] KYC -.adapters.-> EXT[UIDAI KUA, CKYCR, V-CIP,
DigiLocker, NSDL] CON -.adapters.-> EXT2[CIBIL, Experian, CRIF,
AA, Vahan] ```

title: VAHAN glossary of key terms
summary: VAHAN glossary provides plain‑language definitions of key terms used in the vehicle‑registration portal, sourced from official MoRTH and NIC documents.
body:
What each value means, in plain language. Meanings are drawn from the portal and from official MoRTH / NIC / Motor Vehicles Act sources. Where nothing official defines a term, that is stated rather than guessed. None of these are hyperlinks — they are options you select inside the **Report Filters** panel.

## Key terms

- **VAHAN / Vahan 4.0** — MoRTH's national vehicle-registration database, built by NIC. State Registers feed a National Register; Vahan 4.0 is the centralised web version that migrated RTOs onto unified registers. "Vahan running states" = states whose RTOs have migrated to Vahan 4.
- **Registration vs sales** — figures count **vehicle registrations at RTOs, not manufacturer sales**. Back-dated entries and refreshes can change historical numbers. Don't read totals as national sales.
- **Calendar year vs Financial year** — Calendar = Jan–Dec; Indian financial year = 1 Apr to 31 Mar (e.g. FY 2024-2025 = Apr 2024 – Mar 2025).
- **(T) / (NT)** — (T) = Transport (commercial); (NT) = Non-Transport (private).
- **Invalid Carriage / Adapted Vehicle** — a vehicle built or adapted for a person with a disability. "Adapted Vehicle" is the newer statutory term.
- **RTO** — Regional Transport Office: the district-level authority that registers vehicles, issues licences, collects road tax, and issues permits and fitness certificates. Registration numbers encode the state code + a two-digit RTO code (e.g. `MH12` = Pune).

## Archived Flag
- **ACTIVE_COMPLIANT** — a live registration record that meets current data-compliance rules under MoRTH's archival policy.
- **ACTIVE_NON_COMPLIANT** — a live record that fails a compliance rule but is still active in the register.
- **PERMANENT_ARCHIVE** — moved to permanent archive; retained but out of routine active queries.
- **TEMPORARY_ARCHIVE** — held in temporary archive; less frequently accessed than active records.

## Year Type
- **CALENDAR YEAR / FINANCIAL YEAR** — see Key terms.
- **Last 5 FINANCIAL YEAR** — the five most recent financial years.
- **Last 3 Months / Last 6 Months / Last 1 Year** — rolling windows ending today.
- **As on Date** — figures as at a chosen date rather than over a span.
- **1 Month / 15 Days / 7 Days** — fixed short windows.

## State *(family)*
All 36 values are Indian states/UTs; the meaning is the jurisdiction itself. Notes:
- **Telangana** — historically outside VAHAN; began integrating only in 2025, so its historical series may be absent or partial.
- **UT of DNH and DD** — Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu (merged in 2020).
- **Andaman & Nicobar Island** — the Andaman & Nicobar Islands UT (spelled singular on the portal).

## Emission (norms)
- **BHARAT STAGE I–IV** — India's nationwide emission standards, broadly tracking the Euro norms of their time. BS IV was superseded by BS VI for new sales from **1 April 2020**.
- **BHARAT STAGE III/IV** — combined/transition label spanning BS III and BS IV certified vehicles.
- **BHARAT STAGE VI** — current standard, at parity with Euro VI; mandatory nationwide for new vehicles from **1 April 2020**. *(India skipped BS V.)*
- **Bharat Trem Stage III / III A / III B**, **TREM STAGE IV / V** — tractor emission norms (TREM = Tractor Emission).
- **Bharat Stage III CEV**, **CEV STAGE IV / V** — norms for Construction Equipment Vehicles.
- **EURO 1–6 (and 6A/6B/6C/6D/6AD)** — European standard references used in type approval.
- **Not Applicable / Not Available** — no norm applies / not recorded.

## Maker
The manufacturer as recorded in the register (e.g. `TATA MOTORS LTD`, `MARUTI SUZUKI`). AJAX-populated; hundreds of values; known spelling inconsistencies in the underlying data.

## Category Group
Broad vehicle groupings: **Ambulance/Hearses, Bus, Construction Equipment Vehicle, Goods Vehicle, Tractor, Public Service Vehicle, Special Category Vehicles, Trailer, Four Wheeler, Three Wheeler, Two Wheeler.**

## Sub-Category
Weight/purpose splits under the Motor Vehicles Act — Heavy/Medium/Light × Goods/Passenger/Motor vehicle, plus adapted "(Invalid Carriage)" variants and Two/Three-Wheeler **(T)** transport / **(NT)** non-transport. **LIGHT MOTOR VEHICLE** = a transport vehicle, omnibus, motor car, tractor or road-roller whose gross/unladen weight ≤ 7500 kg (MV Act s.2(21)).

## Class
The specific statutory vehicle class (77 values in section 3). Suffix meanings:
- **(T)** transport/commercial · **(NT)** non-transport/private
- **(Commercial) / (Private Use) / (Individual Use)** — the use context
- **(G) / (P)** on e-rickshaws — goods / passenger
- **Snorked Ladders** — not defined on the site; best read as a misspelling of a snorkel/aerial fire ladder.

## Fuel
Covers petrol/diesel, gas (CNG/LNG/LPG/HCNG), dual- and flex-fuel blends, ethanol/methanol, hydrogen (fuel-cell and ICE), and electric/hybrid:
- **ELECTRIC(BOV)** — Battery-Operated Vehicle (electric motor + battery).
- **PURE EV** — battery-electric only, no combustion engine.
- **PLUG-IN HYBRID EV** — hybrid rechargeable from the grid.
- **STRONG HYBRID EV** — full hybrid able to run on electric alone for a range.
- **PETROL(E20)** — petrol with a 20% ethanol blend.

## EV Type
A focused electric/hybrid filter: **ELECTRIC(BOV), PLUG-IN HYBRID EV, PURE EV, STRONG HYBRID EV** — the same four values that also appear under Fuel.

## Status
Lifecycle state of the registration:
- **ACTIVE** — currently active.
- **NOC ISSUED** — No-Objection Certificate issued (usually for transfer to another RTO/state).
- **RC CANCEL / RC SURRENDER / RC SUSPENDED** — Registration Certificate cancelled / surrendered by owner / suspended.
- **CONFISCATED AUCTION VEHICLE** — confiscated and marked for / sold at auction.
- **SCRAP VEHICLE / VEHICLE TO BE SCRAPPED / VEHICLE SUBMITTED FOR SCRAPPING / VEHICLE_SCRAPPED RC CANCEL** — stages of the scrapping process.
- **VEHICLE DE-REGISTERED** — removed from the active register.

## Owner Type
Who the vehicle is registered to — from **INDIVIDUAL** and **FIRM** to the many government categories (Central/State Government, Corporation, Company, Board, Trust, PSU/undertaking, Local Authority, Police, etc.), plus **DIVYANGJAN** (persons with disabilities) with/without the GST concession, education bodies, and **MULTIPLE OWNER / OTHERS**.

## Type, Fitness and Delhi NCR toggles
- **Type** — Transport (commercial) vs Non-Transport (private).
- **Fitness Valid as On Date?** — YES filters to vehicles whose fitness certificate is valid on the chosen date; NO the opposite.
- **Delhi NCR ?** — YES restricts results to the Delhi National Capital Region; ALL STATES shows everything.

## Y-Axis / X-Axis
Set the **rows** (Y) and **columns** (X) of the output cross-tab — e.g. Maker as rows, Month as columns. Options are AJAX-populated; see [section 3]([[03-Report-Filters|03-report-filters]].md#y-axis-single-select-ajax-populated) for the documented (medium-confidence) option sets.

title: Statistics core concepts
summary: Statistics core concepts cover six key ideas, hypothesis testing, Excel tools, and test selection for continuous and discrete data.
body:
The whole statistical half of the programme reduces to about six ideas. It looks like more because
it arrives fast and in unfamiliar words.

## The six

**Y = f(X)** — the outcome you care about is a function of its inputs. The entire method is finding
which X's actually move Y. Everything in Analyse is this.

**Centre vs spread** — mean and median describe the centre; standard deviation describes the spread.
**Six Sigma attacks the spread.** The goal is consistency, not a better average.

**H₀, the null hypothesis** — always the statement of *no* difference. You set it up in order to try
to disprove it. It is written about a population parameter and always carries `=`, `≤` or `≥`.

**p < 0.05** — the difference is unlikely to be chance alone, so reject the null: the effect is real.
A large p means *no evidence of a difference*, which is not the same as proof there is none.

**Empirical Rule** — for normal data, 68% falls within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within
3σ. Chebyshev's Theorem is the weaker version used when normality is not safe to assume.

**Central Limit Theorem** — sample averages behave normally even when the underlying data does not.
This is why a sample can speak for a population you never fully measure.

## Population vs sample

| Population parameter | Sample statistic |
|---|---|
| mean (µ) | sample mean (x̄) |
| standard deviation (σ) | sample std deviation (s) |
| proportion (p) | sample proportion (p̂) |

Testing a population parameter using sample statistics, on normal data, is **parametric testing**.

## Choosing the right test

| Outcome (Y) | X is discrete (groups, categories) | X is continuous (a measured number) |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous** — time, amount, rate | t-test (1-sample, 2-sample, paired) · **ANOVA** for 3+ groups | **Regression** and correlation |
| **Discrete** — pass/fail, category | **Chi-square** · proportion tests (p, 2p) | Logistic regression |

Find your Y down the left, your X across the top; the cell names the test.

**Note for lending work:** most lending data is counts and categories, so expect to live in the
chi-square and proportion-test box far more than a manufacturing textbook does.

## Correlation vs regression

- **Correlation** describes the *strength* of a linear relationship (coefficient r)
- **Regression** tells you how to draw the line that *predicts* — it minimises residuals
- Neither establishes causation

## Doing it in Excel 2010

The **Analysis ToolPak** ships with Excel and needs no admin rights, but is off by default:

> File → Options → Add-Ins → *Manage: Excel Add-ins* → **Go** → tick **Analysis ToolPak** → OK
> Then: **Data → Data Analysis**

That gives Descriptive Statistics, Histogram, Correlation, Regression, ANOVA and the t-tests —
essentially the whole syllabus.

**What Excel 2010 lacks:** native Pareto and histogram *chart* types (added in Excel 2016). Pareto
matters in Six Sigma, so build it manually: sort descending, add a cumulative-% column, plot that on
a secondary axis as a line.

**Google Sheets** has no equivalent panel but the functions are native: `CORREL`, `LINEST`,
`T.TEST`, `CHISQ.TEST`, `STDEV`.

## Design of Experiments — the honest limitation

DOE assumes you can *set factor levels deliberately*. You cannot randomise a live loan file or run a
customer at two interest rates. Applying DOE to an observational process is the real limit of
factory Six Sigma in lending — worth asking the trainer about directly, see [[Questions-To-Ask]].

Related: [[DMAIC-Roadmap]] (steps 7–9) · [[Six-Sigma-INDEX]]

title: Coin collection arrangement methodology
summary: Coin collection arrangement methodology describes sourcing, sorting, and storing coins by continent, sub‑region, country, issuer, and denomination in dedicated boxes.
body:
# Coin Collection Arrangement — Methodology

## 1. Source & scope
- Source: Numista collection export (CSV/XLSX), re-pulled fresh each time.
- India isn't in this collection yet — out of scope for these boxes.
- Four themed sub-collections have their own dedicated 2×5 storage and are excluded from the main boxes entirely: British Round Pound, China Lunar Zodiac, China Peking Opera, China World Heritage. They're listed on the **Series (Separate Storage)** tab for reference only — not counted in any box or page total.
- Coins marked `For exchange = True` are excluded — not part of the permanent collection.

## 2. Counting physical coins, not spreadsheet rows
A row with Quantity > 1, or several rows sharing one Numista N#, each represents a separate physical coin. Every physical unit gets its own position. Duplicates are labeled `(copy 1/2)`, `(copy 2/2)`, etc., so they're never mistaken for a data error.

## 3. Sort hierarchy (five levels)
1. **Continent** — Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania, South America. Alphabetical.
2. **Sub-region** within continent — e.g. Northern Europe, Western Europe, Eastern Africa, Western Asia. Alphabetical. This is what gives browsing continuity: Switzerland (Western Europe) sits near France and Germany, not next to Serbia just because the alphabet says so.
3. **Country Group** — the coin's normalized modern country (Numista's `Country` field). Alphabetical.
4. **Country (Issuer)** — the specific historical/political issuer (Numista's `Issuer` field), shown only where it differs from the Country Group — e.g. Hong Kong and Macau appear separately under China; Ceylon under Sri Lanka; the Soviet Union under Russia. Where Issuer matches the Country Group, this level is simply the same value. Alphabetical.
5. **Denomination** (face value), ascending, within that Issuer group.

Sub-region and Country/Issuer ordering are both alphabetical, for consistency with everything else in the system — not a geographic travel-path.

## 4. Physical boxes: one per continent
- Each continent is its own physical box/binder.
- Ceiling: up to 22 pages (≈440 coins) per box.
- A Country Group's coins never split across a page: if what's left of the group doesn't fit the remaining slots, those slots are left empty and the group starts fresh on the next page.
- Current page counts: Africa 2, Asia 7, Europe 16, North America 5, Oceania 1, South America 1 — 32 pages total, none close to the 22-page ceiling.

## 5. Series — displayed separately, not boxed
Round Pound, Lunar Zodiac, Peking Opera, and World Heritage stay in their own 2×5 storage, untouched by this system. The **Series (Separate Storage)** tab lists what's in each, grouped by series name, purely for reference.

## 6. Adding coins later
1. Export fresh from Numista.
2. Re-run the same filters (exclusions, quantity expansion) and the same five-level sort.
3. Because a gap is pre-reserved at the natural end of each Country Group's block, most new coins slot straight into an existing gap on the page where that group already lives — nothing already placed has to move.
4. A new coin only pushes existing coins onto a later page when that group's gap is already used up. Even then, only the coins after that point on the same box shift — never the whole box, never another continent's box.
5. Each update reports: which coins (if any) moved to a new page, and the page + position for every newly added coin.

## 7. Judgment calls — flag any you'd place differently
- Sub-region for a few transcontinental cases: Cyprus → Southern Europe (not Western Asia); Russia → Eastern Europe; Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia → Western Asia.
- Country Group/Issuer split currently applies to 11 countries: British Crown dependencies, Chile, China, Eswatini, France, Germany, Netherlands, Russia, Sri Lanka, United Kingdom, Yemen.

title: DMAIC roadmap 15 steps
summary: DMAIC roadmap 15 steps outlines the define, measure, analyse, improve, control phases with key actions and common pitfalls.
body:
The spine of the whole method. Every tool taught hangs off one of these steps — when a tool is
introduced and you cannot place it, ask which step it serves.

## D — Define
1. Generate project ideas
2. Select project
3. Finalise **project charter** and high-level map

## M — Measure
4. Finalise **project Y** and performance standards for Y
5. Validate the **measurement system** for Y
6. Measure current performance and gap

## A — Analyse
7. List all probable **X's**
8. Identify **critical X's**
9. Verify sufficiency of critical X's for the project

## I — Improve
10. Generate and evaluate alternative solutions
11. Select and optimise the best solution
12. Pilot, implement and validate the solution

## C — Control
13. Implement control system for critical X's
14. Document solution and benefits
15. Transfer to process owner, project closure

---

## The steps people skip

**Step 5 — validate the measurement system.** In a factory this is a gauge R&R. For a transactional
process measured by human judgement or a system timestamp, it is much less obvious what it means —
and most transactional projects quietly skip it and build on an unvalidated number.

**Step 14 — document and validate benefits.** Usually requires Finance to certify the savings.
Unvalidated benefit is the most common reason a completed project never gets credited.

**Step 15 — transfer to process owner.** Formal handover with a control plan. Routinely skipped,
which is why improvements drift back within six months.

## Phase gates

The five phases are tollgates: you do not enter Analyse until Measure is signed off. That is
phase-gate delivery, and it is the part of DMAIC that maps most directly onto general project
management — see [[Six-Sigma-for-PM-Roles]].

Related: [[Statistics-Core-Concepts]] (steps 7–9) · [[Project-Selection-Criteria]] (steps 1–3) ·
[[Value-Stream-Mapping]] (step 6) · [[Six-Sigma-INDEX]]

title: Vahan portal knowledge
summary: Vahan portal knowledge covers how to pull, clean, and verify public vehicle-registration data from India's Vahan dashboard.
body:
My notes on India's Vahan vehicle-registration dashboard, run by MoRTH and NIC under the Parivahan umbrella. Everything here is about public data and the site itself: how it is laid out, how I download from it, where it trips me up, and how I check the numbers.

## What the portal gives you

Vahan records every vehicle registration at every RTO (Regional Transport Office) in the country. The public dashboard lets anyone see aggregate counts: no owner details, only totals.

The views I use:

| View | What it shows | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Maker-wise report | Maker (OEM) in rows, RTOs or states in columns | Who sold how many, where |
| State-wise view | One state at a time, all its RTOs | RTO-level detail |
| All-India view | National totals for the same filters | The check figure for everything else |

Filters I rely on:

| Filter | Notes |
|---|---|
| State / RTO | Pick one state, then all or one RTO |
| Year and year type | Calendar or financial year |
| Month | Single month within the year |
| Vehicle class / category | See the class table below |
| Fuel | Petrol, diesel, CNG, electric and so on |

## Vehicle classes (MV Act)

Vahan follows the Motor Vehicles Act classes, which split commercial vehicles by gross vehicle weight:

| Class | Goods | Passenger | Weight band |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light | LGV | LPV | under 7.5 T |
| Medium | MGV | MPV | 7.5 to 12 T |
| Heavy | HGV | HPV | over 12 T |

Industry reporting (SIAM) uses different bands: SCV under 3.5 T, LCV 3.5 to 7.5 T, ICV 7.5 to 16 T, MCV 16 to 25 T, HCV over 25 T. The two systems do not line up. SIAM's ICV runs to 16 T while Vahan's medium class stops at 12 T, so any comparison between a SIAM figure and a Vahan figure is approximate unless you regroup by actual GVW.

Groupings I use when summarising:

| Group | Made of |
|---|---|
| Light CV | LGV + LPV |
| Medium CV | MGV + MPV |
| Heavy CV | HGV + HPV |
| Cars, 3W | as listed |

### Vehicle types inside the classes

Under the commercial classes, the portal lists specific vehicle types. The ones that count as regular goods or passenger vehicles:

- Light: goods carrier; maxi cab, bus, educational institution bus, omni bus, private service vehicle
- Medium: goods carrier; bus, educational institution bus, school bus, omni bus, private service vehicle
- Heavy: goods carrier, articulated vehicle, dumper; bus, educational institution bus, school bus, omni bus, private service vehicle

Special-purpose types I leave out of any market view: tractors, trailers, construction equipment, ambulances, hearses, fire vehicles, mobile clinics, cash vans, campers, fork lifts.

### Electric vehicles

For EV counts I filter fuel to PURE EV and ELECTRIC(BOV) only. Hybrids are a separate fuel type and do not belong in an EV number. An early download of mine used the wrong filter and mixed them in.

## How I download

- The maker report downloads as an Excel file with a sheet called "Maker Report". The header sits on the row that starts with `Maker`, not row 1.
- An RTO-level download for a big state is wide: roughly 1,000 to 1,400 RTO columns, plus a Total column at the end that I drop before summing.
- The older Parivahan state-level report puts the header on row 3: Maker, then one column per state or RTO, then Total.
- The month covered is printed in the file's title row. I read the month from there, never from the filename, because a file saved under the wrong name is easy to miss.
- Parts of the site sit behind a CAPTCHA. I solve it by hand and automate only what comes after.

## Quirks and wait times

- **The table loads slowly.** When I automated state-by-state downloads, about 24 seconds per state was the rhythm that worked. Go faster and the download captures a half-loaded table. The file looks fine and the numbers are quietly wrong.
- **RTO names change.** The site renames RTOs and adds new ones often, sometimes splitting a city into zones. Any lookup keyed on RTO name needs checking every month.
- **RTO names are messy.** The same office can appear as `Chennai (South) RTO` or `CHENNAI SOUTH`. To match names I uppercase, keep the words inside brackets but drop the brackets, strip office words (RTO, RTA, ARTO, DTO, SRTO, MVI, OFFICE, RLA, STA, SDM, DTC), drop symbols and collapse spaces. Whatever still does not match gets listed, never dropped.
- **Maker names repeat with small differences.** Trailing dots, "LTD" versus "LIMITED", old and new company names. Keyword matching handles this better than exact matching.
- **Keywords catch lookalikes.** A plain "MARUTI" or "HONDA" keyword pulls in makers that are not the car company, so I keep an exclusion list. Examples from the public maker list: MARUTI INDUSTRIES, MARUTI UDYOG, MARUTI BHIWANI, HD HYUNDAI, HONDA MOTORCYCLE, HERO HONDA, TOYOTA HIACE, TATA ADVANCED SYSTEMS, VOLVO BUSES DIVISION, MAHINDRA DEFENCE, anything tagged (TRACTOR), ROYAL ENFIELD.
- **The same maker lands in different places by class.** A Tata entity can be a major CV maker and a minor name in cars. Group makers per class, not once for the whole file.
- **Registration lags sale.** A vehicle sold late in a month can be registered the next month, so monthly Vahan counts will not match monthly sales figures exactly.

## Checking state totals against All-India

This is the one check I never skip.

1. Download every state for the same class, month and fuel filter.
2. Drop each file's Total column and sum the maker rows.
3. Add up all the states.
4. Pull the All-India view with the same filters and compare.

If the two differ, the usual causes are a state that did not finish loading (wait time too short), a state file from the wrong month (check the title row), or a missing state. Excluding or regrouping makers never changes the grand total; it only moves units between names. So if the grand total moves after a regroup, something was dropped.

## Lessons on scraping and cleaning public registration data

- **Profile before you trust.** List the distinct values in every key column and check matches both ways before reading any output.
- **Count what you consumed.** Files in, rows in, rows matched, rows dropped. A whole category showing zero usually means a file was skipped on a naming test (`Car_` against `Cars_`), not that nothing was sold.
- **Build totals from the rows you print.** A total computed in a separate pass will drift from the visible rows sooner or later.
- **Never add percentages.** Only unit counts add up. A change in share is in percentage points: 8.0% to 9.5% is +1.5 points, not +19%.
- **Leave a share blank when the base is zero**, rather than showing 0%.
- **Check the checker.** Before quoting what a verification step says, confirm it looked at the right files.
- **One mismatch means look for more.** Data defects come in clusters.
- **Fiscal year runs April to March.** April 2026 starts FY27. "Jul'26" in conversation can mean the month or the year-to-date, so confirm which.

## Practical gotchas on my machine

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Permission error when writing a file | It is open in Excel; close it |
| Folder will not delete | OneDrive or Explorer is holding it |
| Excel file will not open from a pasted path | The path was pasted with quotes |
| File reads as corrupt | Download was cut short; check its size |
| A big file shrank mid-write | Pause OneDrive during large rebuilds and recheck row counts |
| Old output mistaken for new | Delete previous output before each run |

title: The eight wastes
summary: The eight wastes of Lean are overproduction, inventory, defects, over‑processing, waiting, motion, transportation, and underused talent.
body:
The core Lean diagnostic. Memorise these — they come up in the orientation and again in project
brainstorming, and you walk candidate problems against the list one by one.

| # | Waste | In a lending process |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Overproduction** | Reports nobody reads; data pulled "just in case" |
| 2 | **Inventory** | Files ageing in an approval queue; pending cases |
| 3 | **Defects** | Wrong account number, incomplete KYC, incorrect amount |
| 4 | **Over-processing** | The same check done twice; duplicate data entry |
| 5 | **Waiting** | Approval queues, document chase, bank response time |
| 6 | **Motion** | Hunting for information across systems |
| 7 | **Transportation** | Handoffs: branch → ops → finance → bank → ops |
| 8 | **Underused talent** | Staff spending time chasing status instead of resolving causes |

Older material calls this the **7 wastes** or **7 mudas** — underused talent is the modern eighth.

## The number that motivates all of it

> Typically **~95% of total lead time is non-value-added.**

In financial services, non-value-added means activity that consumes time, people, systems or
resources but does not increase the value the customer perceives, nor improve the product.

title: Illustrative scenario of a paid Vahan Data API
summary: Illustrative scenario shows how a paid aggregate Vahan Data API could generate ₹12–144 crore yearly revenue.
body:
> **This is an independent, illustrative analysis — NOT an official MoRTH/NIC plan, proposal, or endorsement.** The *historical* figures below are real and cited. The *forward* estimates are scenarios built on stated assumptions and shown as ranges — treat them as order-of-magnitude thinking, not forecasts.

## The real precedent (facts)

India has done paid vehicle-data sharing before:

- Under the **Bulk Data Sharing Policy, 2019**, a commercial organisation paid **₹3 crore** for one year of access to the Vahan (vehicles) and Sarathi (licences) databases.
- The government collected **₹1,11,38,79,757 (~₹111.4 crore)** in total from the scheme.
- Access went to **142 organisations** — including **30 banks, 20 logistics providers, 19 finance companies, 18 insurers, and 5 automakers**, among others.
- The policy was **scrapped in June 2020** over privacy concerns, because that data contained **personal** RC/DL details.

## What's different this time

The new public portal deliberately exposes **only aggregate, anonymised statistics** — no personal owner data. Combined with the **DPDP Act 2023**, selling personal records the old way is off the table. So a realistic paid offering now would be an **aggregate data / analytics API** — registration counts sliced by state, RTO, maker, class, fuel, emission, time — delivered by subscription or per request. Lower privacy risk, and a different (usually lower) price point than the old ₹3 crore personal-data licence.

## Who would pay — potential customers

Segments that already rely on Vahan-style registration data (the 2019 buyer mix is a strong hint):

| Segment | Why they want it | Rough buyer count (India) | Likely tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vehicle financiers** — banks & NBFCs | Market sizing, dealer/territory targeting, portfolio & competitor benchmarking, risk | ~150–300 | Enterprise / mid |
| **Manufacturers** — OEMs & component/Tier-1 | Own-vs-competitor registration tracking by geography, segment, fuel; planning | ~100+ | Enterprise |
| **Dealers & dealer groups** | Local demand & market share, competitor tracking, inventory and target planning | **~15,000 dealers / ~30,000 outlets** (FADA) | High-volume, low price |
| **Insurance companies** (+ brokers) | Pricing, market share, penetration, portfolio mix | ~25–35 insurers, + brokers/aggregators | Enterprise / mid |
| **Researchers & research firms** | Market research, consulting, academia, think tanks, media | ~100+ | Mixed (cheaper for academia) |
| **Data aggregators / resellers** | Build and resell "vehicle intelligence" products and APIs on top of the feed | ~50–100 | Enterprise (API tier) |
| **Fleet / logistics / mobility & used-car platforms** | Fleet planning, supply sizing, pricing, demand signals | ~70–100 | Mid |

**Ballpark addressable buyers:** roughly **~500–1,500 serious enterprise/mid buyers**, plus a **dealer long tail of several thousand** at a low per-seat price. (For reference, the old scheme found 142 buyers even at a steep ₹3 crore personal-data price — so the paying base for a cheaper aggregate feed is plausibly much larger.)

## Illustrative revenue scenarios

Assumes a **tiered aggregate-data API** — enterprise, mid-market, and startup/API tiers — priced well below the old ₹3 crore because it's aggregate, not personal, data.

| Scenario | Customers | Avg annual price | **Indicative annual revenue** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conservative | 150 | ₹8 lakh | **~₹12 crore/yr** |
| Moderate | 400 | ₹12 lakh | **~₹48 crore/yr** |
| Optimistic | 800 | ₹18 lakh | **~₹144 crore/yr** |

**Pay-per-request alternative (illustrative):** at ~₹5 per aggregate query, 100 enterprise users each pulling ~200,000 queries/year = ~20 million queries → **~₹10 crore/yr** from that tier alone, before subscriptions.

**Dealer long-tail (add-on):** a cheap dealer tier — say **₹40,000/yr** — taken up by even 2,000 of the ~15,000 dealers adds **~₹8 crore/yr**; 5,000 dealers → **~₹20 crore/yr**. High volume, low price, and a natural product for OEMs to sponsor across their dealer networks.

*Sanity check:* the moderate case (~₹48 cr/yr) is well within reach of the ~₹111 cr the old scheme earned across its life from just 142 buyers — so these ranges are conservative-to-plausible, not fanciful.

## What would actually shape the number

- **The free portal caps willingness to pay.** If anyone can pull it manually for free, buyers only pay for **convenience, volume, freshness, machine-readable format, and an SLA** — that's what an API sells, not the data itself.
- **Pricing tension.** Too high → firms scrape or do without; too low → under-monetised. The ₹3 crore personal-data tag worked only because that data was unique and irreplaceable.
- **Privacy & law.** DPDP 2023 keeps any offering aggregate-only; anything touching personal data reopens the 2020 controversy.
- **Policy stance.** Government may treat aggregate mobility data as a **public good** (free, to spur innovation) rather than a revenue line — a real fork that changes everything.

## Bottom line

A privacy-safe, aggregate **Vahan data API** could plausibly earn the government **~₹12–50 crore/year** in a realistic case (up to ~₹140 crore in an aggressive one), serving **several hundred** enterprise customers across auto, finance, insurance, and analytics. The bigger strategic question is whether it's monetised at all, or released free as public infrastructure.

title: Six sigma for product management roles
summary: Six sigma for PM Roles explains how the method applies to product and project management work.
body:
Two different questions, two different answers. The framing that resolves both:

> **Six Sigma is a problem-solving method that happens to run as a project — not a project
> management method, and not a product method.**

## Product Management — roughly 40%

Higher for operational and platform products (~45–50%), lower for consumer discovery work (~20%).

### What transfers
- **Hypothesis testing *is* A/B test mathematics.** t-tests, proportion tests and p-values are the
  machinery behind every experiment readout. Most PMs eyeball a dashboard and declare a win
- **DMAIC steps 4–5 — define your Y, then validate the instrument measuring it.** No real equivalent
  in PM training, and the gap causes real damage: teams pick a north-star metric and never ask
  whether analytics measures what they think
- **Y = f(X) is driver-tree thinking** — Amazon's controllable input metrics. Six Sigma adds a way
  to *test* which drivers matter instead of arguing about them
- **VSM maps onto service blueprinting** and user-journey mapping, directly useful for workflow
  products
- **Root-cause discipline** — 5 Whys and fishbone resist the jump to solution

### Where it does not help, and can hurt
- DMAIC assumes the process already exists and has a measurable defect rate. It says nothing about
  whether a product should exist or what to build
- Its goal is **reducing variation**, while discovery needs variation — bets that might fail.
  Applied too hard it quietly kills exploration. This is the standard critique of Six Sigma
  deployments in innovative companies, and it is fair
- It is heavyweight: a full DMAIC runs months, most product calls need a decision by Thursday

## Project Management — content ~55%, experience ~90%

### Covered well
| Area | How |
|---|---|
| Scope | "Select project" is its own step; sizing is treated as make-or-break |
| Quality | The entire method |
| Integration | Charter (step 3), closure (step 15) |
| Stakeholder | Champion, sponsor, process owner roles defined |
| Delivery control | Five phases as tollgates — phase-gate delivery |
| Benefit realisation | Step 14, usually with Finance certifying |

### Not covered at all
Schedule (no WBS, no critical path, no Gantt) · Cost and budget · Risk register · Procurement ·
Resource levelling · Multi-workstream dependencies and programme management.

**If you want PMP-style project management, this is not it.**

### Why the real number still feels high
The areas it skips — Gantt charts, earned value — are the parts people over-invest in and that
rarely decide whether a project lands. The parts it covers hard — correct scoping, a measured
baseline, proving the benefit arrived, a real handover — are exactly where projects die.

And the larger share of the value is not the teaching. It is spending months leading a
cross-functional team you do not manage, against a day job, chasing a busy sponsor. That is project
management learned the only way it is really learned — but it would be worth that for any real
project. **Six Sigma is the excuse to get one, not the source of the value.**

## Where it fits alongside the PM certification

Complementary rather than duplicating — see [[Career-Plan]]. The PM course covers discovery and
product thinking; this adds "can also measure and deliver operationally". For a lending/ops product
like [[Vahan-PRD]], the disbursement VSM analysis *is* the business case for automating a workflow,
rather than asserting one.

Related: [[DMAIC-Roadmap]] · [[Project-Selection-Criteria]] · [[Six-Sigma-INDEX]]
